ERIN: A REVERIE. A magnificent sunset over the Monroe mountains, Ireland, which I witnessed in returning from a delightful sail up Car- /ingford Lough, suggested the foaowing lines. A vessel bounding o'er a watery waste. A range of rugged mountains on her stern, A crimson flush, as if the sky beyond Were lit with blood-red dimes; the flames bespoke The dying splendour of the sinking sun. A wild and wondrous scene; a scene that woke Within the breast of one who stood upon The vessel's deck, a vision. Thus he mused, As in a trance he gazed upon the glory: How like yon scene is Erin's woeful fate; Her sun has set b ood-red, her evening skies Flame with the light of fires incendiary; Her emerald fields are stained, and deeply stained, With life's red tide let flow by murder's hands. Murder most foul, false, and unnatural. Ah night has settled o'er you goodly land : The voyager was sad. Again he mused, And chanced to call to mind the augury'— "When red the sun sets in the western sky, There is a promise of a bright er day." And now A change came o'er the spirit of his dream. The night of blood was past, and morning dawned, Robed radiantly, and leaping laughingly O'er Erin's mountains weirdly beautiful. Assassination's deadly knife was sheathed, And agitation's frenzied tongue was still; The lawless League's fell power was overpast. It wrought no Icnger crimes in freedom's name ; The owners and the tillers of the soil Were both secure, and lived in mutual love, For legislation, like a healing balm, Had worked a gladdening change. Oppression's day And "centuries of wrong " we, e past—forgot, . And kingly justice reigned. The very fields Were greener than of yore, and Ireland was, In truth, an emerald isle. Her valiant sons • And comely maids, in new-found happiness, Were even braver and more beautiful Than in the olden time. No clamour rose Against their brethren on old Albion's shore. They brothers were, in truth, at last; were one In love of law and liberty combined, And one in battiings for humanity. They legally were one; but other bonds tban laws United thein : bonds grand and great and good-- The bonds of loyalty, the bonds of love, The bonds of holy zeal to win the world To henour, virtue, peace, and righteousness. the vision faded from the western heavens, " The fleeting shores receded from his sight," And darkness o'er the waters held her sway. But, to the dreaming voyager, the dream Yet burned with more than visionary hue, And in the future merged a bright reality. Warrirg:on. ARTHIIP. BEN:N.IEI'r.

UPON MY WORD SHE DID! • Her hair was black. "But black," she sighed, " Is very much too cold And so she bleached her locks until They looked almost like gold. A simple satin robe she wore, Which closely to her clung (In fact it was extremely scant), Aud from her belt a lily pale And four sunflowers hung— sour big sunflowers hung. She would not touch a bit of meat, But oft she'd sit and weep, To think the broiled chops were once Part of a baby sheep. "And oh !" she'd moan, "these seared steaks, So full of gravy now" (This was a slight mistake, I think), "Once wandered o'er the fields and meads, Attached to a cow— A gentle browsing cow." She was the most poetic thing ; She wouldn't harm a fly; .‘ Its life is short at best," she'd say— "Oh, pray don't make it die !" The very cat for catching mice In tearful voice she chid, And then at last she married
(And seemed quite glad to ;jet him, too) A butcher; yes, she did— Upon my word she did! —Harper'.3 Magazine.

Our deeds determine us as much as we determine our deeds. The discovery of what is true and the practice of what is good are the two most important objects of life. Life consists in the alternate process of learning and un- learning; bat it is often wiser to unlearn than to learn. He who respects his work so highly and does it so reve- rently that be cares little what the world thinks of it, is the man about whom the world comes at last to think a great de 11. _ _ •

In Eastern Turkey, a missionary in one of the towns, who had noticed the absence of women from church on Sundays, expostulated with the men, and urged them to persuade their wives to accompany them. The next Sunday the women were all present, and as meek and quiet as could be wished. The missionary was delighted, and asked one of the men how they persuaded them to come. He replied, "We all beat our wives soundly until they consented to. come." THE LADY OF TEE PERlOD.—Argelina : "Edwin, thou hest often sworn that did I murmur one desire thou would'st move heaven and earth for its accomplishment." Edwin: "Ay ! that would I, my love! Bid me summon the ele- ments to do thee homage; bid me pluck the anemone from the ocean's depths to deck thy hair; bid me rob the diadem of Majesty of its brightest jewels and place them on thy brow; bid me ride to Sandhills in a third-class carriage on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Beltway. There's nought in the wide world I would not do for thee." Angelina: "Then get me a ticket for the Farneaux TIM GOLD BOOM IX ALMA-TADEMA'S HOUSE.—Farther on is the Gold Room, more antique in sentiment and more radiant than any other apartment in the house. One side is opened by an arch designed by the master of the dwelling, and surmounted by two small semicircular openings over- arching a couple of bread shelves in the thickness of the wall, which are loaded with pottery; immediately below these shelves hangs a gorgeous silk curtain, yellow, blue, and gold. The floor is of ebony and maple; a Byzantine ciado five feet high lines the walls, and supports china or some chance ornament upon its shelf; above this runs a -miniature copy, in ivory set in ebony, of the Parthenon frieze; while thence to the cei!ine and over the ceiling itself spreads the luminous gold in shad's, which gives the room its beauty and its name.—The Magazine of Art. Tate S MEETS OF VENICE.—Many persons are under a great misapprehension as to the means of transit or locomo- tion in Venice. It is a mistake to suppose that there are no streets, and that it is absolutely necessary to go from place to place by gondola. It is true that Only three bridges— the Rialto Bridge of the Middle Ages, and two modern iron bridges—span the Grand Canal which divides the city into -unequal helves: it is true that the city is built upon 117 isiande, intersected by LO small canals and 2,150 passages; but almost every one of the water-streete has a quay or root- path bordeling it, while 400 bridges unite island to Leland. So teat ft is quite possitle to go to every part of the city on foot, although few perhaps would care to do.de se, for theme is not in all the world a more difficult place for the traveller, guided cnly by the " light of nature," to find a given sprit. Tnat spot may be only a few hundred yards away, but to reach it he may have to cross half a dozen bridges, some leading tc the right and some to the left, and traverse as =icy squareh of which there are 3P5: 127 being large equares and 269 smaller equares.—Cities of the Trart4l. THE PIGEON AND TEE Eau:vs.—On a gentleman's estate in Holland one summer evening, a number of birds were noticed to be in a state of unusual excitement. flying about as if they were preparing fcr some important movement cc making a demonstration on a great scale. It soon epteeered' that a "fluttering in the dovecotes" had been caused by the presence of a falcon, which had taken the liberty to carry off a pigenn. The hawk with its victim in its talons was aoariug, into the air, when a company of crows that had wit- =eased the outrage determined To fly after it and rescue their unhappy friend. Keeping up the pursuit fcr a con- siderable time, the plucky crows at length compelled the hawk, which had become exhausted with fatigue and fright, to rot its prey free; arid we may be pretty sure the pocr pig,ecn was very ghd to eseane from the clutches cf the ter- rible falcon.—Little Folks' Magazine. _More than siery veers ago a miller in County Armagh was the means of in-inning a Bihbotiman to the gallows. His life was afterward in constant peril. Many a bullet whistled past him. Tux USK OF TOBACCO.—HOW, then, does tobacco affect the animal tissues? It is not equivalent to the coal of the fire nor to the poker. Where, then, can we find an analo- gous agent? Tobacco has the same effect upon the nerve- cells that water has upon a coal fire. Apply water in small quantity, and your fire will burn more slowly; apply a large enough bucketful, and it will cease to exist. When the cook rakes up the ashes, and covers her fire before going to bed, she performs the same physical experiment as her master, who soothes his nerves with tobacco before retiring for the night. The cook wishes her fire to smoulder during the night. She therefore applies an agent which will check combustion by partially excleding oxygen from her fuel; her master applies to his nervous system an agent which diminishes oxidation and thus seriously interferes with vital action.—Dr. Muir Howie, in "Knowledge." SELF•REGISTERING BAROMETER.—In the January number of the Archives des Sciences Professors Dufour and Amatein describe a simple registering barometer, row in use in the Meteorological Observatory of Lausanne. It depends on the displacement of the centre of gravity of a glass tube containing mercury. The form of the tube may be de- scribed as that of an L leading down to a U by a vertical portion. The lower end is open. The tube swings in thel plane of its angles on a horizontal axis placed above the centre of gravity; with increased barometric pressure it in- clines to the right, with decreased pressure to the left; and these movements are recorded by means of a style attached to the 15 part and applied to a moving strip of paper. By a simple contrivance the pendulum of a clock is made to impart a slight shock every second swing to the tube, so as to destroy any adherence of mercury. The instrument is easily made, and proves very sensitive and reliable. THE STORAGE OF ELECTRIC ENERGY.—IMPORTANT An. VANCE.—It may interest those who have been looking for- ward to a practical application of electric lighting to private houses and to a possibly general use of the enormous forces which, by the aid of electricity, may be placed under ready command, to know that great improvements have recently been made in electrical storage or accumulating batteries. It is stated that these improved batteries are of five times the durability and possess 2± times the storage capacity of those known as the Faure accumulators, and that they are of such a practical construction that they can be readily re- novated when necessary without waste of material, while their first cost is less than that of the Faure. Each cell, of about 43-100 of a cubic foot in size, and consisting of about 601bs. of metallic materials, is capable of containing 400 amperes, and of delivering during eight hours a current of 50. Each cell, in fact, represents over one horse-power of energy for one hour. Public demonstration will be made very shortly, and it is stated that probably within a few weeks, at the Cryet a Palace Electrical Exhibition, 200 in- candescent lamps will be shown running upon one set of 35 large cells of this new construction. A man can never succeed in pocket-picking until be gets his hand in. HOW TO RUN.—I believe I can tell the bOys something that will help them to run better. I was a pretty old boy when I first found it out, but the first time I tried it I ran a mile and a quarter at one dish, and I was not weary or blown. And now I am going to give you the secret: Breathe through your nose! I had been thinking what poor runners we are, and wondering why the animals can run so far, and it came to me that perhaps this might account for the difference, that they always take air through the nose, while we usually begin to puff through our mouths before we have gone many rods. Some animals, such as the dog and the fox, do open their months and pant while running, but they do this to cool themselves, and not because they cannot get air enough through their noses. I found once, through a sad experience with a pet dog, that dogs must die if their nostrils become stopped. They will breathe through the mouth only while it is forcibly held open; if left to themselves they always breathe through the nose. So pos- sibly we are intended to take all our breath through the nose. There Are many other reasons why we ought to make our noses furnish all the air to our lungs. One is, the nose is filled with a little forest of hair, which is always kept moist, like all the inner surfaces of the nose, and particles of dust that would otherwise rush into the lungs and make trouble are caught and kept out by this little hairy network. Then the passages of the nose are longer, and smaller, and more crooked than that of the mouth, so that as it passes through them the air becomes warm. But these are only a few reasons why the nose ought not to be switched off and left idle, as so many ncses are, while their owners go puffing through their months. All trainers of men for racing and rowing, and all other athletic contests, understand this, and teach their pupils accordingly. If the boys will try this plan, they will see what a difference it will make in their endurance. After you have run a few rods holding your mouth tightly closed, there will come a time when it will seem as though you could not get air enough through the nose alone; but don't give up; keep right on, and in a few moments you will overcome this. A little practice in this method will gO far to make you the best runner in the neigh. bourhood.—St. Nicholas. A DELlGirrrri. FLAVOUR. CRA.CROFT'S ARECANUT TOOTR PASTE. Tam INOCULATION OF SHEEP.—The Journal de l'Agri- culture gives details of the new inoculation of sheep, die., by Pasteur's method, now largely practised in France. The vaccinal liquid is sent to its destination in short stoppered tubes (like test tubes). Some are labelled "prenlier vac- cm," others "deuxieme vaccin." The Pravaz syringe is used in inoculation—it has a hollow needle and a graduated piston rod, with adjustable runner. The syringe is filled with first vaccine matter (air bubbles being carefully ex- cluded), and the runner placed at the first division. A man holds up the sheep by the fore legs, while the operator pushes the syring needle under the skin about the middle of the left thigh; then the piston rod is pressed as far as the runner, and the animal is inoculated. Next the runner is moved to the second division and a second sheep is treated. With expertness, about 150 sleep can be thus inoculated in an hour. Twelve or fifteen days after, the operation is re- peated on the right side, with the deuxieme vaccin, which is stronger. Each fill of the syringe serves for eight sheep. Cows, oxen and horses receive a double dose, the two former behind the shoulder, the latter in the neck. The greatest care has to be taken to avoid any kind of impurity getting among the vaccine matter. The syringe must not be used for a second inoculation after some days without thorough purification. A tube of vaccine matter once opened must be used up the same day, or any remainder thrown away. TRY YOUR SEED OATS BEFORE USING.—The Agricul- tural Gazette has received the following very remarkable letter from a known correspondent :—" My oats (about GO acres) got so weathered last autumn that my bailiff wished to have new seed oats this spring, and wrote to two of the leading houses who advertise Black Tartarian seed oats, from whom he received samples; one was at 525. per quarter, weighing 45 lbs. per bushel; and the other at 425. per quar- ter, weighing 42 lbe. per bushel. They were given to my old gardener as usual, who always tries our seed corn in his forcing frames before they are sown. After ten days, out of 100 corns of the former 58 came up, but the remainder were dead and rotten. Out of the latter (at 425.) 100 corns were also tried, and of these 22 came up, although they were put into the frame three or four days before the others, and the rest seemed dead and rotten. The heat in the frame was 80 deg. to 85 deg. The seeds in both cases were clean, and looked very bright and healthy, and in appearance they would deceive any one. My gardener and bailiff are strongly of opinion that they have been artificially dried, which has destroyed the germinating power. It is possible the sellers may not have tried them, and may be ignorant of this; but, if so, what injury may be done to those who bay such. If the poor farmers who rely on the judgment of their seeds- men are to sow bad seed, there will be nothing but loss and complaints next autumn; therefore I beg to impress upon you the necessity of cantionirg your readers and advising them strongly to try all the seeds they may buy this spring, and see if they will grow before they sow them." MUNSTER DAIRY Scrmora—The Committee of the Mun- ster Agricultural and Dairy School have issued their first report on the working of the school since they have taken over its management from the Commissioners of National Education. This Dairy School, for the training of the daughters of the agricultural classes in dairy management, which is, we believe, the only institution of its kind in the United Kingdom, opened its first session on the 16th Aug., 1880, when nine pupils attended; since then four terms have been held, ad 71 girls in all have passed through the school. The girls, who are principally farmers' daughters, have been instructed in the improved methods of making butter, and, as an instance of the benefit of such teaching, several of the pupils who sent butter to the Birmingham and London shows distinguished themselves very meritori- ously, and the butter exhibited by the Superintendent was awarded first prize at each exhibition, as well as the Lord Mayor's Cup at London. The value of the instruction im- parted is being appreciated by the agricultural classes, for whilst of the 17 pupils entered for the November term, 1880, the fees of 16 were paid by landed proprietors or patrons of the school, at the January term, out of a total list of 20, the fees of 15 were paid either by the pupils them- selves or by their parents. The Committee are constantly receiving applications from noblemen and large farmers— some of them from England—to be sent dairymaids who had been instructed in the school, thus opening up to a large class of girls a profitable means of livelihood. The Committee have a difficulty in supplying the demand, for the parents of the girls find them so useful at home that they frequently ref use situations, however liberal the terms may be. In connection with the dairy course a committee of ladies, under the presidency of Lady Colthurst, superin- tend classes for the teaching of plain cookery and sewing, and which are composed only of pupils voluntarily entering. The girls fully appreciate the value of the teaching, and great practinal good has been the result. There are two terms annually held for dairy pupils, opening on the Ist of January and let of July, each lasting for six weeks, the fee being .£3 35.; and two sessions for agricultural students, commencing on the let of March and 20th of August, and lasting for four months, the fee being £7 10s., which in- cludes board, lodging, Ste. Farm experiments are carried on in the growth of crops, &c., the results being afterwards published. The distribution of prizes won by the young girls who are pupils at this institution took place lately at the Model Farm, at the close of the winter session. Mr. M'Kenzie said he had great pleasure in acting as judge of the butter. The prizes were given, not for the superior quality of the butter, but for the way in which it was manipulated, and he should say that there was a great im- provement over the previous occasions on which he judged. Nothing could be nicer than the way it was made, and it was most creditable to the pupils. Dr. Sullivan said the committee expected that each of the girls wou'd be a mis- sionary in her own district, carrying home with them any ideas they might have picked up at the school. They should always recollect that some of them, at least, had brothers, and it would not do to let the girls have all the knowledge and find their brothers ignorant, and they ought, therefore, to encourage their brothers also to come and learn. The boys' term would commence on the Ist March, and the present pupils could not do better than to get their brothers to come and avail themselves of the advantages which the institution afforded.

XXIII. The chief object of the preceding articles has been to show clearly and conclusively, and on the most unimpeachable evidence of the eminent statesmen, politicians, writers, and thinkers, whose very words have been quoted, that our present land system is not really 'beneficial to the landed proprietors, is oppressive and unjust to the tenant farmers, is demoralising to the agricultural labourers, and as limiting the produce of the soil and the capital and labour employed in agriculture, injurious to the welfare and prosperity of the whole nation. Ist. Let us take the Landlord's case. Many of those who constitute the landed aristocracy, and those outsiders who are struggling and hoping to get within the charmed circle, argue that it is part of the political and social system of this country to preserve landed estates in families, and that as it is on this basis alone an hereditary House of Lords is possible or justifiable, the system must be perpetuated, even at the risk of all the evils shown to exist by the preceding articles. The experience of the past few years will doubt- less have diminished the number of these professed believers in the doctrine of "whatever is, is best." The landlords' rents have been gradually declining; they have felt equally with their tenants the pressure of bad harvests and foreign competition. As life tenants they are powerless to sell the lands which they have not the means to improve, and a de- creased rent roll leaves in many cases a comparatively small margin of income after the annual payments to all the in- cumbrances are made. The motto, "Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform," has become the order of the day in the private and domestic establishment of many a landed pro- prietor, who would, however, scout the idea of being con- sidered a disciple of Richard Cobden. Moreover, it would be well for those bigoted and prejudiced supporters of our present system who may not have felt the pinch, to remem- ber that our Land Laws were made by landlords, long before the people had the power of controlling the Government of the day which they now possess, that a system which passed muster before the Reform Bill of 1832, when the people had little or no part in the legislation of the country, is beeoming every day more antiquated and out of joint with the times since the Reform Act of 1868, with a more extended fran- chise still in the immediate future. The day is fast ap- proaching when the rank and file of the nation, or as Lord Sherbrooke (ad Mr. Robert Lowe) calls them, "our new masters," will no longer tolerate that a privileged upper class shall be continued in their exalted station by means of artificial laws specially devised for that object, when the people have realised the fact that those laws operate injuri- ously to the nation as a whole, and that the game is not worth the candle, or in other words, that our landed aris- tocracy is not worth the heavy price we pay for it. A sa- gacious Conservative statesman many years ago said, "I am afraid we shall have an ugly rush some day," and it is the object of Land Law Reformers, who are true Conserva- tives, to prevent either the necessity or possibility of any such "ugly rush," or of even such an uprising of the " many " again t the " few " as we have had in Ireland. The Irish Land Question, in consequence of agriculture being almost the only industry in that country, would have inevitably presented itself for solutionlf Devitt and Parnell had never been born. Mr. Parnell and his satellites have merely seized the opportunity afforded by the admitted evils of a defective and objectionable land system, and util- ised them for political purposes, coming into notoriety on the crest of a wave of which they were not the cause, but have used for their political objects, which are quite distinct from the tenants' grievances. Our Eng- lish land question, in consequence of our trade and manufactures, is not so urgent and imperative, nor has the disease taken so acute a form, but it will none the less de- mand attention, and the longer it is deferred, the more ob- jectionable and drastic will be its treatment in the opinion of those who cling to our present system. It is no use such: a staunch Tory as Lord Cairns introducing a Bill on Land Law Reform into the House of Lords, professing to deal with admitted evils resulting from Primogeniture and En- tail, but practically designed to do nothing more than prop up our present system. Such temporary and shallow expe- dients even if adopted cannot possibly be permanently satis- factory, and the only legislation which will or can be effec- tive must be in the direction of " Free Lend," every land- owner having the legal right to sell or leave his land by will to whomsoever he may think proper. The more the ownership of land is spread among an ever increasing num- ber, the better will it be for the 'owners of large estates. Every man added to the landowning class, even if he only purchase the house he lives in by means of a Building So- ciety, is another Conservative,in the true sense of the term, and with his stake in the country he may be reckoned as on the side of law and order. The sooner our landed aris- tocracy and their supporters abandon the idea that the balk of the soil of this country is to be kept absolutely in a limited number of families, generation after generation, irrespective of changing circumstances, and whatever the effect on the nation at large, the sooner they will recognise the inevitable, and it is one of the most cheering signs of the times that some of our most distinguished and far-seeing Peers are identified .with the promotion of the wise and moderate:reforms necessary. They see clearly that to pre- vent " topsey turvey " legislation, it must be anticipated and obviated by more etatesrnanlike measures. As a speci- men of what we may expect to have proposed, in the ab- sence of timely changes, we have the scheme of what is called "The Land Nationalisation Society," which is totally impracticable and undesirable, for it proposes to do away with all private ownership of land, which is to belong to the State. This is not the place to go into all the peculiar features of this extraordinary suggestion, which is merely I mentioned as a sample of what is possible to the minds of some, in the absence of more rational reforms taking the wind out of their sails. 2nd. Our land system does not suit our tenant farmers, who have suffered so much, especially recently, from bad laws and bad harvests. What do they require chiefly ? Lord Hartington's answer is "Greater freedom in the conducting of their business, and greater security for their capital." When will the farmers get this freedom and security? Whenever they make up their minds to have them. Whenever they look after their own interests, by making themselves thoroughly acquainted with their needs in the shape of legislation, and combine to insist upon their repre- sentatives in Parliament passing the necessary measures. Whenever they begin to think and act for themselves instead of, as is too generally the case now, voting blindly for their landlords, or for the candidate or the nominee of their land- lords, thereby earning what should be a name of reproach, "polled cattle." If tenant farmers would only combine in every county constituency, they have the power either to elect a candidate of their own choosing ; or as in the case of the North Riding election, the landlord's candidate, for the sake of obtaining their votes, would find himself obliged to pledge himself to vote for measures which he is bound after- wards to support, however bitter the pill. It is not an un- common thing to hear a farmer say, "A' never meddle xvi' politics," ignoring the fact that politics meddle with him, and that the Land Laws which especially affect his business have been made by landlords, with a very due regard to their own interests in preference to his. When farmers awaken to their own strength at the polling booth, and to their power to affect the course of legislation, they will soon have their grievances remedied, and substitute a real Act for the protection of their tenant right, instead of the sham Agricultural Holdings Act of the Tory Government, which provided that no landlord should rob his tenant unless he wished to do so. The farmers have the game in their own hands, if they only knew it. They have now the protection of the Ballot, which is secret, whatever may be insinuated to the contrary. They can, therefore, vote for whoever they think fit, and if they would only form branches of the Farmers' Alliance in every county, or divisim of a county, and unmistakeably pronounce in favour of the abolition of the Law of Distress as regards agricultural holdings, the amelioration or abolition of tithes, a real Agricultural Holdings Act, the reform of railway rate, the abolition or a very considerabte modification of the Game Laws, and all the other legislative reforms that the most intelligent among the farmers have already advocated, the thing would be as good as done, as the county members would be obliged to carry out the behests of such a considerable portion of their constituents, or forfeit their seats at the next election. Another thing, farmers as a body must begin to read more. It is surprising to think that the men who carry on thebnsi- ness of farming, numbering hundreds of thousands, with millions of capital invested in it, do not read more on the subjects relating especially to that business. Of course there are manylarmers who take an active, and intelligent, and prominent part in all that concerns agriculture, but there is still a great body of them who eptertain a sort of prejudice against what they call "book laming" and "fancy farming," whereas by taking and reading weakly a newspaper which deals extensively with agricultural sub- jects, or a purely farmer's paper, like the Mari: Lane Ex- press, they would obtain information worth many pounds In the course of a year. The latter paper deserves the sup- port of every tenant farmer fcr the outspoken way in which it has always defended and maintained his Cause. If the farmers were better posted up in what affects them they would not be so liable to be gulled by Parliamentary candi- dates as they often are now. Fair speeches and vague promises are not always followed by specific performance, and the candidate who succeeds best in humbugging his audience at election time often goes into the wrong lobby of the House of Commons when farmers' questions are being h voted on. 3rd. Oar present system does not suit the agricultural labourers, whose abject condition is a disgrace to our civi- lisation. They have, however, grown up under, and become accustomed to the system, and do not always realise their position as compared with their class abroad under more favourable Land Laws. Even admitting that, is it not a national question that thershould be gradually and surely elevated from their present level, so productive of crime, immorality, and pauperism, and so utilised that their bone and sinew ;hall not only be employed to benefit themselves morally and materially, but to swell the tide of national prosperity to an extent they have never hitherto done ? While there are millions of acres in this country not culti- vated to the extent they might be, there ought to be no oc- casion for the labourers either to increase the ranks of the "hewers of wood and drawers of water" ill our large towns, or to transfer their labour to foreign conntriee to augment that foreign competition which has already been 'so severely felt. At present, owing to their not possessing votes, the labourers do not get that attention from Parliament to which they are entitled considering their numbers. It is under- stood, however, that before the diesolution of the present Parliament the county franchise will be extended, and that will help the agricultural labourers to help themselves. 4th. We come to the people at large, the general public., for the interests of every other bnsiness, trade, or occupa- tion, are affected by the prosperity or otherwise of the great industry of agriculture, involving, as it does, the fccd of the nation, the employment of capital and labour, the amount of rates and taxes, and the activity or otherwise of the home trade. In November last, at Rochdale, Mr. John Bright

said, we have arrived at that time when feelings of hostility to Government and Parliament are for the most part extinguished, and when generally throughout the nation— in all the boroughs it must be so, where all the householders have votes,—there must be a conviction that if Parliament is wrong and does wrong, if reform is delayed, if evils are perpei uated, it must be because a sufficient number of our people are not acquainted with the circumstances of the cases, and don't themselves take that active and wise part in Parliamentary Elections which the Constitution expects of them, and which it is their interest to take. That is the whole question. The general public are, however, fast awakening to the imperative necessity of reforms in our Land Laws in the interest of all, whether inhabitants of town or country, whether peer or peasant, farmer or shop- keeper. It has been the object of the writer to stimulate in some degree that public interest, to add to that public know- ledge by pointing out in as clear and simple a manner as possible the evil consequences of our present Land Laws, and the direction which reforms should take. The various arguments and illustrations have been designedly confirmed or supported by well known public men of high authority, and if these articles have created an increased interest on the subject in the minds of any of the readers, and a con- viction of its importance, and the absolute necessity for re- forms, then the writer's object has been accomplished. Let those reforms be wise, well considered, moderate, and gradual in their operation; let the arguments for and against be thoroughly threshed out in a statesmanlike manner in Par- liament before action is taken, and the result cannot but be of the most satisfactory character, and not the less sure for being cautions. Such reforms "broad, based upon the people's will," will effectually dispose of

div.p: THE ENGLISH LAND QUESTION.

ILIESTRIOTTs IIIISHItEN. No. X.—JOHN PHILPOT CURRAN. Is true freedom but to break, Fetters for our own dear sake, And, with leathern hearts, forget That we owe mankind a debt? No ! true freedom is to share All the chains our brothers wear, And with heart and hand to be Earnest to make others free. They are slaves who fear to. speak For the fallen and the weak, They are slaves who will not choose Hatred, scoffing, and abuse Rather than, in silence, shrink From the truth they needs must think, They are slaves who dare not be In the right with two or three."—Lowell. The French Revolution took all Europe by surprise. Its effects were immense. • Continental monarchs looked on it with amazement and dismay, for, on a large scale it illus- trated hew powerless they were against popular talent com- bined with popular force. The spectacle presented to their gaze—that of a self-emancipated people seating itself upon the very throne from which it had hurled its hereditary occupant—was by no means a pleasant one for them to con- template. At the same time the nations over whom they ruled with an iron hand suddenly became animated with a new-born vigour and unaccustomed aspirations. " The democratic principle in Europe," to use the words of the illustrious Grattan, " was getting on and on like a mist at the heels of the countryman, small at first and lowly, but eoen ascending to the hills and overcasting the hemisphere." This principle made its way to England, where the better genius of the Constitution prevailed against its allurements, and England stood like a rock in mid-ocean receiving only the spent spray of the revolutionary wave that surged around her. It passed on to Ireland, where it was welcomed with open arms by a people who had been long ripe for any desperate experiment. There had been in Ireland no sabsi• dence of the ground swell of agitation which had been pro- duced in 1782. The memory of the Volunteers was still fresh in the minds of the people, while the traditions of past oppressions and the spectacle of existing abuses served to alienate the people from England. In 1793 a society was formed calling itself "The United Irishmen." The idea of its formation seems to have originated with Samuel Neilson, but its organiser, the framer of its declarations, its penman, was Theobold Wolf Tone. The society originated with the intention of securing, if possible, "a radical reform in the representation of the people," and its promoters declared that "no reform can be adequate or useful, satisfactory or just, unless all Irishmen of every description shall be equally and fairly represented." There can be little doubt but that numbers of those who joined the Union at its first formation were actuated by the purest patriotic motives, and were de- sirous of obtaining ne,cessary reforms by constitutional means. But while this was the intention of the rank and file of the Union, the leaders thereof had other and revolu- tionary aims. In concluding in his diary a description of the part he took in the formation of the society, Tone says: —"To break the connection with England, the never-failing source of all political evils, and to assert the independence of my country—these are my objects." Revolution, and not Reform, was clearly the aim of Tone and his coadjutors from the first. In 1795 a change came over the spirit of the society. The recall of Lord Weetmorland and Lord Fitz- william raised the sinking confidence of the Catholic party. The well-known bias of the Earl's political opinions was warmly in favour of fresh and full concessions, and it was supposed that Emancipation was at hand. While the Roman Catholics were buoyant with high expectation arising from the noble Lord's appointment to the Irish Lieutenancy, his sudden recall crushed their hopes and augmented their dis- affection. From this period their hostility to any monarchi- cal form of government appears to have become inveterate, and the first test required of the United Irishmen—one in which the Reformed Parliament was distinctly recognised— was instantly exchanged for another purely democratical. The initiatory oath taken henceforward by the United Irish- men was thus worded :—" In the awful presence of God I, —, do voluntarily declare that I will persevere in endea- vouring to form a brotherhood of affection among Irishmen ' of every religious persuasion, and that I will also persevere in my endeavours to obtain an equal, full, and adequate representation of all the people of Ireland. I do further declare that neither hopes, fears, or rewards, or punish- ments shall ever induce me, directly or indirectly, to inform or give evidence against any member or members of this or similar societies, for any act or expression of theirs done or made collectively or individually, in or out of this society, in pursuance of the spirit of this obligation." The society increased in numbers. 'The Government took alarm, and adopted means to crush the spirit of rebellion. An Insur- rection Act was passed in the spring of 1796, and this was followed up by the suspension of the Habeus Corpus in Octeer. But the policy was suicidal, as all repressive policy, unaccompanied by ameliorative measures, assuredly is. We will not dwell noon the history of that dark period. If oar readers wish to become acquainted with the woes and wrongs which the Irish people suffered at the hands of their Saxon tellers in the years of 1796, '97, and '9B, let them read caret nut' Maxwell's or Gordon's "History of the Ee- -1 e'lion in 1798," or better still, the History of the United Irishmen, in four volumes, by R. R. Madden, and though not gifted with a seer's vision, we dare predict that their slumbers will be rally disturbed for many nights in conse- quence, while their waking hours will be haunted with horrid scenes of scourging, torturing, rapine, blood, and murder. It will be sufficient for us to observe that the se- verities inflicted upon the peasantry by the Government were impolitic in the extreme. They re-acted against the Government. The feelings of the people were exasperated, not subdued. At length', on the 23rd of May, 1798, the storm burst over the land, and all Ireland was in rebellion. The struggle was short and sanguinary, and ended in the defeat of the insurgents. Fifty thousand of them are said to have perished in the attempt. Twenty thousand fell in fighting for the Crown. Thus in a single year seventy thousand human beings were sacrificed. Well may the his- torians of the two countries recoil from the details of the scenes of that disastrous period, and well may they let fall the curtain over scene S that were equally disgraceful to both. The man, however, who at this time occupied the first position in the public mind was, beyond all question, John Philpot Curran. The leading counsel in the trials of the Conspirators, he defended them with a vigour, and a courage, and a talent, less like the emulation of an advocate, than the zeal of a friend. A brief description cf two or three of these historical trials may not be uninteresting to the readers of The Examiner and may recall to their minds the names of men who, had they not failed in their attempts, would ere now, have been regarded as the Waehingtons, the Kossuths, and the Garibaldis of Ireland. • After the trial of Hamilton Rower, to which we referred in our last, the next State trial of importance was that of Mr. William Jackeon. Mr. Jackson was a clergyman of the Established Church. He was a nathre of Ireland, but had for several years resided out of Irelaeal. At the period of I the French Revolution he passed over to Paris and formed political connections with the ruling powers there. From France he returned to London, in 1794, for the purpose of procuring information as to the practicability of an invasion of England, and f:orn thence he proceeded to Ireland on a similar mission. Taking an attorney, named Cockayene, into his confidence, the latter informed Mr. Pitt of Jackson's proceedings. Jackson was arrested and committed to stand his trial for high treason. He was committed to pi son in April, 1794, but his trial was delayed till the same moeth in the following year. He was convicted and brought up for judgement on the 30th April, 1795. The report of Curran's defence of Jackson will be found in Howell's State Trials. It was, as he observed, a nan ow case, and afforded few materials for the display of eloquence. An unusual spectacle, however, was presented. when he was summoned to hear his fate pronounced. He had a day or two before made some allusion to the subject of suicide. The utmost precautions had been taken to prevent this. His food was always cut to pieces before - being brought to him, the gaoler not venturing to trust him with a knife and fork. This precaution he ridiculed, and said that the man whq feared not death could never want the means of dying, and that as long as his head was within react of the prison wall he could prevent his body being suspended to , scare the community. At the moment they regarded this as a mere casnal ebul- lition, and did rot give it much attention. .But on the morning of the 30th of April, as he slood in the dock, his frame was observed to be in a state of-violent perturbation, but his mind was still collected. He beckoned to his coun- sel to approach him, and making an effort to squeeze him with his damp and nerveless hand, uttered in a whisper. and with a smile of mournful triumph, the dying words of Pierre—" We have deceived the Senate." Some consider- able time was occupied by the counsel addressing some arguments in Court in arrest of judgment, during which the condition of the prisoner was becoming worse. 'Curran pro- posed that he should be removed, as he was in a state of body that rendered any communication between him and counsel impracticable. Lord Clonmel thought it lenity tc

the prisoner to dispose of the question as speedily as possible. The windows of the Court were thrown open to relieve him, and the discussion was renewed. At length, while Mr. l'onsonby, who followed Mr. Curran, was urging further reasons for arresting the judgment, their client sunk in the dock. The Court then adjourned. An inquest was held the next day. A large quantity of metallic poison was found in his stomach. To save himself and his family the shame of an ignominious execution he 141 anticipated the punishment of the law by taking poison. Independent of this awful scene, the trial of Jackson was a memorable one. It was the first trial for high treason which had occurred in the Court for upwards of a century. As avmatter of legal and of constitutional interest it estab- lished a principle of the most vital importance to the com- munity having any pretensions to freedom. Against the authority of Coke and the reasoning of Blackstone, it was solely decided in Jackson's case that in Ireland one witness was sufficient to convict a prisoner upon the charge of high treason—that 'the breath which Cannot taint the character of a man in England shall in Ireland blow him from the earth."

Passing over two or three of Mr. Curran's great forensic exertions, we come to one of the niosr. successful, if not the most eloquent, of his efforts at the Bar. This was his de- fence of Patrick Finney, who was brought to trial in Jan., 1798, on a charge of high treason. The case derived addi- tional importance from the number of his clients, for in addi- tion to the prisoner at the bar he was virtually defending, there were fifteen others against whom there existed the Caine charge and the same proofs, and whose fate would have imme- diately followed had the evidence against Finney prevailed. The principal witness for the Crown in this case was an in- former named James O'Brien. The infamy of his previous life and morals, and the improbabilities and inconsistencies of his story were•the subjects to which the attention of the Jury was called. Curran knew that the only means by which his client could be saved was by impeaching the credit of O'Brien. This he did, and with marvellous success. In his speech Curran developed the atrocities of the man in such colours that he, who, in the early part of the trial comported himself with insolence, was for a mo merit apal led by Mr. Curran's descriptions of his villainies and by the indignant fury of his glances. He was observed by the Advocate to be taking shelter from the storm of invective in the crowd which thronged the Court, and the Advocate did not fail to take advantage of this circumstance : —" Wheat was the evidence of the innocent, unlettefed, poor farmer Cavanagh ; pursuing the even tenor of his way in the paths of honest industry, he is in the act of fulfilling the decrees of his Maker, he is earning his bread by the sweat of his brow.' when this villain less pure than the archfiend who brought this sentence of villain, action on mankind, enters the habitation of peace and honest industry, and not content with dipping his tongue in perjury, robs the poor man of two guineas. Where is O'Brien now ? Do you wonder that he is afraid of my eye ?—that he has buried himself in the crowd ?—that he crept under the shade of the multitude when this witness would have disentangled his evidence? Do you not feel that he was appalled with horror by that more piercing and peniatrating eye that looks upon him, and upon me, and upon us all ? At this moment even the bold and daring villainy of O'Brien stood abashed. He saw the eye of Heaven in that of an innocent and injured man. Perhaps the feeling was consummated by a glance from the dock. His heart bore testimony to his guilt, and he flect for the same. Do you know him, gentlemen of the jury? Are you acquainted with James O'Brien? If you are, let him come forward from that crowd where he has hid himself, and claim you by a look." He concluded in his own peculiar and characteristic manner This is the great experiment of the informers of Ireland to ascertain how far they can carry on the traffic in human blood. This cannibal informer, this demon O'Brien, greedy after human gore, has fifteen other victims in reserve, if from your verdicts he receives the unhappy man at the bar—fifteen more of your fellow citizens—now in gaol depending on the fate of the unfortunate prisoner, and on the same blasted and perjured evidence of O'Brien. Be you then their Saviours. Let your verdicts snatch them from the ravening man, and interpose between your- selves and endless remorse. The character of the prisoner has been given. Am I not warranted in saying that lam now defending an innocent fellow subject on the grounds of Eternal Justice and immutable law? and on that Eternal Law Ido call upon you to acquit my client. I call upon you for your justice! Great is the reward, and sweet the recollection in the hour of trial and in the day of dissolu- tion, when the casualties of life are pressing close upon the heart, or when in the agonies of death you look back to the justifiable and honourable transactions of your life. At the awful foot of Eternal Justice I do' therefore, invite you to acquit my client, and may God in His infinite mercy grant you a more lasting reward than that perishable crown we read of which the ancients placed on the brow of him who saved in battle the life of his fellow citizens. In the name of Eternal Justice I do implore you to interpose between the perjurer and his intended victim, and if ever you are assailed by the hand of the informer, may you find an all powerful refuge in the example which as jurors you shall set this day to those that might be called upon to pass upon your lives —that of repelling at the human tribunal the intended effects of hireling perjury and premeditated murder. And if it should be the fate of any of you to count the tedious moments of captivity in sorrow and in pain, pining in the damps and gloom of the dungeon, while the wicked one is going about seeking whom he may devour,' recollect that there is another and more awful tribunal than any upon earth, which we mast all approach, and before which the best of us will have occasion to look back to what little good we may have done on this side the grave. In that awful tribanal—oh ! may your verdict this day assure your hopes and give you strength and consolation in the presence of an adjudging God. Earnestly do I pray that the Author of Eternal Justice may record the innocent deed you shall have done, and give to you the full benefit of your claims to an eternal reward—the requital in mercy upon your souls." The result of this defence was that the Jury were com- pelled to acquit Finney, and at the next sitting of the Court the fifteen other prisoners were likewise discharged. Of the perjured O'Brien, "the wretch," to use Curran's words, "who could dip the Evangelists in blood," we would add that he came to an ignominious end. Two years after this trial he was himself placed in the dock on a charge of mur- der. By a kind of retributive justice the counsel who had rescued Finney were appointed to conduct the prosecution. He w.as found guilty and condemned to death, and so pre- dominant were the feelings of terror and detestation which his past conduct and action had excited, that his execution was accompanied by shouts of the most universal and horrid exultation.

div.head: DEPARTURE OF THE EMPRESS OF AUSTRIA.
div.p: DEPARTURE OF THE EMPRESS OF AUSTRIA.

Satutday's hunting h ardly calls for any particular report except that it was Her Majesty's farewell day with Sir Watkin Wynn's hounds.. There was even a finer field than usual, the place of assembly being near Whitchurcb, and about five miles from the Abbey. Before .quitting the field the Empress tool z occasion to express her acknowledgements to the "Prince in \Vales" for the hospitality and kindness she had experienced during her hunting tour, and with gracious regards to all, together with best wishes for excel- lent sport in days to come, Her Majesty bade Sir Watkin and Miss Wynn adieu. The Empress, who has, on the whole, spent a very enjoyable season in hunting with the Cheshire and other local packs of hounds, left Wrenbury on Monday morning, precisely at half-past nine. The railway arrange- ments having been quite complete, Mr. Neele was in charge of the train throughout to Dover. The .Empress looked wonderfully well, and was attired in a black broche silk dress, sealskin jacket trimmed with fur, and fur hat with ostrich plume. She chatted with Lord Hopetoun, who was on the platform, and departed amid the cheers of a large crowd. The Empress alighted at 3-45 p.m. at Addison-road station, London, and was greeted by the Duke and Duchess of Teck, Earl and Countess Granville, Earl and Countess Spencer, the Austrian Ambassador. and the Countess Karolyi. The Empress conversed for about twenty minutes with the principal personages assembled in the ladies' waiting-room, which had beer luxuriously furnished for the occasion. The train left at 4-20 p.m., when the Empress resumed her jour- ney to Windsor, on a visit to Her Majesty. The Prince and Princess of. Wales met the Empress at luncheon at the Castle.

div.head: ATTEMPT UPON THE LIFE OF
div.p: THE ATTEMPT UPON THE LIFE OF
THE QUEEN.

It is officially announced in the Court Circular that the Queen has received telegrams congratulating Her Majesty on her recent preservation from 'danger from all crowned heads, the President of the United States of America, from several of the foreign Governments and British Ambassadors abroad, and from many bodies and institutiens in Great Britain and Ireland, India, and the colonies. The man 11PLean, who on Thursday week deliberately fired a pistol at her Majesty, was brought before the Wind- sor magistrates the following day and remanded, after some formal evidence had been taken. The Queen, it is gratify- ing to know, has suffered no ill effects from the outrage perpetrated upon her, and she has not only had the satis- faction of receiving from all classes and sections of her people the most profound and heartfelt expressions of sym- pathy and congratulation at her happy escape, but has also received from the representatives of foreign Powers in Eng- land, and direct from foreign Courts, the warmest felicita- tions upon her safety. At public meetings in England congratulatory resolutions have been promptly and sponta- neously adopted, and in various law courts and other public places touching references have been made to the startling event. _ .

With reference to the mental condition of the would-be assassin, the following letter has been published :—"Sorer- set and Bath Lunatic Asylum, Wells, March 3rd, 1882. Dear Sir,—l have seen in to-day's paper an account of an attempt to shoot her Majesty the Queen by a man named Roderick 111‘Lean. It may be of service for you to know that a man of that name was a patient in this asylum for twelve months, and was discharged last July. The man who was here had a sister, Caroline M.!Lean, living at 112, Earl's Court-road, Kensington. I was not in charge of this asylum when 111`Lean was here, but I understand that he had been apparently quite well for some months beforz.• his discharge. From the similarity of the names, and the description given in the paper, I fancy it possible that this is the same man.—l am yours faithfully, A. LAWADE, M.A., medical superintendent." Eton boys distinguished themselves on the occasion of the assault upon the Queen, and in acknowledgment of their loyalty the Queen on Monday had them all at Windsor Castle, for the presentation of an address which they had prepated congratulating her Majesty on her escape. The whole school, numbering seven or eight hundred, attended, and the Queen in her brief reply expressed her sincere pleasure at receiving their congratulations, and hoped that their loyalty to the Royal`Family would ever continue, and that they would always uphold the honour and glory of this ancient kingdom. The boys were highly pleased with their reception, and cheered her Majesty lustily. The attempt on the life of the Queen has raised a discus- sion as to the sovereign who has reigned longest. It is of course known that her Majesty is the senior ruler of all Europe, and that her reign exceeds that of any other monarch. But the Emperor of Brazil has really been a sovereign longer than any other, since he succeeded to the throne on the 4dication of his father in April 1831, though he was not deCiared of age until July Ist, 1841.

THE BISHOP OF MANCHESTER ON THE ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION. The-Bishop of Manchester devoted his sermon on Sunday' evening, at the Manchester Cathedral, to the subject of the attempt upon the life of the Queen. Ho said the nation's sentiment of loyalty received a great shock when it got noised abroad that for the seventh time in her reign the Queen had been exposed to danger and outrage at the hands of one of her subjects. It was almost incredible that any Englishman should lift his hand against his Queen. And what a Queen we had sitting upon the throne. In the ficrce light that beats upon the throne the Queen had stood the test of the closest scrutiny. She had been emphatically a sovereign who had done her duty with no other aim befcre her but her -country's good, and it was and ought to be ft proud thought to Englishmen that their sovereign was re- vered over the whole civilised world. Yet such a Queen but for the special providence of God, who had so often shielded her, was not safe from the assassin hand of a crazed lunatic. Happily it seemed to be proved that such was a true description of that man. One would never believe in the existence of a regicide conspiracy amongst Englislilmen. England had prospered wonderfully under her monar&y, and we should be foolish to lend a credulous ear to those who were given to change and were always threatening change.

div.head: INDIAN BUDGET.
div.p: THE INDIAN BUDGET.

ABOLITION OF COTTON DUTIES. A despatch from Calcutta gives a summary of the,lndian Budget, which Mr. Baring had introduced in the Legislative Council of India. The total cost of the Afghan war is now set down at £21,611,000. Turning to the year 1882-3, the statement deals fully with the opium question. It contests the views of the Anti-Opium Society, and announces that the Government does not intend to abandon the Bengal monopoly. As regards the low cpium estimates taken in 1881-2—namely, £6,500,000 net—it is pointed out that the real point at issue is to what extent the Government can take off taxes in reliance on the opium revenue. This de- pends upon the nature of the tax taken off. There would be no objection to taking off the salt duty, in partial reliance on , opium, as it may reasonably be hoped that the loss by the reduction will be to some extent recouped by the increased consumption of salt. The estimate of the opium revenue for 1882-3 is taken therefore at £7,250,000 net, being £588,000 less than tbe regular estimate it 1881-2, and £1,200,000 less than the actual receipt of £lBBO-1. The salt duty is to beat once reduced to a uniform rate of 2r per maund everywhere except Burmah and the Trans-Indus districts of the Punjab, where the existing lower rates are maintained. This involves a reduction of duty amounting to 30 per cent. in Bengal, and to 20 per cent. elsewhere. The loss of revenue is esti- mated at £1,423,000. Dealing with tile Customs duties, the statement says that the issue the Government has had to decide was not whether direct should be substituted for in- direct taxation, but what form the remission of taxation may best take. It is pointed out that the defects in the present tariff, as regards the cotton duties, are so great that some change is absolutely necessary; that the duty on white and coloured goods cannot be maintained if grey goods are allowed free entry; that the general import duties involve an amount of friction, scrutiny, and interference with trade in- commensurate with the revenue they produce, and that their maintenance is indefensible if the cotton duties are abolished, If new taxation had tole imposed it might be necessary to bear with some of these evils, but under actual circumelatices there is no reason why the benefits of Free Trade should any longer be withheld from India. It has, therefore, been resolved to abolish all import duties, except on wine, beer, spirits, liqueurs, arms and ammunition, salt, and opium. The net loss to the revenue is estimated at 'Ll,lOB,OeO. If

tbe opium estimate were taken in 1882-3 at £6,500,G60 net, as in 1881-2, and the salt duty were not to be reduced, there would still remain a surplus of £0D7,000 after the aboltion of the import duties.

div.head: DUNECHT OUTRAGE.
div.p: THE DUNECHT OUTRAGE.

The investigation into the Dunecht outrage was concluded on Saturday, and the two men—Kirkwood and Philip—were liberated in the afternoon. The greatest excitement pre- vailed amongst the crowd in the neighbourhood as the pri- soners were undergoing final examination, as there ,was a gBneral impression that the case against them had failed. The authorities apparently have been unable to obtain:evi- dence sufficient to justify them in ,recommitting Kirkwood and Philip to prison, and there only course was to set them at liberty. It is stated, on reliable authority, that. an anonymous letter was received by Lord Crawford, stating that, should he allow the authorities to extract information respecting the outrage from Kirkwood and Philip, the body of his late father would he destroyed, and naming the chemicals to be used in its destruction should judicial proceedings be per- sisted in. This statement has, however, since been con- tradicted.

Mr. Prentlce,,Q.C., the Commissioner, gave judgment on Thursday, in the Virmingham municipal election case, seating Mr. Frank Wright (Liberal), subject to a scrutiny. • A list was issued on Thursday morning of 587 suspects confined in various Irish gaols on March Jet under the Pro- • tection Act, againct 512 90 confined on February Ist. On Thursday morning Mr. Romer informed Justice Chitty .that the plaintiffs .in the action to restrain the removal of Jumbo had decided to carry the matter no further. The in- quiry as to the damages sustained be Mr. Earnurn from the plaintiffs' action would go on at Mr. Barnum's risk, The • learned judge said that in that case the action would be dis- missed with costs. A further seizure of" Alta keland "was made on Wednes- day night at Bandon station, consisting of seven parcels, containing five hundred copies, intended for towns in the west cf Cork. One thousand copies were also seized at Cork. The iccue boars date Liverpool, February 25. Shortly after 12 o'clock on Thursday a fire brolo out in the third storey of the premises of Mr. N. Fish, ca.tinet- maker, Church-street, Darwen, owing to some pitch getting on fire. The Corporation Fire Brigade was quickly in attend- ance, and the flames were extinguished, but not before con- siderable damage had been done.
