div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 11, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 11, 1882.
FOREIGN INPELLIGENUE.

. _ The sentence of death passed on the prisoners in the recent Nihilist trial has been commuted to varying terms of im- prisonment. A subscription has been started in New York, and is headed by the Mayor of that city, in aid of the refugee Jews arriving there. A telegram from Belgrade intimates that Prince Milan has accepted the title of king, and will henceforth be known as King Milan I. of Servia. A Vienna telegram states, an accident has occurred in a mine near Teplitz, owing to the falling in of a shaft, by which 40 men have been killed. The French Government has introduced, and the Chamber of Deputies has passed, a bill conferring on the communes the right of electing their own Mayors. The announcement is made from Berlin that the Sultan contemplates visiting Western Europe, in which case we should no doubt have the pleasure of seeing his Majesty in England. The female prisoner Jessie Helfmann, charged with com- plicity in the murder of the late Czar, and sentenced to death, but respited on account of her condition at the time, has died in childbed. The Rdssian Government has prohibited the entry of British Indian goods into its possessions in Turkestan, with the exception of tea, indigo, and muslin textures, but on these heavy duties are imposed. A sensational "rumour from Brussels," prominently pub- lished by an evening paper, and alleging an understanding between Germany and France for the cession to the latter of the Grand Duchy of Luxemburg is, we learn—and as appears on the face of it—a pure invention. A telegram from Calcutta states that Ressildar Mahomed Azful Khan, C. 5.1., has been appointed British agent at Cabul. The Ressildar has served in this country as aide- de-camp to the Prince of Wales, and was attached to the suite of his Royal Highness during his visit to India. Marshal Bazaine is about to publish, at Madrid, a work on the siege of Metz, in which he promises to give a clear and full account of the events which led to Lhe capitulation.' The volume is intended to answer all the charges made against him; and it will doubtless be read with much in- terest. _

A Russian journal announces that the Chinese Govern- ment has decided to build three new towns on the Russian frontier, with permanent garrisons of 2,500 men each; and that the Russian Government, on the other hand, is en- deavouring to form settlements on the frontier of emigrants from the interior. _ _

According to a Cairo paper, reputed to be the organ of the National party, an engineer has been instructed to make a careful examination of the Suez Canal, and to report where it would he most desirable to erect fortifications with a view to the preservation of the territorial security of the country. In amusing scene took place in the Italian Chamber of Deputies, on Saturday. Because there were not present a sufficient number of members to form a quorum, the Presi- dent severely censured the faithful and industrious minority because of the absence of the faithless and idle majority, who, he said, were by their conduct injuring the business of the country. Distressing accounts are given of the effects of the floods in the Valley of the Mississippi. The water is still rising, and the physical •sufferin, of the people is descrilb:A as ap- palling. One hundred thousand dollars have already been voted for the relief of the destitute; but this amount has been found to be inadequate, and a proposition to ask for $1,000,000 for the repair of the levees has also been under consideration. A telegram from Oran states that advices from Mecheria confirm the news of the defeat, with great loss, of 1,500 in-' surgents from Fignig by a French detachment on the 2nd! inst. The French captured 18,000 sheep and 300 camels.' Another French column surprised by forced marches a con• tingent advancing to join Si Sliman. One hundred of the enemy were killed in the engagement that ensued. The telegram adds that these insurgent defeats have product a great impression amongst tbe disaffected tribes. The Vienna Allgenteine Zeitung publishes intelligence from Moscow stating that Custom House officers in that,city had opened several cases of men's hats which had 'been lying for some time in the depot unclaimed by the con- signee, whose address could not be fourid. On openitg the cases suspicion was excited by the unusual weight of some of the hats, which, on examination, were found to have a double crown, the space between the real and false crown being filled with explosive material, which, on beingthrown to the ground, would have the ef.'ect of a bomb. The authorities are making an investigation, which, 'however, , has been without result up to the present.

The Pope has made another vigorous speech in cupport of his claim for the restitution of the temporal newer. Ad- dressing the members of the Sacred College who congratu- lated him on his birthday and the anniversary of his coronation, Leo XIII. asserted that the Roman question could never be settled, either by silence or by the action of time, so long as the Pontiff continued under the domination of others and his dignity and liberty remained unprovided for. He expressed the conviction " that civil society, im- pelled by the increasing threats of demagcg,ic passion, would sooner or later turn to the Church and invoke those great principles of order, religicn, and morality of which the Roman Pontificate is the guardian and vindicator." A SCENE IN COURT IT ST. PETERSBURG.—During the late political trial the prisoner Isaieff demanded that the ' revolutionary proclamation issued after the assassination of the late Emperor, and addressed to his successor, should be read out. The President replied that, as such perusal was not, in his opinion, necessary for the defence of the accused, his request could not be complied with. The prisoner then stated that he considered the reading of . the proclamation as highly important to him, whereupon the President, much to the astonishment and consternation of those present, read out this inflammatory sheet, tecmine• with Censive allusions to the late Emperor, and warning till present Czar against; following in his footsteps. It is said that the Minister of; Justice, who was present in the ,court, showed marked signs of displeasure at this incident. A ToucaiNo STORY FROM romPEti.—A Naples correspon- dent writes:—" Two or three weeks ago a touching .'iscovery was made during the excavations at Poropeii. In one of the narrow streets were found the signs of human remains in the dried mud lying on the top of the strata of the lapilli reaching to the second floor of the houses, and when the usual process of pouring plaster of Paris•into the hollow le by the impression of a body had been accomplished there came to light the form of a little boy. Within the house oppositil to the second floor window of which this infantile form lay were found a gold bracelet and the skeleton of a wcman, the arms stretched towards the child. The plaster form of this could not be obtained, the impression being too much destroyed. It is evident the mother when the liquid mud began to flow, had put her little boy out of the window into the lapilli in the hope ofeaving him, and must no debt have been overwhelmed. The plaster'figere of the child'has not yet been placed in the little museum near the entrance of Pompeii, but is kept in a house not far from the Temple of Isis."

ANOTHER SPEECH BY GENRAL SCOMELEPE —A Cracow telegram says :—The Czas publishes the following intern- ger.ce from Warsaw :—Shortly after his 'arrival here. General Scobeleff, accompanied by General Paniutyn, went to the Stemkowski luncheon bar, where General Paniutyn met a Polish acquaintance, to whom he said that General Scobeleff desired to have the pleasure of taking wine with him. Hearing the Generars,name mentioned, all the persons presznt immediately gathered round the party, when General Scobeleff said :—" Geßtlemen, I do not know what

the Goyernment thinks of you ; but 1 wish the best to the Poles, and sincerely desire that they may • form one •body with us, as Servia and Bulgaria should do. Are we not all bvethren ? You must consider that if there were no Russian garrison here you would have a German one." General ,`•cobeleff here paused, and as a number of people were coming into the restaurant he -resumed speaking in French as follows :—" In the last war commanded the 'l6th Regiment, which is regarded as the bravest in the service, because its officers are Poles. Since that time I have learne& to respect and esteem them. 1 now raise my glass as the representative of the Russian nation and drink to our commovFatherland. Long live Poland:" The Times correspondent says :—The stormy and rainy weather which usually prevails at this time of the year has set in all about Dalmatia, and, it appearc, in many parts of Herzegovina also. This may account for the fact that no news of any fresh operations has been received for the last , two days. iPossibly, however, this maw 'be due to the situa- tion having been quite changed by the last operatian. by which the larger bodies of the insurgents were dislodged and in a great measure broken up, so that new plans and dispositions ,must now be made to deal with the insurrection in this new phase. The accounts of Bosnia would appear to be reassuring. From the fires . which are still to be seen on the heights above Livno the existence of insurgents is suspected at this border-point between Bosnia and Herzago- vina ; but in general a decidedly better disposition is reported. The sight of the strong reinforcements has had its effect on the Mahometans and Catholics, who thereby are relieved of their anxiety and are glad to have the pro- tection of the troops.. The Orthodox show great depres- sion, for, if they had any hopes from the movement, they have been compl,etely destroyed. Otherwise there can he no complaint against them. It is otherwise in the districts actually in insurrection. Though partly forced, most of the able-bodied men bad at one.time :joined the insurgent bands, but it is believed that many of these will take advantage of that process of decomposition which seems to have set in to return quietly to their homes. "17.:HE INSURRECT,A-ON IN THE HERZEr;OVINA.. ! " Mr. Evans, the llfizehester grdian correspondent," sayc a telegram published in the Globe, "use been ordered to leave Austria within three days. The reason assigned is that he had sent incorrect news respecting the insurrection." It is also said that his home was the "centre of a con- spiracy," Mr. Evans bac since been arrested. A Vienna correspondent says that a remarkable fact in connection with the insurgents in Bosnia and Herzegovina is that while hitherto disagreeing among themselves on account of difference of religion, they are now united in one common eau,ee against Austria, and Mahometans add Chris- tians fight side by side. Too much importance is not attached, the correspondent adds, to the recent successes of the troops, ()wing to the fact that the insurgents were enabled to carry off their dead, thus showing that they did not fly in disorder, but withdrew regularly. A Vienna correspondent says, with regard to the Mikan rizing,, that in the Crivoscie (ristrict it is reported that all the fortifications are complete, and the total submission of the insurgents there is shortly expected. They are, it is added, suffering terribly from the torrents of rain end the lack of pro,,io • •"-iocs The Herzegovina insurgents are also reported- as being thoroughly discouraged.

The Premier has given £5O to the new college of music. The Earl of Wilton died at Melton Mowbray on Tuesday morning, in his 83rd year. The deceased peer is succeeded by his eldest son, the present Lord Grey de Radcliffe. At the annual meeting of the Liverpool Branch of the Religious Tract Society, Dr. Ryle said the name of the society on any publication was a guarantee of the purity and excellence of the contents. The majority which voted for the exclusion of Mr. Brad. laugh was made up of 219 Tories, two Tory Home Rulers, 13 Liberals, and 24 Home Rulers of both sections. The minority was composed of 237 Liberals and five Home Rulers. _ _

Arrangements have been made for the Queen's departure for the Continent on Tuesday next. Her Majesty will travel vid Cherbourg, and will, it is hoped, reach her destina- tion between four and five o'clock on Wednesday evening. She will remain at Mentone till April 11, and on the return journey will spend a night in Paris. The Jubilee Fund of the Congregational Union of England and Wales, which was commenced at the meetings of the Congregational Union held it: October, at the Free Trade Hall, Manchester, now exceeds £112,000. Among the recent contributors to it is Mr. Henry Lee, M.P., of Sedgley Park, who has given £2,000. On Sunday, the body of a man known in Wolverhampton for many years as "Jimmy the Brick "—at one time a noted pugilist—was found drowned in the canal. He appeared to have been in the water a fortnight, and it is supposed he fell in when under the influence of drink. His back was broken, but this is attributed to the passage of boats over him.

At the Central Criminal Court, on Tuesday, James Harris and David Atkins who were acquitted on Monday of setting fire to the picture "Monarch of the Meadows," were charged with its theft. The prisoners were found guilty, Harris was seatenced to seven years' penal servitude, and Atkins, who was strongly recommended to mercy, was ordered to enter into a recognisance to appear and receive judgment if called upon. A sculling match for a stake of £lOO was rowed on Tuesday afternoon, over the course between Putney and Mortlake. The competitors were Sylvie Gook-in, of Boston, Mass., and John Largan, of Wandsworth. The betting was 7t04 on Gookin, who got 'off best. Several fouls occurred, but Largan got to the front at Hammersmith, and won by three lengths. The umpire gave his decision in favour of Largan. A week ago the committee of the Cobden Club sent a unanimous invitation to the Earl of Derby to take the chair at the club's annual dinner this year. Lord Derby, in reply, asked Mr. Potter, M.P., to meet him and talk the matter over. Mr. Potter saw his lordship at St. James's-square, on Monday. Lord Derby expressed his entire concurrence in the Free Trade views advocated by the club, and after some conversation on the English land question, he informed Mr. Potter to convey to the committee his acceptance of their invitation.

ELOPEMENT—Particulars of a heartless elopement from Bolton have just come to light. The wife of a tradesman, during the absence ot her husband, eloped, leaving behind her five children, whose ages range from two to ten years. The fugitives were traced to Oldham, where, after staying a few days, the man abandoned the woman and returned to Bolton. The woman is described as prepossessing and aged 29, and the man a year older. Mr. William Miller Coultate, J.P., Burnley, died on Saturday evening. He was a surgeon by profession. For the last 13 years he had been the leader of the 'Burnley Town Council, and for 30 years he had taken a prominent part in all public movements. He was a county magistrate, borough magistrate, senior alderman of the borough, pre- sident of the Liberal Association, governor of the Burnley Grammar School, and senior trustee and chairman of the trustees of the Burnley Mechanics' Institution. Colonel Brine and Mr. Simmons attempted to cross the English Channel in a balloon on Saturday. They left Canterbury at half-past eleven but at three the balloon fell into the sea, and they were picked up by tbe Calais steamer Foam. Mr. Simmons said that when picked up by the steamer they were drifting into the North Sea, and would probably have gone towards Norway, it being quite hopeless to think of reaching either France or Belgium. They passed several steamers, but, not knowing that they needed assist- ance, the crews simply cheered them. RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT STRATFORD. On Saturday , morning, shortly after ten o'clock, an accident occurred just outside the Stratford station on the Great Eastern Railway to a local train from Woolwich. The train left the Stratford Market Station in due course, when everything appeared all right; but on reaching the top of the incline, which extends about a 'quarter of a mile from the station, the engine "slipped " the points and ran off the line on to the abut- ment et an iron bridge, which runs along the line at that point. After striking the ironwork, the engine turned on to its sif,e, and embedded itself into the earth. Two carriages were smashed, and six persons were injured. They were taken to the Stratford Infirmary. An interesting Case has been decided at Glasgow, in vrhich the liability of a master to provide medical attendance for his domestic servant was involved. The master was a dairy- man ; the girl in question Was attacked with scarlet fever, and was removed at her request to her aunt's. Subsequently slr„ was removed to a hospital, where she only lived a few hours. At the hospital in question six gc.ineas is charged for each patient, whether the stay be long or short, and the treasurer sued the dairyman accordingly. The Sherriff ,-Ided that the employer is under no legal obligation to pro- ide medical attendance for his servant.

THE ADVENTURESS AND HER PETS.—A Birmingham taxi- dermist on Saturday received a note from 31. J. Furneaux, dated "Her Majesty's Prison, Birmingham," asking him to keep her two poor pets—dogs she had sent to be stuffed— until she knew what was going to he .done in the case. The adventuress continues—" They will not be much in your way, and I regret to add now that I have not a home to place them' neither have I one friend to Whose faith and confidence I could entrust them, unless one lady friend relents towards me. P.S.—I should have answered at once, but really I coul4 not do so, as letters are limited, and I had others to write."

The annual meeting of the Association of Municipal Cor- porations was held in London on Tuesday, Mr. Joseph Dodds, my., presiding. The report stated that the position of the association, both in regard to the number of its members and the subscriptions to its funds, was in a-satisfactory position.l A resolutien had been passed by the Council declaring that the private electric lighting bills introduced into Parliament was an unjustifiable interference with-the rights of municipal corporations and other local authorities, and-that the same should be opposed; that the attention of the Government should be called to the subject with a view to prevent their further progress;, and that the Government should be re- quested to consider in what way facilities can be given for the promotion of electric lighting by local authorities, when they desire to adopt it, and do not wish to promote a local bill of their own. THE MALMESBURY ELECTION.—OOIOIIOI Miles was on Tuesday elected member for Mahnesbury, in place of the late Mr. W. Powell, who was lost in lie balloon Saladin. The Polling was considerably closer than at the general election, when Mr. Powell received 603 votes against 310 returned for Mr. A. G. Kitching, his Liberal opponent. Tues- dav's numbers were—for Colonel Miles, 491; for Mr. Luce, 433: the Tory majority being thus reduced from 293 in 1880 to 56. Mr. Powell was first elected in 1868, when he had a majority of 23, and he held his seat unopposed until the contest in 1880. He was, too, the first Conservative who sat for the borough since the passing of the Reform Bill in 1832 land it may be that the material reduction in the Conserva-' tive majority is the forecast of the return of the little , borough to its original Liberalism. THE WORKINGTON MYSTERY.—The coroner's inquiry in regard to the death of the girl Lucy Sands, who mysteri- ously disappeared from her home at Workington on the evening of December Sth, anti whcse body was found last Wednesday morning buried beneath a mound of cobble stoncs on the North Side Road, near that town, was resumed at Workington Bridge Station on Tuesday. Dr. Highet and Dr. Hogg stated the results of the post-mortch.; examination, I and their evidence made it clear that the deceased had been murdered, though possibly life was not quite extinct when she was laid on the way side and covered with stones. There were several marks of violence on the body, bat the process of decomposition was so far advanced—the features themselves being beyond recognition—that the medical witnesses were unable to specify the _particular act of violence which was the immediate cause of death. The inquiry was further adjourned for a week. The police have not as yet made any arrest in connection with the crime. I THE QUEEN AND LORD BEACONSFIELD.—The monument

which Her Majesty commissioned Mr. R. C. Belt to prepare for the perpetuation of the memory of I.;lrd Beaconsfield has just been completed and erected in Hughenden Church. It is placed immediately above the seat habitually occupied by the late Prime 111 inister. Tho spot was, it is stated, selected by Her Majesty; and the monument is a touching record of that friendship which can SO rarely exist between sovereign and subject. The centre of the memorial is occupied by a profile portrait carved in low relief in etatuary marble, placed within a quatrefoil cartouch, which is flanked by buttresses and crowned by a carved and crested canopy in which figures a heraldic hatchment of the late Earl's arms and supporters. Beneath this is a tablet bearing the followinz dedication, penned by the Queen' her Gel f

To the dear and honoured Memory of Ben.jam'n Earl of Beaconsfield. This memorial is placed by his gra•eful and affectionate Bover,ign and friend Victoria It I. "liing love him that spealieth right." February 27, 1882. Proverbs xvi. ln. The whole of the architectural • Farroundings are in strict accord with the architecture of the church itself, and are wrought in Sicilian marble. • MRS. GIRLING AND THE SHARERS : EXTRAORDINARY PRETENSIONS.—MTS. Girling, the head of the Shaker com- munity, who are still located on the borders' of the New Forest, has written a remarkable letter, stating that the late reports of the sickness and death of "the mysterious woman , known as Mary Ann (Arlin,. " are without foundation. She says, however, that some weeks ago she felt "very weak in body and depressed in spirit, even beyond ordinary mea- sure, but the main .cause was the hardness cf people's hearts and their unwillingness to believe the truth and the light which is come." Proceeding to illustrate what she means by the "truth," she asserts that "notwithstanding all iappearances, this mysterious woman, known to tie world as Mrs. Girling, "is no less a person than the re-incarnation of the Great Fa.ther of love who is come again, making her body the abode of His second appearing, and the "print marks" of the evidence of His form:: suliencg now appear- ing upon her body.

The death of Mr. Samuel Walters, the well-known marine painter, is announced. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone arrived at Windsor on Wednes- day evening on a visit to her Majesty. The ex-Empress Eugenie, who had been on a visit to the Queen, proceeded from Windsor to London on Wednesday. Barskimming House, the residence of Sir W. F. Miller, of Glenlee, one of the finest old mansions in Ayrshire, was on Wednesday totally destroyed by fire. The Times has reason to believe that Mr. George Grove will be invited to take a leading part in the management of the new Royal College of Musia, with the title of director of the institution. _ _ _ _

A serious disturbance took place on Tuesday night at Fleetwood, between a number of soldiers belonging to the Bth regiment of foot and some local sshermen. Several on both sides were severely cut and bruised. The Blackburn Cattle Market was re-opened on Wednes- day, after being closed for three weeks owing to the preva- lence of foot-and-mouth disease. The market has been thrice closed during the last twelve months in consequence of the prevalence of cattle disease in the borough. Earl Spencer on Wednesday received an influential depu- tation, representing 40 cities and towns, who urged that greater assistance should be given to provincial museums by the Department of Science and Art. Earl Spencer stated, in reply, that the Department expected soon to be able to afford a larger amount of aid to local museums. On Tuesday night the shop of Mr. John Wainwright, watchmaker and jeweller, Tulketh-street, Southport, was entered by thieves. Besides other articles of value, there were taken twenty gentlemen's silver alberts, a number of private gold seals, a child's silver spoon, stamped "J. W. and C 0.," and a number of gentlemen's gold studs. A fire occurred on Wednesday, at the mansion known as Boldon Lawn, near Sunderland, the residence of Captain Farrens. The house was completely gutted, and the con- tents, with the exception of the dining and drawing-room furniture, were destroyed. The loss, estimated at between £3,000 and £4,000, is said to he covered by insurances. It is announced that letters to or from soldiers or sailors serving abroad, in order to be sent through the post for a British postage of one penny, must not exceed half an ounce in weight. The name, rank, and description of the soldier or sailor must be stated in the address of the letter; and if the letter is from a soldier or sailor the commanding officer must sign his name. The Oswaldtwistle Local Board have attached their seal to a petition to Parliament for leave to bring in a bill by which the Gourlay disputes will be settled. It is stated that there is now only one member who refuses to sign the agreement for a settlement, and it is confidently expected that the proceedings will go on without any further obstacle, the standing orders having been set aside. A serious accident occurred on Wednesday night at the Thomasson Gymnasium, Bolton. A clerk, named William Rothwell Bridson, of Waterlco-street, was attempting to vault over a horse, when his foot slipped, and ran with his chest full tilt against the wooden structure, being thrown back on his head with such violence as to render him insen- sible. He was conveyed to the infirmary, where he lies in a dangerous condition. Cumbrians and others who have made inquiries will be pleased to know that subscriptions for old Mr.' Greaves, the author of "D'ye ken John Peel ? are received by Messrs. Coward, booksellers, Carlisle. Although the famous hunting song has sold by thousands, Graves never received a penny for its sale. At the ago of Sti he is not only destitute, I but all his family are dead, and he is now alone in the I world.

Charles Dickens's original manuscript of the " Christmas Carol," which has especial value as being the only manu- script of Dickens's in England not contained in the South Kensington Museum, has been bought by a firm of London booksellers from a bookseller in Birmingham, for 250 guineas. The only other manuscript of Dickens's in the hands of the general public—that of "Our mutual friend" —is in the bands of an American.

A preliminary order for the establishment of a School Board in Birkenhead is about to be issued, considerable de- ficiency in the elementary school accommodation having been proved to the satisfaction of the Education Department. An inquiry will no doubt be demanded, but the case for the establishment &I a School Board will probably prove unaswcrable. _ .

Mr. Arthur Arnold and Mr. B. Armitage, the members for Salford, addressed a meeting in that borough on Wednesday night. Mr. Arnold said he looked upon the institution of a grand committee of the House of Commons for Inlaid as the possible beginning of the settlement of the claims of the Irish people. He did not, in his view of the possible future, exclude the hopes that such committee might hold an annual session in Dublin for dealing with purely Irish busi- ness, just as another committee might hold an annual session in Edinburgh for the transaction of purely Scotch business.

LORD REDESDALE'S RELIGIOUS TEST.—The example of Lord Reclesdale is likely to prove infectious. We may ex- pect to hear that the following notices of motion have been given in the House of Lords—A Bill to renew the Test and Corporation Act. by Lord Harrowby ; a Bill to repeal the Catholic Emancipation Act, by Lord Oraninore - a Bill to revive the Conventicle Act, by Lord Cairns; a Bill re-enact- ing the provisions of the Statute De heretico comburendo, by Lord Salisbury. Thus it would seem we are in fair way of regaining the orthodoxy and piety of our illustrious ancestors. Nor, perhaps, neml we altogether despair of witnessing Mr. Bradlaugh at the stake.—Pall :Vat Gazette. THE CHANNEL TUNNEL.—OR Saturday, the scientific parliamentary committee appointed to inquire into the • Channel Tunnel scheme, with a view to its defensi- ,bility, visited Dover. They first proceeded to Biggin-street, • where the terminus of the original scheme is proposed to be ccnstrncted, and thence to Fan Hole, St. Margaret's. They I were accompanied by Major-General Newdigate, command- ing the south-eastern district, and Colonel Gordon, command- ing the Royal Engineers. The party included about 20 aentlemen, amongst whom were General Adye, Professor Newdeaate, and the Inspector-General of Fortifications, Royal Engineer Department. They afterwards proceeded Ito the South-eastern Channel Tunnel works at Shakespeare I Cliff, accompanied by Sir Edward M.‘tkin. HARVEST PROSPECTS IN INDIA.—A Times Calcutta tele•l gram says :—The note of alarm regarding the harvest pros- I pects in Mysore lately sounded by the local papers is I evidently considered by the Government as premature. An official communique states that there has been no material change in the situation since Decembdr ; that rains were not plentiful, but that the crops did not fail, and prices were not high : that the present condition is the natural consequence of a•short rainfall lastlear ; that in certain places drinking water is rather scarce, and the spring crops will be short; but there is nothing in the circumstances to cause anxiety or alarm. The official weather and crop report is to the same effect. The Bangalore paper, however, thinks this picture too hopeful, and says that after two,dry seasons another year of insufficient rainfall will exactly reproduce the conditions of the great famine of 1877 NAVAL OFFICERS DISMISSED THEIR SHIP—The court- martial on Lieutenant Grant, commanding, and Lieutenant S. H. Carden, navigating, her Majesty's gunboat Banterer, charged with neglig,en tly suffering their ship to be stranded off the coast of Galway, concluded on Wednesday, at Devonport. The prisoners in their defence stated that they did not anchor their vessel under Black frlead, outside Gal- way Harbour, as they might have done, because a change of wind would have exposed them to the force of the gale. The weather was overcast, and they did not see the light of Galway town in time to port the helm in accordance with sailing directions, and they were just about to do so when the vessel struck. A statement was read showing that Lieutenant Grant had been reprimanded and cautioned by a cmrt-martial for stranding the Merlin at Gal way last year. Both prisoners were severely reprimanded and dismissed their ship. An interesting reminiscence of the Queen in connection with the Bedfordshire Regiment has just been brought to light. In 1860 her Majesty visited Aldershot and was present at a grand review, subsequently visiting the female hospital in the South Camp. .While there she was informed that one of the patients was mometarily expecting confine- ment, and before the Queen left the wards the child (a girl) was born. The mother was the wife of a soldier of the 16th (Bedfordshire) Regiment, named Stinson. The Queen desired that the child should be named Victoria, and, upon leaving the hospital, sent down a box of clothing for the infant, a christening cap, 5:c., and directed that .-05 should be invested for the child, to remain with interest until Victoria Stinson should attain 21 years. The regiment subsequently proceeded to Canada, and the money was invested in Toronto. The stipulated period has recently expired, and the money— now amounting to £l2—has been just handed over to the gratefal recipient of her Majesty's bounty.

A DISCIPLE OF DICE TURPIN.—At the London Mansion House, on Saturday, Ernest Edward Thompson, ía lad thirteen years of age, was charged on remand, before Alder- man Sir Robert Carden, M.P.. with robbery from a jeweller's shop. Mr. Wontner. solicitor, who appeared for the defence, • now stated that the lad's parents were living apart, and he had been placed under the care of a schoolmaster at Brixton. His character had hitherto been irreproachable, but he bad been in the habit of reading sensational stories, one of which, called "Dick Turpin," was found upon him when arrested. On the day in question the boy's father had taken him from school to be photographed, and he .had stupidly given him a quantity of drink, under the influence of which he com- mitted the theft. Sir Robert Carden said the prisoner had stolen a silver ring and four scarf pins from another shop, and he should send him to a reformatory. Mr. Wontner protested against this course being taken, for it would ruin the lad to mix with the ordinary inmates of a reformatory. —Sir Robert Carden said in that case ,he should commit him for trial, and he formally remanded him for the completion of the depositions. THE ENGLISH CHURCH UNION EXPELS A BISHOP. At. the last meeting of the Council of the English Church Union, they unanimously pronounced the Rev. T. W. Moss- man to have ceased to be an associate mernter of the Union. Mr. Mossman is rector of East Torrington, in the diocese of ' Lincoln, and the Council have it upon documentary evi- &nee that on the 30th of August, 1879, be went through a form of conferring priest's orders upon a deacon of Or, Church of England, privately, in his own house. Mr. Mos.,-_ man upon being requested to explain what he had claimed for himself all the powers and prerogatives of a Bishop of the Church of Christ, but he has failed to tend, any proof that be has received from any competent source episcopal rank and episcopal jurisdiction in the place where the alleged ordination is said to have been performeii. The Council of the English Church Union are, therefore,' f opinioh that by thus acting, Mr. Alossman has committed a very grave offence against the discipline of the Church of England, and as the English Church Union was constitutpd "to defend and maintain unimpaired the discipline of the Church of England," no other colit•se than that of removin the "bishop's" name from the roll of menbers was possiblu
THE STATE OF IRELAND.
Mr. Forster has announced his determination not to appear as a witness before the House of Lords' Select Committee on the Irish Land Act.

Moroney, the farmer who was recently shot for having paid his rent, died on Saturday afternoon in Talla work. house, where he had been lying for some days past. One thousand pounds reward has been offered for inform& tion that will lead to the conviction of the murderers of Police-constable Kavanagh, at Letterfrack, county Galway, on February 9. The police on Monday seized a number of rifles, with bayonets attached, and a quantity of military cartridges, in the house of Bridget Murphy, at Waterford. Six arrests were made at the time.
On Wednesday, for the first time. in Dublin, a garotter was whipped. The punishment was severe, and blood was drawn. The prisoner yelled and struggled violently, but he was held fast by weights.

Seen ballad singers were charged at the Dublin Police Court with having sung and sold in the public streets bal- lads calculated to incite persons to murder informers and to excuse the murder of Bernard Bailey, the victim of the Skipper's Alley tragedy. The accused were discharged on their own bail in £lO each.

The agitation of the suppressed Land League is spreading in the county of Armagh. A hut for the accommodation of an evicted family has just passed through the county town, sent by tilt Ladies' Land League. A proclamation appears in the Dublin Gazette placinF, the greater portion of the three baronies of the county under the operation of the Arms Act. A Parliamentary return shows that up to the 24th Feb. last, 72,408 applicatibns to fix fair rents have been made to the Irish Land commission. In 2,365 cases rents have been fixed, while 841 applications have been dismissed or with- drawn. 704 appeals have been lodged, of which 56 have been disposed of. Lease ls have been declared void in 33 cases. _ _ _

Another return shows that the total amount of advances made to tenants for purchase of their holdings, under section 26 of the Irish Land Act, up to January 28th last, was £1,579. The amount of advances made under sections 24 and 35 of the same Act was £7,817; the advances under the last-named sections sanctioned but not completed amounted to £16,094.

The Press Association is authorised to contradict the statement published in some of the London newspapers to the effect that a scheme is afoot for payment of the Land League members for their services in Parliament. No pro- posal of the kind has been discussed or even suggested among Mr. Parnell's followers, or by the central authority of the Land League. A return has been issued from the House of Commons of agrarian offences throughout Ireland during 1581, from which it appears that the total number reported was 4,439, in 3,953 of which the offenders were neither convicted, nor made amenable, 1,725 of the latter class being in Munster, 1,123 in Connaught, 751 in Leinster, and 354 in Ulster. The total number of offences reported in each province wag 414 in Ulster, 833 in Leinster, 1,957 in Munster, and 1,235 in Connaught. Mr. Pat. Egan, the treasurer of the Land League, writing to some of his retainers in Parliament, says that he does not intend to claim the seat for Meath. Michael Davitt, he says, was the deliberate choice of prelate, priest, and pople, "and his return was a solemn and defiant protest against the brutal and truculent policy of coercion." It is under- stood that Mr. Egan will be nominated, and, of course, elected when the new election takes place. It is believed that the Government are in possession of in- formation which will lead to a criminal prosecution for the ! murder of Bailey, the supposed Fenian informer, who was shot dead on Saturday night week. On Saturday morning six men were arrested simultaneoirsly in different parts of the city under warrants signed by the Lord-Lieutenant, charging one of the men as a principal in the crime of mur- der, and the other as accessories to murder. The warrants were issued under the Coercion Act.

The Daily News special correspondent in Ireland, who has been making inquiry into the relations between landlords and tenants in the county of Limerick, states that on many estates, both there and in Tipperary, the rents, with or with- out a deduction, have been lodged in bank to the joint credit of the landlord and tenant, the tenant binding him- self, or at least promising, to give his signature for the withdrawal of the money the moment the suspects are re- leased.

As a party of the Swinford police were patrolling on Sun- day they came up with a large drilling party in a wood. They managed to capture a considerable number, but many others escaped by swimming across a river, and making off through the wood, On the march back to barracks with the prisoners, shots were fired inside a garden wall, and the I police, thinking they were attacked, were thrown into dig.. order, when six of toe prisoners escaped. A Militia drillbook was found on the ground. Mr. Justice Barry, in opening the assizes for Care, on Tuesday, regretted to see a spirit of lawlessness manifesting itself, and remarked that with the exception of three all the crimes committed were agrarian. rhe murder of the farmer Moloney was a disgrace to civilisation. Yet he did not think the condition of the county such as to produce a feel- ing of despair. Chief Justice May, in opening the Leitrim Assizes on Tuesday morning, said there was evidence of the :.existence of secret societies and illegal combinations to deter men from paying rent, but at the same time the county might fairly be congratulated on its immunity from numerous outrages such as disgraced neighbouring coun- ties

div.head: N ISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: N ISCELLANEOUS.

Mr. Edwin Jones, forngerly a famous advocate at the Eng- lish bar, died on Saturdly. A building manufactory, and machinery exhibition is to be held in the Bingley Hall, Birmingham, in April and May. Arrangements have been made for the establishment at Milford, near Stafford, of a convalescent hospital, as a memorial of the late Sister Dora. The cost is estimated at £2,000, and towards this Miss Lonsdale gave M,2000, being the net proceeds of the sale of her " Memoir of Sister Dora."

_ Afire broke out on board the steamship Missouri, of the Warren Line on Monday afternoon soon after she had been berthed in the Alexandra Dock, Liverpool, on her arrival from Boston. It was extinguished with some difficulty, and the damage to the cargo, which was considerable, was chiefly caused by the water poured into the hold in process of sub- duing the fire. A painful case was witnessed on Monday in the streets of Lower Gornal, near Sedgley. A boy named Hobson, in suddenly running across a street, was knocked down by a cart, and the wheels, passing over his head, killed him in- stantaneously. The mother witnessed the sad occurrence and fainted. In falling she dropped a child out of her arms, which is said to be badly injured. The members of the Chester Farmers' Club passed a reso- lution on Saturday, urging that a bill should be introduced into Parliament to relieve landlords from restrictions as to the sale and improvement of land, and to ensure to tenants compensation for improvements and full security of tenure. It was decided to forward the resolution to the Premier and to the members for Cheshire and Flintshire. On Saturday, as the ferry steamer was approaching the Woodside stage, Liverpool, a man jumped overboard. One of the crew jumped in after him, after which a beat was lowered, and both men picked up. The would-be suicide, who appeared to be a man in good position, was insensible when taken to the Woodside Stage, and was immediately taken to the receiving house, where he was promptly attended to, and efforts made to restore animation. In the Queen's Bench Division, on Saturday, Mr. Justice Grove had before him a case in which the North London Tramcar Company was sued for compensation for injuries to a little girl two and a half years old, who has been knocked down and run over by a car in Gossvell-street. One foot was cut off by the wheels, and the'other foot and leg were so crushed that amputation was necessary. The jury, in giving £4OO damages, conveyed a suegestion that the money should be invested for the benefit of the child.

At Grafton' on Saturday night, a quarrel took place be- tween two labouring men—Elijah Smith and Samuel Brooks —and they went into the road to "fight it out." After fighting several minutes Brooks was knocked down and was carried into an adjacent public-house, in an insensible con- dition. He was afterwards removed to the infirmary at the Alcester Workhouse, where he died shortly afterwards. Smith ran away, but being captured, was lodged in the lock- up at Stratford-on-Avon.

A disgraceful scene took place at the •.-neeting of the Sal- vation Army at Oldham on Sunday night. Stones were thrown on the top of the skating rink, where the army hold their gatherings; and a crowd, numbering about 1,000 persons, attempted to break in the doors. The entrances were barricaded, and it was with the greatest difficulty that the roughs were prevented from committing violence. The army have made nearly two hundred converts in their first week's visit to the town. Over 7,000 persons attended the services on Sunday. Publicans ought to be well aware that the mere exhibition of a card in a billiard-room bearing the words, '• Betting strictly prohibited," will not free them from responsibility for alloWin, betting to go on unchecked in presence of them- selves or their servants. In a Lonnon Po-eice Court, a pub- lican who had charged an admission fee to witness a billiard match, and had exhibited the no-betting card in his room, was fined 10 a day and costs for failing to personally or by deputy follow up that warning when wagers were made in presence of himself or his servants. In view of the impending legislation in regard to the liquor traffic, the Irish Temperance League is holding meet- ings in different centres in Ulster, at which resolutions are adopted urging the Government to introduce a measure giv- ing practical effect to the local option resolution which the House of Commons has twice passed, and calling for a re- newal of the Sunday Closing (Ireland) Act, which expires next October, and the extension of that measure td the five cities and towns now exempted. Meetings had already been held in 13 towns in Ulster,and they will be continued during the next few weeks. FIRE IN A SHIPPING MILL—At ten minutes to eight on Monday morning a tire broke out at the spinning mill of Mr. Massey, Trafalgar-road, Burnley, which contained about 30,0 T spindles. It appears to have originated through the heating of the main shaft. 'Notwithstanding the efforts of the local tire brigade and the use of the appliances on the place, the flames got a firm hold of the building in which the engine-house is situated.. The roof fell in about nine o'clock. One-half the machinery in the works isdestroyed, and the damage is many thousand pounds. It was thought the, one-half the works would be saved.

On Saturday night, deliberate attempt to murder was made at Kingsbridge, North Devon. A dentist, named Wm. Elliott, lodging at a boarding houhe kept by Mrs. Polyblank, has lately been addicted 'to drink. His conduct became erratic, and on Saturday night he quarrelled with the ser- nt girl, and threatend tc shoot her with the gnu he carried with him. Miss Polyhlank, daughter of the proprietress. interfered, whereupon El:iott followed her to her bedroom, and shot her. The bullet struck the young lady under the left eye, and she lies in a most precarious state. Elliot was .tlisarmed after a severe strugg e. SINGULAR ACCIDENT :AT HANLEY : TWO LIVES LOST.— An explosion of benzolice and fireworks, resulting in the .death of two persons and injuries to two others, occurred at lranley early on Monday morning, the victims being a widow named Cooke and her family. Whilst the family were asleep a benzoline lamp in the room in which the mother and two daughters slept, which was left alight on their re- ' tiring, set fire to the bed. The fire exploded the lamp, and also a quantity of fireworks stored away in the same room. One of the daughters died immediately on being extricated from the flames, and the other died in the infirmary during the day. The mother and one of her sons lie in the infirmary suffering from severe burns. ATHEISTIC FUNERALS. Some atheistic funerals in the public cemetery of Kidderminster lately induced the local burial board to take counsel's opinion as to their powers of control. Counsel held that the board could not prevent any burial service, provided it was not blasphemous or tending to a breach of the peace. Counsel was, further, of opinion that atheists had no right to the use of the nonconformist chapel at the cemetery, and that a mere oration over a dead body was not a funeral service within the meaning of the Burials Act. Any person who at the grave delivered an ad- dress tending to bring.into obloquy or contempt the Chris- tian religion or belief in God would do an act tending to a breach of the peace. acd be punishable by fine and imprison- ment. The foundation stone of a new high school for girls, at Chester, was laid by the Duke of Westminster on Monday, when his grace took occasion to comment on the great pro- gress of elementary education since the passing of the Act of 1870, and the claims of higher education to attention now. This manifestation of interest in the education of the classes above those for whose benefit elementary schools -are intended is a healtle7 sign, and may, it is to be hoped, be taken as indicative of a growing conviction that uncertified seminaries and private adventure schools are not fit places, either from a sanitary or an educational•point of view, for the children of well-to-do people to commence their educa- tion in. The new schocl for Chester is on rather a grand scale, £4,500 being estimated as the cost of the building and the teachers' residences, though the Duke of Westminster has given the site.

SINGULAR AND FAT&L'EXPLOSION.—The town of Brad- ford has been the scene of a singular and fatal explosion. On Friday night the main sewer in Thornton-road was blown up, at intervals,icr a long distance, by the explosion of gas evolved, it is believed, from chemical refuse which bad been discharged into the drain from a manufactory. A.O the result of the explosion several persons were seriously maimed, amongst these being a married woman named Bridget Kaine, aged 35. _dust as. she emerged from one of the mills in close proximity to the scene ot the •explosion, she was thrown violently to the ground by an iron grating hurled from the manhole. She had one of her legs broken. She lingered at the the infirmary until Saturday morning, when she expired in great agony. The occurrence discloses a new and formidable street danger, into which full inquiry must be made.

MYSTERIOUS MURDER AT 'FINCIILEY.—A very remarkable murder has been discovered at Finchley. On Thursday night week a villa at Friern tßarnet was broken into and a considerable quantity of property stolen. On Saturday evening two gipsies found in a wood at Finchley the body of a young man who had avidently been murdered. He had been shot in the throat and stabbed in several places. Near to his body, and concealed in some undergrowth, was found a portion of the property stolen from the Nilla at Friern. It is believed that the deceased man, whose name is unknown, had broken into the house with a confederate, and that they quarrelled in the wood over the division of the plunder, with a fatal result to one of them. An inquest on the body was held at Finchley, on Tuesday. The deceased was identified as a gipsy named Heber Butler. The medical evi- dence showed that the deceased had received numerous stabs, evidently from a long-Waded dagger or knife. The jury returned a verdict of "Wilful murder" against some , person or persons unknown.

THE CESSION OF THESSALY TO GREECE. - A banquet was held in London on Saturday evening, which, if a Con- servative Government had been in power, could not have been held at all, .or would have taken place under very different circumstances. Its object was to celebrate the peaceful close of the work of the Greek Committee by the , cession of Thessaly to Greece. Lord Rosebery presided, ' and, giving honour to whom honour was due, attributed the pacific solution of the Greek question to the labours of Mr. Goschen, Lord Granville, and Sir Charles Dilke. His only regret was that the Greeks of Epirus have had to be left under the Turkish yoke, but he looks forward to a time when the Greeks, by the force of good conduct and progress, will lead the revival of a great Christian nation in the East—a nation which, apart from any s'entimental ideas, would be a bulwark to British interests in that part of the world, guarding, as it would, the Eastern Mediterranean against the encroachments of the Russian power. Lord Dalhousie, who proposed the Greek Committee, claimed praise for the Government for the manner in which it had through a long and trying period urged the claims of Greece, but did not forget to give due credit to the Greek Committee for keep- ing the question alive at a time when the-prospe.cfs of a fair and peaceful settlement were least hopeful.

div.head: SPEECH BY THE CHIEF .SECRETARY.
div.p: SPEECH BY THE CHIEF .SECRETARY.

Mr. Forster, who has been visiting the West of Ireland, went down to Tullamore on Monday, and, after moving freely about the town without an escort, and inspecting the convent school, made one of those straightforward, manly speeches with which the right honourable gentleman occa- sionally varies the even course of his ordinary utterances. His theme was his visit to the West of Ireland, the object of which, he said was to see if outrages were as bad as he had bees told they were at Dublin Castle, and whether he could not find a way to mend matters. He had to confess that the state of things as he found them was terrible, and that it was true that men were terrorised over by a vicileut minority, and maimed and murdered for doing what before God and man it was their duty to do, and he called upon the Irish people to rise against this tyranny and say that it should no longer be allowed to exist. Mr. Forster, with much pathos, described his visit to the workhouse where the poor man murdered by Moonlighters at Tulla lay dying, and told how his wife went on her knees to his murderers and and prayed thorn not to kill the father of five innocent chil- dren. The Government, Mr. Fcrs.ter said, was determined, and he was determined, to put a stop to such outrages as these, which disgraced the name of Ireland; and he im- plored them, though they might join whatever constitu- tional movement for ihe redress of grievances they pleased, to purge the country of these villainous crimes. In answer to a cry to release the suspects, he said that as soon as the Government could say that outrages had ceased, and men were not maimed and murdered for doing their duty, this would be done. The Chief Secretary was quietly listened to throughout, and His speech, in the circumstances under which it was delivered, must be regarded as the strongest appeal yet made to the Irish people in the cause of law and order.
The Quebec Legislature met on Wednesday, and elected Mr. Tailion as Speaker. _ _

On Thursday -morning the parish church of Sun(lricige, near Sevenoaks, was netrly destroyed by fire. Mr. Bulkeley Hughes, the Liberal member for Carnarvon Borough, died on Wednesdavnight. He was 8,5 years of age. _ _
—A correspondent telegraphs:—The repeal of the Indian import duties has given great satisfaction in Oldham, and a s ciety foimed for the purpose of agitating the repeal is now dissolved.

Mounted police, armed with cavalry swords, are now em- ployed after dark on the Thames EmOnkment. The terror excited in the public mind in consequence of the outrages recently committed I.T gangs of roughs has been such that the Embankinent is now practically deserted by the public after nightfall. The Sultan of Turkey, being slightly indisposed, has post- poned the final reception of the German special mission, which had been fixed for Thursday at Constantinople, and it is now arranged that the mission shall have an audience to take leave of his Majesty on the 14th inst. . An old man named Pickard, aged SO years, an inmate of the Alms Houses at Bedworth, near Coventry, has disap- peared in a remarkable manner. He has recently been under the impression that.othe Queen had granted him a large sum of money, but from some cause or other he was prevented obtaining possesSion of it. He left home in search of the supposed fortune a week ago, and has not since been heard of.

On Thursday three boys, named Henry Clarke, John Thomas Price. and James Halliwell, were charged with breaking into the Earnwortl4 Theatre on Sunday. The pri- soners effected an entrance by the removal of some boards from a side door. They broke open six boxes, strewed some 9cwt. of ctage properties about Eh* floor, and stole three pistols, two 'daggers, and a purse of " flash " sovereicrns. Prisoners were all committed for trial.

<IMMO 1N CHANCERY.—The argument on the motion brought by Mr. Berkley Hill on behalf of himself and aq other fellows of the Royal Zoological Society to restrain the president and council of the society from parting with the elephant Jn mbo, was concluded on Wednesday before Mr. Justice Chitty. It was elicited that the council of the society had received .c. 2,000 purchase money, but it was urged that the contract was not binding, inasmuch as it had been entered into by a committee, and the council bad no power to delegate its functions. Mr. JuFtice Chitty he'd that the evidence was against the plaintiff's contention. In his opinion the council'of the Zoological Society bad acted in good faith in the exercise of their discretion, and that being so it was no part of the duty of the court to invFsti- gate the circumstances. On all grounds the motion and must be refuscd with costs. The Egyptian Monarch, in which the animal was to have been taken across the Atlantic having sailed for New York, an endeavour wit! now b the A , ssyrian Monarch, of. the same lie mne,wdhe to hi: which sisap m b dvheirtiseyd to sail on the 22nd inst. :rom Lon- don. Jumbo has not yet shown any disposition to enter the travelling carriage prepared for his reception, which thu remains Outside the elephants, recreation ground. The num- ber of visitors to the Zoological Gardens is still very :arge daily. There is nothing more nourishing and warming in cold weather than a cup of really good Cocoa, but the difficultv has been to obtain it pure. This may be secured at a cost a one halfpenny for a large breakfast cup by using Cadbury's Cocoa Essence, which goes three time,s as far as the adulterated and starchy compounds ordinarily sold, the smallest packet making fourteen breakfaiit cups of strong Cocoa.—Advt.

dealing with other members returned. Had Mr. Bradlaugh presented himself at the table in the ordinary way and offered to take the oath, the course followed would have been less ob- jectionable; but in this instance that was not the case, and the precedent having been established, what is there to prevent its extension, and awkward resolu- tions being passed with regard to other duly elected members whose views on particular questions may not commend themselves to the majority? In the future discussions on this question it might almost be as well to bear in mind that oaths or even affirma- tions are not required from the members of all legis- lative assemblies. A Parliamentary paper was issued only the other day containing repo* upon the political oaths or affirmations required from the members of foreign legislative bodies, and while it is usual to re- quire either the one or the other from the members in most of these assemblies, still in others nothing of the sort is required. In Austria no oath is taken by the members of the legislative assemblies, but they are obliged to make an affirmation; in France no oath or affirmations are required from the members of either legislative assembly ; in Germany neither oath nor affirmation is required from the members of the Reichstag or Imperial Representative Chamber; in Roumania no oath or affirmation whatever is required from a member of either the Senate or the Chamber of Deputies to enable him to take his seat as such; in Sweden, only the Presidents and Vice-Presidents of the two Chambers are required to take the oath; in I Norway no oath is required, and so on instances might be multiplied. But after all even if Mr. Majoribanks's amendment had been carried, and a bill in accordance therewith had passed through the House of Commons, it would in.the House of Lords have assuredly met with the fate of all Liberal mea- sures, and on that account it is probably as well that it has not been carried. In the Upper House, on Tuesday, Lord Redesdale introduced a bill—which- has been read a first time—to prevent the admission of Atheists into Pariiament. It applies to both Houses, and requires that every peer and every person elected to the House of Commons shall, before taking his seat, declare that he " solemly, sincerely, and truly believes in Almighty God." Whether such a measure will ever become law remains to be seen. We will only add that from the ranks of unbelievers in the past legislators have been found, and it is fair to pre- sume that from the same class, if they are not de- barred, may be recruited the ranks of the statesmen of the future.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES,
div.p: LOCAL NOTES,

During the week Mr. Robinson Watson has conducted a series of special religious services in St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel, Runcorn, and has won golden opinions from all for the tact and Christian courtesy he has manifested in cir- cumstances which are always open to much criticism from the religious as well as the general public. Mr. Watson may be described as rather a "son of consolation," than a "son of thunder"; and I am able to state that the efforts put forth have been "much blessed." Many who were, spiritually, asleep, are said to have been quickened into life, and some who were" dead" have been "quickened." One of the most singular things in connection with Mr. Watson's services are the capital mid-day audiences which he draws togPther. The meetings will be continued on Sunday and several of the days of next week. The evils of the custom of practical joking, of which some of the rising generation are far too fond, have been illus- trated in a very sad way at Runcorn during the past week. The details of the case will no doubt be found under your

local news, and, though the remark may not really be par- ticularly opportune, as the accident happened at. one of the stores of the Co-operative Society, I may state for the in- formation of the management, that there are loud complaints from customers at some of the branches concerning the amount of tomfoolery indulged in by lads who are employed to serve. In fact, many people who are favourably inclined to the principle of co.operation, strive to avoid going to some of the stores in consequence of the terrible amount of time which has to be wasted before they can be served. When this state of matters is further aggravated by a view of a couple of youthful assistants larking in an adjoining room, or keeping cus- tomers waiting whilst they sally upstairs in quest of a side of bacon, human patience reaches its limits and sensible people leave for other establishments where their wants can be supplied in something like reasonable time. The employ- ment of ycuths as assistants in a busy place of business, unless they are very well under control, is a penny wise and pound foolish policy. I suppose that when other trades- men hear of such a mode of conducting business, they must quietly "chuckle " at the way in which the directors of the stores play into their hands. Rome was not built in a day, says a well known proverb, and some co-operators have much to learn before they will arrive at the perfection of shopkeeping which has been reached by their old com- petitors.

Judging from the report of a case which appeared in your local columns last week, the chiefs of the Salvation Army at Runcorn can say what Paul could not, for the apostle re- marks "We wrestle not with flesh and blood." It seems that the other day a young man named Peck entered the Foresters' Hall, Runcorn, in a fuddled condition, and intent upon having some fun. He, however, appears to have begun the warfare without counting the cost, for no sooner had he entered the place then he was seized by Lieutenant Wood— apparently a very valiant champion of the faith, who wou!d have proved invaluable to the defenders of Bunyan's town of Mansoul—and carried out of the building. This is mus• cular Christianity with a vongeance!

The decision given at the Eddisbury Petty Sessions in the proceedings taken for alleged cruelty to a donkey appears to have considerably exercised the mind of a writer in a sporting paper, who volunteers his opinion that the magis- terial wisdom of Eddisbury appears to exist only in fiction, and after saying that he would not express his opinion in the matter, proceeds to state, " I will venture to bet that if a bench of lunatics from Prestwich had been appointed to de- cide the case, their decision would have shewn at least equal intelligence of the Eddisbury magistrates." The above is rather strong language after declining to express an opinion in the master, and I am inclined to think that if the writer had been acquainted with the local circumstances be would have cordially approved of the magistrates' decision. I understand that some wag has been making capital out of one of the defendants in the case, mid has addressed a letter to him on behalf of Barnum's organising agent, in which he says "As agent for Mr. P. S. Barnum, the Great American Showman, I am purchasieg the largest NN lid animals that are to be found in the world for the pw pose of forming a monster menagerie. Amongst cther quadrupeds already bought is the elephant now in the Zoological Gardens, London, which is about eleven feet in height and six tons in weight, and known by the name of "Jumbo." It is intended to ship hint to America shortly, and I want some one to carry him from his present home to the ship, about one mile distant. lam told that you are an unusually strong man, and one that has carried a donkell with the greatest of ease. Will you, therefore, undertake the above cominis.siou. I will under- take to give you £25 and all your expenses, also it might lead to Mr. Barnum engaging you to remove other large animals in different parts ef the world that have been and will be bought for the collection. There were 25 members present. SUDDEN DEATIL AT WIDNEs. A child, named William Morley, aged one year and ten months, the son of William Morley, Cholmondeley-street, Widnes, died on Saturday under circumstances which may necessitate a coroner's inquiry being held. The child appears to have been healthy from birth, and until Friday last suffered from no ailment whatever. It was then, however, taken ill, but was better on Saturday morning. In the afternoon, how- ever, it again became worse. Dr. McDonnell was sent for, but when he arrived the child was dead. It had never been attended by a medical man. The deceased, we may state, is the child of the Mary Morley who was last week com- mitted for trial at the Liverpool Assizes on three separate counts.

In 1878 the per centage of children who attended school in comparison with the number on the books, was 77727; in 1879, 79180 ; 1880, 79 209 ; in 1881, 79610. Ap- plications had been made to the Guardians by the inquiry officers for the payment of fees for 131 children, and orders were granted in 116 cases, the total cost amounting to £22 ss. 11d. The expenses of the committee during the year amounted to £llO 95., and after taking credit for the sum of £3 18s., which had been repaid for costs, the charge to the ratepayers was about id. in the £ on the rateable value of the district.—The report was ordered to be printed.—The estimated expenditure for the ensuing half-year ending Michaelmas, was £75. THE VICAE OF FAIINWOETH ON THE ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION OF THE QUEEN.—At the Farnworth Parish Church, on Sunday morning, the Vicar (the Rev. G. Bond) in the course of his sermon alluded to the dastardly attempt made upon the life of the Queen. He said that it was our custom to pray for our Sovereign Lady Queen Victoria, in church, and so it was, perhaps, fitting that they express their joy at the preservation of their beloved Sovereign; for now it seemed that their prayers were answered. She was a monarch who had thegreat sympathy of her subjects, and her subjects sympathised with her when in the hour of danger. There were some people who supposed that she had little influence in the politics of the country, bet in this they were mistaken. Both the Queen and her late husband, Prince Albert, did exercise an influence, and exercised it in such a manner as to show, he thought, that no constitutional change in this respect could be for the better. Then her life had been one long and bright example of simplicity and purity. The Poet Laureate hadwell said concerning it Her Court was pure, her life serene; God gave her peace; her land reposed; A thousand claims to reverence closed, In her as mother, wife. and Queen. Her influence had made itself felt upon society, and reached every grade and class of her subjects. And there was another reason why they should sympathise with the Queen in the peril through which she had passed—she would not have run that risk had she not been our Queen. The preacher, after expressing a hope that by the mercy of God the Queen might long be spared to us, went on to allude to the world-wide sympathy the attempt upon Her Majesty's life had called forth, and to the eager enquiries which the telegraph had flashed from all parts of the world—not only from the crowned heads of Europe, but from independent communities as well. And what would have been the con- sequences had the assassin's bullet found the billet which he in his darkness and criminality intended it should? That day their ordinary service would have been replaced by one of mourning, and in place of rejoicing at her plovidential escape, they would have been called upon to mourn the greatness of her whom they had lost, and whom it would be so difficult to replace.

OAKLAND-STREET WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.—A novel Bible lesson for the benefit of the teachers, friends, and others connected with this place of worship, was given on Monday evening by Mr. Turner, of Frodsham, when there was a good attendance, at least 200 people being present The Rev. J. H. Cummings occupied the chair, and was sup- ported by Mr. Whitley, Mr. Wynne, of Liverpool, and others. The Chairman said he had great pleasure in being there that evening, but he would not take up the time of the meeting by making any ltngthy remarks, as he considered that it was to hear Mr. Turner that so goodly a number of people had assembled, and not to hear him. He held that the Sunday school work was a noble work, and he hoped thatjhe teachers present would derive no inconsiderable benefit from the lesson they were about to receive at Mr. Turner's hands. (Applause). He also begged to assure Mr. Turner that he had to deal with a school, in which the teachers were very earnest in the work in which they were engaged, and that the scholars also were eager to learn. Mr. Turner, on rising to give the model lesson, made some pre- liminary remarks, in the course of which he observed that all his life he had more or less been connected with educa- tion. He was brought up in a Sunday school, and remained there until he became teacher. He fulfilled that office until he was called to woik of a more public and prominent character. After some further remarks, he proceeded to give the model lesson. Mr. Turner selected the fourth chapter of St. Mark's Gospel, thirteen verses of which were read by the class. Mr. Turner then questioned them upon the subject matter of the lesson, and the answers were given in a correct and intelligent manner, which did credit to the training of the Oakland-street class. A short address upon after which the chairman called upon Mr. Wynne, f Lriovere; pool, to read a payer, the subject being " How to prepare Turner, and how to deliver Bible lesson, and how to the piessuggested by the lesson was then given by Mr. manage a Sunday school class.' The paper touched at some length on the details of Sunday school management, on at- tention to which success in a great measure depends. He was listened to with interest and frequently applauded. At the conclusion of his reading, he made a few remarks upon Sunday school work. Mr.. Whitley then moved, and Mr. Hunt seconded a vote of thanks to Mr. Turner for his lesson, and to Mr. Wynne for b.is leading, and to the scholars and others who had taken part in the lesson.

RELIGIOUS TRACT SOCIETY. FORMATION OF A WIDNES AUXILIA.ItY.—On Tuesday evening, a meeting was held in the Waterloo-road schoolrooms, Widnes, for the pur- pose of forming a branch of the Religious Tract Society. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams occupied the chair, and Mr. Richard Butcher attended as a deputation from the Parent Society, and there were also on the platform the Revs. J. H. Cummings (Wesleyan Methodist Superintendent), J. Tesseyman, and W. H. Duggan (Parish Church Curate). There was only a poor attendance. The Chairman, alluding to the small number present, said they often found that a poor beginning resulted in a good ending. Their assembly in that place might be looked upon as a somewhat novel gathering, as there oad not been a similar meeting in the town before. The Religious Tract Society was no longer young, by the age of man' having been founded in the year 1799, within one year of tre close of the eighteenth century. Their object was to spread the glory of God's word, and its, operations were world wide. The publications of the society found their way all over the globe. Indeed, he could not say how many dialects they madetheir appearance in. They made it in the strangest of all strange countries, China; in the wilds of America; penetrated into the most distant parts of Africa rand in all these places the publications were received and read with interest. The speaker next went on to refer to the influence of the fourth estate, and said it was a power which, since the time when Caxton established his first rude press in London, had been an increasing one. But, alas, they knew very well that in every town in the United King- dom there were places where books with a pernicious purpose were sold; and they were aware from the revelations in their police courts that these unmentionable periodicals were found in the pockets of many criminals. The Religious Tract Society had provided a better class of literature for the juvenile population of the country. Having spoken in high terms of the Boys' Own Paper and the Girls' Own Paper, which were published by the society, the Chairmanwent on to refer to the great number of tracts which were published by it, which amounted to 81,000,000. He concluded by an appeal to those present to do what they could in a pecuniary sense to advance the interests of the organisation.—Mr. Butcher next addressed the meeting. He briefly sketched the history of the society, which, he said, owed its origin to an idea first suggested in the year 1799, when a number of friends met in London for the purpose of attending the approaching meeting of the London Missionary society. The suggestion was mentioned to Rowland Hill, a relation to that Rowland Hill to whom we owed our system of penny postage, and met with his approval. A meeting was afterwards held in a London coffee-house, on the 9th May, 1799, and the society was formed. The total amount received during the past year by the society was £33,373 Os. 11d., which included con- tributions and subscriptions, and the whole of this was avail- able for missionary objects. The expenditure during the year had been £46,625 15s. 2d., which consisted of foreign money grants, foreign grants of paper, electro-types, grants to emi- grants, to domestic applicants for tracts, circulating libraries, and colporteurs. Mr. Butcher went on to describe the work of the organisation in France, where a branch was established at the time when the power of the Commune was at its height, and since then it had grown immensely. There were 35 to 40 parish institutions in Paris alone, and 38,000 Pro- testant parishes in beautiful France. The Boys' Own Paper had proved a success beyond the brightest expectations of the society, and this fact was proved by the fact that after it had been in circulation six months, five out of seven of the worst papers issued by one publisher had died from want of proper support, and the circulation of the other was greatly crippled.—The Rev. J. H. Cummings moved the following resolution:—" That the work of the Religious Tract Society commands itself tb this meeting, and that, to further its in- terests, an auxiliary be established, and an annual meeting held in Widnes."—The Rev. J. Tesseyman seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously, and with acclama- tion.--On the motion of Mr. Butcher, seconded by Mr. W. Treacy, senr., the Revs. J. Wright-Williatns and J. H. Cummings were appointed secretaries for the district; after which the proceedings terminated.

WIDNES PARISH. —Writing in the lirerpool Parish, Messenger for this month, the Vicar of Widnes says : " The arrangements for the annual tea party, directed by the churchwardens, and carried out by an energetic band of lay helpers, resulted, as careful forethought generally does result, in success ;—success in numbers, tea ptoper, enter- tainment, and financial profit. In the report of the annual tea party of Feb. 7, 1878, we may note that in the face of very evident care, the tea itself was a money loss, for while the subscriptions amount to -e3O 19s. 6d., the nett sum realisel was £2B 15s. id. Again, the meeting of 1879 re- ports subscriptions as £23 55., and the nett proceeds as £l5 Gs. 7d. Last year, the subscriptions were £29 75., and the amount handed to the churchwardens £3l 2s. 10.!Ed., the balance being on the proper side; and we may be pretty sure it will so result on this occasion. And how has this been effected? Not. we venture to say, by greater care, but by more lay help,—more voluntary labour. The large item which used regularly to appear for fitting up tables, has quite gone in 'Bl and 'B2, in cansequence of an energetic sidestnan, and a friend or two, doing the work themselves, for love of the Church. In some of the years now gone,the annual tea party seems to have been almost the only oppor- tunity for stating the details or broad lines of parish work, and for enlisting the practical sympathy and per- sonal assistance of those well disposed to the Church. This would certainly not describe the position now. Opportunities for such have, fortunately and unfortunately, quite lost the charm of rarity among us. They come in the disguise of Sales of Work," Christmas Trees," Fortnightly Entertainments," Special Entertain- ments,' Sze., with all the large amount of personal labour devolving upon every individual connected therewith. These over and above the labours, regular and special, incident to the Sunday school and temperance work. In the face of all this, financial success in the old institution (the tea party), is very satisfactory." ACCFDENTS AT WESTON CHEMICAL WORICS.—A man named John Costello, who was engaged unloading a flat at the Weston Chemical Works, on Monday, had the ends of two fingers taken off by a crane. The other day a man named Thomas Stanton, living in Granville-street,Runcorn, while crossing a plank stumbled and fell into a caustic pot. One of his legs was very severely scalded. Both men are doing well under Dr. Mouritz. SERVICE OF SONG AT PRESTON Boo.—On Monday evening the choir of the Primitive Methodist Chapel,, Run- corn, assisted by a few friends, rendered Mr. Billingsley's new service of song, "The Basket . of Flowers," in the society's chapel, at Preston Brook, in aid of the circuit fund. The chapel was filled to excess and many manifestations of approval were shown during the rendering. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Billingsley and the choir for their kindness in coming to Preston Brook.
