SID CONSEQUENCES OF PRACTICAL JOKING AT RUNCORN. —Within the last few days, an event has happened at Runcorn which has" caused a great *amount of gossip. It appears that a girl named Elizabeth Cartwright aged about 13 whose father lives near the Doctor's Bridge, and keeps a stationer's shop, was sent to the Co-operative Stores, in Church-street, with her father's tea, he being the manager of the Boot and Shoe Department. Whilst waiting there, a young man tamed Walter Lacey, 18 years old, an em- ploye of the society, who lives in Norfolk-street, began to teaze the girl, who evidently became somewhat annoyed. As Lacey.was going through the door he felt a sudden pain in the back of his left leg and on turning round found that be had been struck by a pair of very sharp scissors, which being thrown by the girl with some violence, had penetrated an artery. The wound was bound up and the youth walked home. He suffered great pain and Dr. Robinson was called in, the leg becoming worse. Dr. Mouritz was consulted on Thursday last, who, seeing that mortification had set in in the . .

foot, perceived that an operation would be necessary and ordered the immediate removal of the sufferer to the Royal Infirmary at Liverpool. The friends of the young man offered some objection to this course, but saw the necessity of the doctor's instructions being complied with on Tuesday, ' and on that day Lacey was taken to the Infirmary. The eminent surgeon Dr. Bickersteth, was telegraphed to by Dr. Mouri:z, to undertake the case, and on seeing the patient, stated that his life would be saved only by prompt amputa- tion of the leg above the knee. The surgical operation was successfully carried out by Dr. Biekersteth, who deserves every praise for the assiduous attention he is now paying to Lacey, who is in a most precarious condition and in danger of losing his life.

RUNCORN UNITED -METHODIST FREE CHURCH HOME AND FOREIGN MISSIONS.—The annuai sermons on behalf of this society were preached on Sunday, by the Rev. J. Bil- lington, the pastor. On Monday evening the missionary meeting took place. Mr. Linton, of Liverpool, presided, and on the platform were the Revs. T. M. Booth (ex-president of the conference), J. Billington, and J. D. Thomas (Con- gregationalist). After a few brief remarks from the Chair- man, the Rev. J. Billington read the report, which showed that Runcorn had contributed as follows during the twelve months :—Public collections, £3 108. ; and subscriptions, £4 Is. sp. Widnes: Public collections, £2 12s. 61c1.; sub- scriptions, 198. Bd.; total, £l3 4s. id. The expenses were £2 3s. 4d., which left the nett sum .£ll Os. 9d. During the year they had also received £2 4s. towards the relief of the members in Jamaica.—Mr. Thomas Snape remarked that he had always had a strong attachment to all missionary agencies, which had been strengthened by his having had the honour and privilege of being one of their connexional, Foreign Missionary Committee. He felt sure that the ap- parent diminution of interest in missionary operations was not real. It was a fact that the income of their missionary societies was growing, the demand for labourers was increas- ing, and every year theY had a large number of agents at work in the various .fields. Certainly their missionary meetings were not as crowded as in the early days of the en- terprise, when they had men present who had been in unknown countries and could tell tales of absorbing and thrilling interest. He then dealt with the charge that they were neglecting the heathen at home to look after savages abroad. He maintained that this statement was certainly ,ot correct as far as their own society was concerned, as part of its regular work was to do something for the heathen at home. Another objection was that missions had proved a failure, or, at least, that the success attending them had been in no degree commensurate with the money expended. He, however, felt sure that if they took into account the difficulties which the labourers in foreign fields had to face, they would come to the conclusion that their success had in- deed been marvellous. He instanced the work which had been done by Moffat, Williams, and Carey, and reminded them that the last named famous Orientalist had a relative

in the person of one of their neighbours—Mr. Eustace-C;e; (of the firm of Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., Widnes), who was his grandson. In conclusion, the speaker referred in eloquent terms to the wonderful work which had been done in Mada- gascar, by the agents of the London Missionary Society ;and to the fact that the earth was in two many places still full of the habitations of cruelly, as was proved by the horrible doings of the Kings of Dahomey and Burmah.—The Rev. T. M. Booth, who attended as the deputation, first spoke of the vast responsibilities which rested upon all Christian churches in relation to this great cause. His own interest in mis- sionary operations was as great to day as it had ever been, and although the prospect was, at times. somewhat discourag- ing, he had no gloomy forebodings. Since 1830, the num- bey of their members on their foreign and colonial stations had increased from 3,632 to 7,332. (Applause.) He urged them to do what they could by prayer and giving of their substance, to help forward the good cause.—The proceed- ings concluded with the passing of votes of thanks, which were moved by the Rev. J. I). Thomas, hnd seconded by Mr. Mathew Ternperley.
WIDNES PROPERTY OWNERS AND OCCUPIERS' ASSOCIATION.

--- - - . The annual meeting of this association was held yester- day at the officers' room, Volunteer Hall, Widnes. Major Cross, chairman of the Local Board, presided; and there were also preeent Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Eustace Carey, S. Muspratt, J. L. Muspratt, B. Stringer, J. Matthews, G. I. J. Wells (secretary), F. Heyes, F. H. Pank- burst, W. H. Kershaw, Frank Gaskell, and D. Forster. The minutes of the last annual meeting were read and approved.

'Mr. J. L. MESPRATT moved a vote of thanks to the repre- sentatives of the association upon the Local Board and Board of Guardians;for the manner in which they had dis- charged their duties during the Nat twelve months. No doubt the ratepayers were entitled to say that the calls upon them were at present heavy, but he thought this fact arose from faults which had been committed in years past, which it was nearly impossible to remedy by any course of action which ought to be adopted at present. The tasks which the representatives of the association had had to discharge of late had certainly been of a disagreeable nature, but the manner in which they had carried out their dottes was deserving of much commendation. Mr. STRINGER seconded the motion, which was passed unanimously. The CHAIRMAN had pleasure in acknowledging the com- pliment on behalf of the members of the Local Board. The remarks made by Mr. Muspratt were well founded. The Local Board had, in past years, drifted into expenses before they really knew where they were, but as soon as their posi- tion was really found out, everything was done to remedy the state of things. He had the satisfaction of telling them that to-day the finances of the Local Board were in a better state than they had been in for a great many years indeed. Mr. MerrnEws responded on behalf of the Board of Guardians. He said he must admit that it was hard work to do justice to the township of Widnes upon that Board, and he was of opinion that, it was not represented as it ought to be. Widnes was of sufficient importance to demand a stronger representation in the future than it had had in the past, and he hoped that this state of things would he remedied at a very early date. It appeared to him that Widnes wastreated as a sort of scapegoat for all the other townships, and those present would no doubt have noticed. on reading the reports of the Guardians' meetings, that not a word was said in the way of criticising St. Helens. Widnes had to stand the full brunt of adverse criticism, and if the township had a larger representation on the Board of Guardians—to which it was most certainly entitled—they would, perhaps, be able to defend its interests better than the small number of Guardians who had now to stand in the breach when attacks were made upon it. (Hear, bear.) He was sorry that he was not gifted with ability to speak with greater fluency on behalf of Widnes. The CHAIRMAN said the next matter they had to consider was how many members they should place before the rate- payers as candidates. _ _

n Mr. S. Mutpnarr thought they could not do better than re-appoint tlitir present representatives upon both bodies. Mr. WELLS Said he had received a communication from Mr. Heyes stating that he should not be able to stand for re-election upon the Local Board, and suggesting that Mr. Peter Longton be appointed in his place. The CHAIRMAN was very sorry to hear that Mr. Ileyes had come to this decision. As far as he (the speaker) was concerned, if he were to consult his own belings, he should positively decline to be pat in nomination again, but there was a duty devolving upon them as citizens, which made him feel he waS bound to do what he could to advance the interests of the township. He hoped that Mr. Hayes would reconsider his decision. Mr. HEYES : I have been reconsidering it for some time, and the mote I do so, the plainer does it become to me that it is my duty, unfortunately, to retire. Mr. nMArrxEws said be might state that though willing to do his best for the township, he could not see his way to taking both the position of a Guardian and a member of the Local Board. Mr. WELLS moved, and Mr. E. CAREY seconded, a motion in favour of the Rev. Father Finegan being nominated as a candidate for the Board of Guardians, which was passed. Mr. S. MUSPRATT proposed, and Mr. HEYES seconded, a motion in favour of the association having their full repre- sentation upon the Local Board, which was agreed to. The CHAIRMAN said that the former candidates were Messrs. B. Brown, H. Gasket', • jun., F. Holes, John Matthews, and himself. Mr. J. L. MusruArr moved that the association should " run " the old members, with the exception of Mr. byes, and that Mr. Peter Longton's name be substituted in the place of that gr!ntleman's. Mr. PLmtuuttgr seconded the proposition, which was passed.

The CHAIRMAN said the retiring Guardians were Mr. Matthews, Mr. Gerrard, and Mr. Sadler. Mr. MerrilEws remarked that he should be glad to see the Rev. Father Finegan on the Board, as he was sure be would make a very good member. The CHAIRMAN thought there was no doubt that they would soon have an increase in the number of Guardians representing Widnes.

was —resolved that the Rev. Father Finegan be nominated as a Guardian, in the place of Mr. Matthews. It was agreed that the Canvassing Committee should be re-appointed, with power to add to their number. Mr. WELLS said that he had acted as secretary to the association since its formation in 1875, and he was of opinion that some other members shonld now take the duties. He understood that Mr. Frank Gaskell had kindly consented to do so, and he should have much pleasure in proposing that he be re-appointed. On the proposition of the CHAIRMAN, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Wells for his services. Mr. CAREY and the CHAIRMAN supported and seconded the proposal to appoint Mr. T. Gaskell secretary, and it was carried with acclamation.

Mr. E. K. MrsPRATT spoke strongly upon the high poor rate from which Widnes was suffering, and expressed a hope that something would be speedily done to reduce it. Mr. STRINGER said this state of things arose from some omission in the past. Mr. KERSHAW : Oh that is an old cry. Mr. STRINGER maintained that it was a cry with some force in it; and he then referred to the conduct of some previous collector. This terminnted the proceedings.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.-
div.p: LATEST NEWS.-
DON CARLOS.

It is rumoured at Madrid that the Pretender, Don Carlos, has renounced his claims to he throne of Spain in favour of his son, who is about 10 years old. This step, says the Madrid correspondent of the Dailg .2VemT, is advocated by the Ultramontanes and the Carlists, who declare that the Pretender has become unpopular since the last civil war, chiefly on account of the numerous scandals connected with his travels. Carlism inspires the present Government with no fear, since the majority of the bishops and clergy declined to associote with it in the pilgrimage. THE BOER OUTBREAK.

We learn from Durban, in a telegram of Thursday's date, that the Boers have been repulsed in two attacks made on the position of the Chief Montsiva, their loss in the second engagement, which took place on the 25:h ult., being 38 men, including the commander. It is announced that Sir Henry Bulsver has appointed a Special Commissioner for Zulu affairs, Sir Hercules Robinson's Commission being suspended in respect of Zululand. THE INSURRECTION IN TUNIS. SEVERAL BRITISH SUBJECTS KILLED.

A Tunis telegram of Wednesday says :—lnsurgents ap- peared suddenly yesterday in the vicinity of Kairouan. Be- sides carrying off a large herd of cattle, they attacked a pro- vision train, killing several British subjects and an Italian, and wounding many others. Ali Ben Kalifa continues to send letters to different tribes, inciting them to a general rising. A telegram on Thursday from the same source says :—A telegram received here from Kairouan states that only one man survived yesterday's affair, when the insurgents at- tacked the provision convoy on its way from Susa to Kairouan. An anxious crowd of relations of the cart drivers employed in the convoy are now thronging the telegraph office. It is believed that the Maltese drivers will leave the French commissariat service in a body. The 4th Zouave regiment has arrived here.
THE WORKINGTON MURDER.-APPREHENSION
OF A MAN.

lOn Thursday afternoon the Workington police visited the West Cumberland Iron and Steel Works, at the north side of Workington, and there apprehended a young man who works at the ironworks as an extra hand. The prisoner was conveyed to the police station in a cab, and the greatest ex- citernent prevailed in the town, large crowds of persons assembling near the police station. Suspicion has rested on the prisoner from the discovery of the crime, and he has previously been interrogated by the police. It appears that the night the unfortunate girl Lucy Sands was last seen she went to the prisoner's garden at the north side, which is situate close to where the body was found. Two other young women were also there, and it is reported that their state- ments to the police have been that Lucy Sands left them to meet someone else. She was never afterwards seen alive. •

LIVERPOOL COTTON BROKERS' EXCHANGE. A meeting, which was numerously attended by cotton merchants, spinners, and others interested in the establish- ment of a Cotton Exchange in LiN erpool, was held in that city on Thursday afternoon, when a president, secretary, and list of directors for the year were appointed. Mr. F. Muir, who presided, gave a long explanation as to the cir- cumstances which have led a number of merchants and spinners to determine to establish a Cotton Exchange, and said that in consequence of the infringement by brokers on what was considered the legitimate province of merchants, and the refusal of the Cotton Brokers' Association to take any steps to remedy those practices of which merchants complained, the latter had almost been driven to take the course which they are now following. He also stated that the prospects of ultimate success were very encouraging, for afready there were 189 subscribers to the new Exchange, representing 141 firms. The new Exchange is expected to be opened in three or four months. THE DIVISION ON MR. GLADSTONE'S MOTION.

In the first division on Thursday night, upon Mr. Glad. stone's resolution regarding the Lords and the Land Act, fourteen Home Rulers voted in the majority, and one Con- servative Home Ruler in the minority. In the second division fourteen Home Rulers again voted in the majority, and sixteen advanced Home Rulers and one Conservative Home Ruler in the minority. The majority included Messrs. Cowen, Torrens, Walter, H. W. Fitzwilliam, and Sir Nathaniel de Rothschild. No English or Scotch Liberal voted in the minority.

div.head: DASTARDLY OUTRAGE ON A YOUNG LADY.
div.p: DASTARDLY OUTRAGE ON A YOUNG LADY.

A dastardly outrage wns committed on Thursday night at Madeley, Shropshire, on a young lady named Miss Nellie Birbeck. As she was returning home from a friend's house she was ;topped by two men in a lonely part of the road. Her assailants threw a handkerchief over her face, and de- manded her purse, which she gave them. They afterwards threw her down, and attempted to strangle her. Her cries were heard, and assistance came. One of the men has been apprehended. FOUNDERING OF A BARQUE: 25 LIVES LOST. ,

Intelligence received from Lloyd's on Thursday morning states that the well-known barque City of Dunedin, 1,074 tons, belonging to Maryport, has foundered in the Atlantic with her crew of 25 hands. She sailed from Pensacola on the 4th November last for England with a yaluable cargo, and has never since been heard of. She ought to have reached her destination two months ago, therefore all hopes of her safety are abandoned. DESPERATE FIGHT WITH A BURGLAR.

At Manchester, Thomas I-Idwards was remanded on a charge of shopbreaking and wounding a police-officer, on Thursday morning. Prisoner and another man broke into' the shop of a tea niirchant, but were disturbed Ist the police. A canal runs at the back of the premises' and, rushing out of the way, the burglars met a policeman. Prisoner knocked him down with a crowbar, and ran across the lock-gates. A police- officer knocked the prisoner down with his staff and secured him. The policeman is in a dangerous condition. EXTRAORDINARY DISCOVERY.

An Oldham correspondent telegraphs:—On Thursday morning, a representative of the press was invited to the Wellington Mill, Oldham, to judge for himself of the extent of cotton adulteration. He was shown a bale of cotton which, amongst others, was purchased at Liverpool on the 23rd ult. Near the top was a layer of common sand about two inches deep, and in the centre another layer about the same depth. Over one-fourth the bale was sand, which appeared to have been shovelled on the cotton.
THE RECENT ATTEMPP ON THE QUEEN.

EXAMINATION YESTERDAY. The magisterial inquiry into the attempt by Roderick M'Lean to assassinate Her Majesty at Windsor, on the 2nd instant, was resumed yesterday morning, in the Town Hall, Windsor. The magistrates on the bench were the Mayor (Mr. Devereux), Mr. Pooley, Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Wellman, Mr. Pearle, Mr. Dewe, Mr. Webb, Mr. Beach, and Mr. Tuck. Prince Leopold. accompanied by General Ponsonby, drove up to the court shortly before 11 o'clock, and stayed during the greater part of the proceedings. The court was crowded, a number of fashionably dressed ladies forming part of the assemblage. Mr. Stevensori, solicitor to the Treasury, again appeared to prosecute. Mr. Edmund Thomas appeared for the relatives of the prisoner whose interests he watched. Shortly after 11 o'clock the prisoner was put iota the dock. The prisoner, who entered the dock in a state of apparent calmness, was received with hisses, which were immediately suppressed. He looks a great deal better since his arrest. He sat at the end of the dock, with his side towards the bench, and gave furtive attention to what transpired. A slight difficulty arose at the outset. 111`Lean was not directly represented by a legal gentleman, and Mr. Steven- son asked openly in court whether any one was present to act in his behalf. Mr. Haynes, solicitor, announcei that he was present to represent, with the assistance of Mr. Thomas, ! the prisoner's family.—Mr. Stevenson pointed out that his :1 question was not without its importance. Failing the pos- session of a direct representative, the prisoner would have I the right of himself cross-examining the witnesses.—Mr. Haynes replied that he had no further instructions for the 1 present, and refrained from assuming any immediate respon- sibility with regard to the prisoner.--Without further die.

cussion, the matter was allowed to rest here.—Jos. Turner, ot the Great Western .tiailway, submitted a plan of the Great Eastern Station at ‘S'iodsor, showing the Queen's waiting_ room, the gate through which the Royal carriage passed, the spot where the bullet was found, mid the place where M‘Lean stood—it was now the prisoner's right to cross-examine, and when asked to do so, he rose and said, "I understand I am represented by a solicitor and counsel."—The Mayor: The solicitor ishere on behalf of your iantily.—Frisoner : I leave the case entirely in their hands :(resurninghis.seat and sud- denly rising). ireserve my defence.—The Mayor: Very well. —Mr. Councillor Errington, of Sunderland, examined by Mr. T. R. D. Stevenson, said:—On the 2nd of March I was in Windsor watching the arrival of her Majesty. I was about twelve yards from the barrier, and I observed her Majesty get into the carriage. Just as the carriage was moving off I heard some cheers from a crowd of boys who were standing by. They were Eton boys. I observed a man standing just on the inside of the barrier. His arm was pointed towards the carriage. I heard the report, and saw the puff of a pistol fired by the prisoner. His arm and pistol were aimed at a point two or three feet below the top of the carriage. I saw a gentleman close to the barrier, and he rushed forward and seized hold of the prisoner. I under- stand it was Mr. Hayes. (Superintendest Hayes, now in uniform, stood up and witness recognised hitn, remarking that he wasdifferently attired.) I also noticed someone strug- gling with the prisoner's arm. I asked the man who get the pistol from the prisoner his name, and he said it was Mr. Burnside. (Mr. Burnside also stood up, and was recognised by the witness.)—Francis Orchard, fifteen years a footman in the service of her Majesty, said :—I came from London on Thursday with her Majesty, who drove from Windsor Station in a closed landau, pulled by a pair of horses.. I saw a man pushing his way to the front with his arm out- streched. He was about six or seven yards from her Majesty,and I saw the dash of the pistol whiclehe fired. He aimed about six or seven inches above the panel of the Carriage. Her Majesty was on the off side of the vehicle,. and Princess Beatrice was next to her, being nearest the prisoner. The Duchess of Roxburge was also in the oaraiaga Prisoner declined to cross-examine either of these witneases —Edward Don, postillion to the Queen's carriage, said: We had got the ponies just out of a gentle walk before we got to the barrier. We were about nine' or ten yards from the barrier when I heard the report. I looked round, and saw a man standing with his arm stretched straight out from the- shoulder and pointing to the carriage. I could net see what was in his hand.—James Hudson, an outrider of the Royal I Mews, raid: I preceded the carriage from the Great Western !Railway Station, on the arrival of Her Majesty, as outrider. I was just going outside the barrier when I heard a re- port. I looked round and saw a man with his arm pointed towards the Queen's carriage.and presenting a pistol. I did not see any smoke emanating from it. The carriage was going straight towards the gate, and was about ten yards from the man. The pistol looked a new one—something I like that now produced. I went straight on, ' and the carriage followed directly to the Castle.— Lord Chestney Wilson, a student at Eton, said :—On Thu s- day I went to the Great Western Station to see the Queen arrive. I saw her Majesty enter the carriage. I was inside the barrier. I heard a report. The prisoner was standing with a pistol held at arm's length, and was two yards or a yard and a half in front of the crowd. It was a pistol or revolver which he grasped which I could not make out. I was stancting a few yards inside the barrier and was about seven yards from the man, being situated between the door- way and the barrier. Prisoner's aim appeared to be directed to about the top of the panel. Inspector Hayes seized the man, and another man ran up. and I went up and gave him "one "over the head with my umbrella. I was dragged off. The prisoner in the dock is the man.—Leslie Murray Robertson. another Et on boy, said: I was with the last Witness, and I too heard the report, and saw prisoner aiming at a little above the panel of the car- riage. I mean the panel of the carriage window, and to the right. I am able to say that the pistol was pointed upwards and not downwards.

P.C. Benjamin Houghton, of the metropolitan force, stationed at the Castle; Mr. W. J. McCloskey, of the Star and Garter Hotel ; Mr. J. G. Smyth, stationmaster ; and Mr. C. Noble, chief inspector of the Western Railway police, were eacbiexamined, and subsequently INl‘Lean was committed for trial. In the evening the prisoner was removed from Windsor police station to Reading gaol. He passed through Windsor quite unnoticed, but received a hostile recognitien at Slough,

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS. Earl KIMBERLEY, replying to Lord Carnarron, said he had no additional information as to fighting between the Boers and natives in South Africa. Lord LyrroN moved for copies of the Indian correspon- dence respecting public works in that country.—The Slate Mines Gunpowder Bill was read a second time.—The Consolidated Fund Bill haring been passed, the House adjourned.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. NOTICES.-Mr. W. "Salmi gave notice of his intention to ask whether the Government intended to introduce a bill to extend the purchase clauses of the Irish Land Act. 11. a. CHAPLIN gave notice to move a resolution iitana; that the Land Commission, as at present constituted, was totally inadequate to deal with the business before the court, and stating the propriety of amending the Land Act so as to facilitate the hearing of the application for fixing rent.

JUMBO.—Mr. Asumv, replying to Mr. Labouchere, said the Board of Trade had directed an inspection of the arrange- ments on board ship for conveying Jumbo to America. The inspectors were directed to ascertain whether the cage was sufficiently strong and secure as to provide for the safety of other passengers, and also that their health and ventilation was not interfered with in providing for the transport of the animal.

THE ARREST OF MR. ROURKE.—Mr. FORSTER said it was true that James Rourke, of Dublin, had been arrested.—Mr. HEALY condemned the arrest as an act of oppression, and said the crime Rourke had committed was being the partner of Egan, the treasurer of the Laud League. All attempts to crush out the league would prove fruitless. He moved the adjournment of the House.—Mr. SEXTON and Mr. GRAY condemned the arrest, which would destroy the successful business now in operation in Dublin.—Mr. FORSTER said Mr. Rourke being in partnership with Egan in trade had nothing to do with his arrest.— Mr. MITCHELL condemned the "no rent" manifesto as the present cause of crime in Ireland. Jle urged Irish members to obtain its withdrawal, as maintaltfing it was traitorism to the Irish cause and cruelty to the Irish people. He accused many of the Land League party in that house as wanting the courage of their opinions. The discussion was continued by Sir P. O'Brien, Mr. Red- mond, Mr. Leamy, and Mr.Comrnins.—Colonel COLTEMRST regretted that the "no rent" manifesto had been jus.ti6ed in that House. He considered the subscribers to the document responsible for the terrible outrages that now disgraced Ireland.—Mr. MACIVER said the true cause of the arrest of Messrs. Parnell and Dillon was because they had answered the speeches of Mr. Gladstone.--Mr. FORSTER gave that statement a direct denial.—Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN said peace was hopeless in Ireland as long as they kept Messrs. Par- nell, Dillon, and others in prison.—Mr. BIGGAR did not be- lieve increased crime had been caused by the no-rent manifesto. Mischief was brought about by the obstinate and headstrong policy of the Irish Government —Mr. GILL believed that had it been known that nearly 1,000 persons would have been cast into prison the Coercion Act would never have been passed.—The House divided, when there voted for the motion 16, and against 147. SOUTH AFRICA.—Mr. COURTNEY, replying to Mr. Gorst, said the Government had no additional news from South Africa to that already published. FUNDS IN CHANCERY.—On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. S. Lnion•rox called attention to the.unsatisfactory :manner in which the list of dormant funds in Chancery was published. He moved a resolution that in future the lists of unclaimed money belonging to suitors should be published, alphabetically arranged, with names and address of persons criginally entitled, date of order or decree, and amount unclaimel.—The ATTORNEY- GENERAL did not tbink the plan suggested would be an improvement ; but, on the c mtrary, it would increase liti- gation. Information could always be obtain-d by employ- ing a respectable solicit,r.—Dr. LYON thought an officer ought to be appointed.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

LIVERPOOL CORN, FRIDAY.— There was a moderate • at- tendance at our Exchange thi, morniag, and t'.e mlrket for wheat was rather firmer than yes:-erday ; a fair business being transacted at a decline of from Id to 2d from last Tuesday's prices. Flour was also a shade firmer, but not active. Indian corn was Ii moderate request at 5s 100 to 5s lid per cental for new mixed American. old was firlit at 6s Id per cental, whilst round sold at 6s to fit 3d per ceutal. Bea is were slow of sale at a decline of about §d per cental from the quotaTion of last market day; Egyptian sold at is ld to is 21, and mixed at 7S per cental. WAERINGTON POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley and Captain Reynolds. A TAILOR'S RECEPTION IN A "EERANGE COENTRE."— Andrew Moffatt, a tailor, a native of Carlisle, but last from Manchester, was charged with wilfully breaking a window in the shop of Messrs. Jesper and Co., Sankey-street, on Friday night, doing damage to the amount of £4 10s.—It appeared that the prisoner was on the tramp, and went to Messrs. Jesper and Co.'s workshop to beg money towards his lodging. The men told !aim they could not relieve him but one of them generously shared his tea with the prisoner. Afterwards prisoner got up, and swore he "never saw such a town as this," and, on getting to the door, said he would "break windows before be went far." He was in a pas- sion, and broke a new spring on the door by the force with which he threw the door open. Prisoner then went into the shop and solicited relief from the shapinan, who was engaged with a gentlemen, and on the shoprean asking him if he did not see he was engaged, prisoner threatened him. About a quarter of an hour afterwards a stone was thrown through a plate-glass window, which was shattered. lo one, how- ever, saw the stone throe n, but the chopman gave it as his opinion, from the way the window was broken, that the prisoner had thrown it from the passage between the District Bank; and Mr. Connor's shop, where Le would be in the dark. The Chief Constable remarked that the stone must have been thrown with considerable force. Soon after the prisoner left the prosecutor's shop, he accosted two women in the street, end with an , oath said "there would be crime com- mitted in the town before long," as "he could not stand it any longer." P.S. Cox apprehended the prisoner, who, when between Bold-street and Messrs. Jesper's shop, said "If these get me locked up for this, I will do something for them when I come out."—Prisoner denied that he had broken any window, and said he had been nine weeks on the road, and "would back he had not eaten 3d. worth during the week." —The Bench said it was not absolutely brought home to the prisoner that he threw the stone, but they had no moral doubt in their minds but what he broke the window, and that he was a dangerous, loose character. He would have to find two sureties of £5 each to keep the peace six months, or in default, go to gaol one month.—Prisoner : I am very sorry lam a stranger in such a country as this. lam in- nocent of the window.—The Bench: We have no doubt that you are a very bad character.—Prisoner was then removed in custody. Moen:ay.—Before Captain Litton and Major Cartwright. A CANDIDATE FOR THE CHIEF CONSTABLESHIP.—ChaS. Henry McCosta was charged with being a vagrant, having been found on the grounds at the gas works, with intent to commit a felony.—On Saturday evening, about half-past five, the prisoner went to the gas works and told the man in charge he was a detective from Scotland Yard, London. Hadland, the lodge-keeper, replied "Why, you are not big enough to be a detective. Where is your authority ?" "I have my card, my whistle, and my handcuffs, and I have made eight arrests to-day," was his answer. The prisoner afterwards made his way into the retort room. He would, , he affirmed, soon have Mr. Hunt's place. (Laughter.) lie I was atterwasde given into enateely.—lie stated he was suffer- ing from delipium tremens at the time, and did not EIIOW what he was doing.—Mr. Hunt said the prisoner stated he was a draughtsman and had been a gas manager in North Wales.—Captain Litton said as the prisoner had been in prison since Saturday he would be discharged on promising to leave the town. A DESERTER.—Patrick Coulter, a fine looking fellow, was charged with being a deserter from Her Majesty's 6th regiment of foot, stationed at Colchester.—lnspector Berry proved the case, and the magistrate recommended the pay- ment of the usual reward to the officer.—The prisoner was remanded to Walton to await an escort. MISCELLANEOES.—Peter O'Brien was charged with having, on the 26th February, made use of obscene language in Buttermarket-street. P.S. Bowen said the defendant was using very bad language as the people were returning from church. Defendant was fined ss. and costs.—Michael Jeffrey, a labourer, was fined in the costs for wheeling a barrow on the footpath, in Wilson-Patten-street, on the Ist Inst.—John Flannaghan, carter for Mr. Pierpoint, seedsman, Bridge-street, was charged with causing an obstruction in that street by allowing his horse and lorry to stand there a long and unreasonable time. It was proved that on the 25th ult. the defendant allowed his lorry to stand 20 minutes in the street, and he was ordered to pay 3s. 6d.—Joseph Lee, Elizabeth Hayes, Rot Maskell, and Thomas Unsworth, were all charged with having their chimneys on fire, and they were each fined is. E.EHOoL ATTENDANCE CASES.—Archibald Brown, book- keeper, Church-street, was charged with not fulfilling the requirements of the Elementary Education Act. Mr. Riley, the inspector, said that the boy was uumanageable, and suggested that the boy be sent to an industrial school. The case was adjourned for a fortnight to give the boy another trial.—John Haslam, of General-street, pleaded guilty to not sending his daughter regularly to school. Mr. Riley said the child had been absent over 100 times since November, and a fine of ss. was imposed.—Jehn Branwood, coal dealer, Haydock-street, was summoued for neglecting the schooling of his son. Mr. Riley proved that the boy was absent 241 times during the last year, and consequently he could not be preeented for examination. Since January he had been away 39 times. Defendant pleaded sickness in his family, but had no evidence to support his plea and was fined ss. The daughter of Philip Hankinson, Bank Quay, was shown to have attended school irregularly, and her father was fined ss. The girl, who was twelve years of age, was unable to read and write.—John Wilcock, Bank Quay, made his third appearance for neglecting to snd his son John (12) to ecbool, and he was fined ss.—A similar penalty was imposed on Esther Travis for neglecting to send her daughter to school—On a like charge Pat Loughlin, 12, Dolman's-lane, was fined 55., which penalty was also ordered to be paid by Wm. Egerton, Elizabeth-street, for not sending his daughter, aged 12, to school. When the Bench announced the penalty, Mrs. Egerton, who appeared, went into a great temper, and said she wished Mr. Riley had a 'dozen of 'em" (children), and applied an insulting epithet to him. She was ordered from the court.—A fine of ss. was inflicted upon John Mather, Hardy-street, in regard to his step-daughter, Rachael Buckley, and upon John Pritchard in regard to his daughter Jane. TUESDAY .—Before Captain Litton and Major Cartwright. STEALING AND RECEIVIN G.—James Tickle and John Tickle (father of the first-named) were charged with stealing from the slaughter-house of James and Alfred Bowcock, in Proffit's-yard. Church-street, on the 24th February, 941bs. of fat, value 19s. Od., and on the rd instant, 631bs. of fat, value 145., their property. John Tickle, the father, was further charged with receiving the fat knowing it to be stolen.—On the days named the father went with the fat to 31r. Burgess's candle works on Friar's Green, and offered it for sale. On the first occasion the foreman at the works was rather suspicious as it was mixed with pieces of beef fat, and he questioned the elder prisoner abeut it, but the latter said "he got it from his son and it was all right." The foreman gave the father a credit note to take to the shop, which he did and he received the money. On the 3rd inst. the father visited the works again and offered 63Ibs. of fat for sale, but as it was similar to the last lot Jones (the fore- man) said it was stolen and retained it. The younger priso- ner presented himself on Saturday morning and asked for the note, but Jones refused to give it up. On Monday the younger prisoner presented himself again, area after remark- ing that he did not care if Alfred Bowcock had not seen the fat, told Jones he did not need to make such a noise about it, as "he would put him' all right." The Chief Constable was however communicated with, and the matter was placed in the hands of Inspector Singleton whose enquiries re- sulted in the apprehension of the prisoners. The younger prisoner, who worked odd days for the prosecutors, and re- sided with his father at 19, Carlisle-street, Cockhedge-lane, was in the habit of purchasing, skins from the prosecutors which he dressed and sold, and he maintained that the fat was got from the skins he purchased.—Mr. James Bowcock, on being called, stated that he had notice a deficiency in the weight of fat, and that the pieces produced were such as appeared to have been cut from the pieces in the slaughter- house. As to the fat being obtained from the skins, he stated that if the younger prisoner had done his duty to them while they were his (the prosecutor's) property such fat would not have been found upon them.—The Bench consi- dered the prisoners were equally guilty, and they were each sentenced to two months hard labour. come a member of the church by that very fact, and all else beyond that was simply left to the conscience of the indi- vidual to settle between him or her and their Maker. This had been the steadfast policy of their people for the last 150 years. He had lately gone through the history of their own chapel, and he could speak with perfect confidence; they were simply carrying out the policy which had obtained in that chapel for the last 150 years; and he believed he might make the stronger claim, that they were in the main upholding the same doctrines that were preached there 150 years ago. They were in perfect accord with the policy which ' had ruled in that old place for that long period, of having no authoritative creed by which they could include that man or exclude that, or exercise any dominion over his conscience in any way. And it had this full advantage, that they could see good in every other .Christian sect, and in those who were non-Christian. He hoped they had strength of mind enough, and respect and , confidence enough, he their own principles to see good even in those who were not Christiaus. All were Christian in their eyes who were evidently striving to live a Christ-like life in a Christ-like spirit. And it was lefcause they had adopted this as the policy of their lives, leaving all else to be settled by the conscience of the individual, that they had stood up for free thought and free speech, perfectly confident that Christianity was its own best defence, and that the principles which underlay Christianity were so great that , they would commend themselves to the conscience, and to the intelligence of the world, if only they were permitted to have fair play. (Applause.) But there was another part of their policy. They had met for a social gathering, and would cut down the speaking as much as possible. They would mingle it with amusement, under the profound con- viction that they best showed their gratitude and reverence for the Giver of All Good by enjoying His gifts with pure and simple, yet joyous hearts. .(Hear.) "His is not the least thankful heart," as the hymn expressed it," that tastes these gifts with joy." For his own part, he perfectly be lieved that they were doing as much a religious act when they took the pleasures of life which Providence permitted them, to lighten what would otherwise be intolerable. They were doing as much a religious act in properly using the - pleasures and enjoyments of life, as they were when they stedfastly strived to perform its duties. Religion if it were worth anything, should go into every nook and corner of life, and while it was its life and the strength of life, it should also be its sunshine. (Applause.) Mr. W. LONG then addressed a few words to the audience, remarking that he went back 1,800 years for his faith, and that was a good deal longer than 150 years. If a man took the New Testament as his guide through life, and tried to form his own opinions upon that, it would give him sufficient thought ; if he followed its teachings he would lead a life that would make blue a happy man while he lived, and a man who was happy while he lived was always a happy man when he died. (Applause.) The Rev. S. A. STEINTIIAL said he must candidly confess that he was rather taken aback when he entered the room and saw the gathering that night. He must congratulate his good and old friend Mr. Richard Filcher, in being able to see before him such an assembly as was gathered there to greet him on their annual festival day. (Applause.) It looked to him as if the congregation to which Mr. Filcher ministered was really in a healthy condition, and the promise that they saw before them that 'evening was a great en- couragement to him to continue that active and useful work to which he had so faithfully devoted himself during the , past years. It promised, too, a future for the old Cairo- street congregation which they all must rejoice in, because they knew that Cairo-street had a history of which a coagre- tion might well be proud—(iiear, hear)—and had a bittory of which it was proud. It also showed 'that it had a future to which it could look forward with equal certainty that it would justify tn'e highest anticipations . which might be -raised .by such a gathering as that. Of course they all were familiar with that old history of Cairo-street, and they knew what names were connected with the history of the congregation that had met there now for generations. They knew they all looked back to the time when from Warrington came forth the real life , of all their churches, when their ministers, men of such I high names as Aikin, Priestley, Enfield, and Taylor, were trained at Warrington. They knew what great things, therefore, were done for the scientific side of the theology of the churches of which Cairo-street formed one important feature. They knew, too, that Cairo-street bad not only been well-known in the past history for giving to them the foundation of a scientific theology, but they remembered the efforts of some of their ministers who had been equally renowned in the field of philanthropic work, and whose benevolent labours for their fellow men would not soon be forgotten by those who had the privilege to know Francis Bishop and Philip Carpenter. (Applause.) He must say that when he thought of those who had gone to their reward, and looked upon the assembly before him, he felt indeed as if their spirit were amongst them still ; and that that combination of scholarly and earnest 'research into theological truth, com- bined with practical interest on the every day questions of ordinary life, secured for the church the right position that it ought to hold. They firmly believed that it was a good and a wise thing to search into the foundation of truth, and to build upon a certain foundation. But mere theological learning after all was but a poor thing unless it inspired every earnest heart with a religious love and faith that showed itself in deeds of sympathy and kindness, not only to the members of the household, but to the whole com- munity in which that church was placed. Cairo-street had that tradition, and he was glad to think that those who were at present working there under the able guidance of Mr. Pilcher were keeping up that tradition, and were widening the influence of their church, and were helping to break down some of those division lines which , only too deeply had scored themselves upon modern society, and to unite in earnest work a variety of opinions, while there might be a unity of strength underlying that variety. (Applause.) He felt assured that he was speaking not only to those who really were members of the Cairo-street con- gregation. He knew that there was a sufficient kindly spirit to cetera this liberalism of Cairo-street, and it chewed itself in members of other churches being amongst theni that night. (Hear, hear.) It was a pleasant thing to think that they could feel this cordial unanimity of sympathy one with another amongst this variety of opinion. They who were called Unitarians fancied—he did not think they were very far wrong in fancying it— they had been very much mis- apprehended in days gone by,—that people thought them a j very dreadful kind of religious people, believing rather in 1 negative than in positive truths, and much more likely to criticise and pull (Lawn than to accept and edify those with whom they were connected. The past year, in which they had been engaged in a variety of work, was just one of those years that it was well to dwell upon,because they had during that year done one thing, at any rate, to show how truly affirmative was the basis of that religiousness which brought them together. He thought if he were to look beck in the history of Unitarian work during the past twelve months, theone feature that would strike him would be the fact that the Unitarian Association in London was able to bring together ten men of various schools of thoughteto lecture to the world at large in London and elswhere, upon, not the negative points of Trinitarian or Unitarian controversy, but upon those greet fundamental principles on which they believed all true religion was based. (Hear, hear.) If they looked through the. volume that bad since been published of the affirmative lectures of those men, he was certain those who did not lee- long to the Unitarian congregation would be surprised to find how much they held in common. Not but what they would find out there were differences, but they Would find that the essential truths of religion were held in cemmon by them all ; and the Unitarians believed they had the additional ad- vantage over the rest of the churches that they could stand in the controversy which was the pressing controversy of the present day in a very powerful position indeed to meet those difficulties which were most pressing upon thought- ful minds at present; because the affirmative truths which they put, forward as the fundamental truths of all religion were truths which did not in the slightest degree come into conflict with any of the scientific enquiries of the present day. (Hear, bear). He pointed out that the questions which divided the world at the present time were not those which divided the churches in olden time, and spoke of the efforts which were being made to erect new churches in the various suburbs of Manchester, in which, at the present time, none of their free churches could be found. There was one thing that had happened in the past twelve months in which all churches alike were interested, hut which they had hailed with the greatest gratification. He referred to the publice- lion of the revised version of the New Testament. He ex- plained that few many years the ministers in their free churches and Unitarian churches had been dwelling upon the importance and the necessity of a revision of the Bible, and said he believed that the publication of the revised ver- sion of tbe New Testament had been of essential service to Higious progress. It had knocked on the head, he thought. altogether the old superstition that the words in the English Bible were inspired words, and it had done a say with certain opinions that they as Unitarians had long since declared ought to be done away with, and they had now a really, fair representation of that which Ilk original writers produced. In conclusion, he expressed his opinion that the book would make its way, and referred to the great demand there had been for the revised version. Mr. C. BROADBENT said he was sure all prhent would feel that they had been fully repaid by having the privilege of hearing Mr. Steinthal's interesting address. (Hear, hear). It seemed to him Mr. Steintlial had taken a Very accurate measure of the position of the leading features of the pre- sent time, and it had often occurred to Mtn how paltry it was to find people quarrelling over more or less trifling points of doctrine and still more trifling points of vestments when there was a real great eantroVersy between those who professed religion, and that, he was sorry to say, the enormous number who professed and lee. tiered in no religion and no God. (Hear, hear.) Surely all those who did their best to be religious, and did believe in Almighty God might unite in their efforts to stem the tide of ir-religion and to try to convert these who were desti- tute of any religious belief whatever. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the tendency of the time was towards unity rather than towards the divergency which had been such a curse in days past. (Hear, hear.) He prOposed a most hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Steinthal for his presence that night. (Ap- plause. Mr. T. BIRCECA.T.L seconded the 'proposition, and said while Mr. Steinthal was speaking of the past history of the-con- gregation he touched upon some things which' found a very strong and deep echo in his heart. Referring to the Sunday- school, he said they owed a great deal of its excellent organization and influence to those esteemed gentlemen whom Mr. Steinthal had named—Mr. Bishop and 'Mr. . Carpenter. (Hear,ihear.) Its influence continued to extend, ..ind he could see it in • the United States of America to-day. . There were young men there who received their first intpire- tion in Cairo-street school, and he could tell them.e.indi- e

MID-CHFSHIRE ITEMS. The directors of the Altrincham Gas Company have, it is stated, declined to accept the advance made in their remuneration from £3OO to £5OO, voted at the last meeting of shareholders. On Sunday afternoon, a tire was discovered in the steeple of the Parish Church, Sandbach, which, but for the prompt and timely assistance rendered, might have proved serious in its results. On Monday evening the Rev. T. W. Norwood, vicar of Wrenbury, gave a lecture in the People's Hall, Nantwich, on the "Nantwich Parish Church." Ile chair was taken by Captain Cotton, of Reaseheath Hall. There was a good attendance. On Sunday evening, the Rev. F. Carter, pastor of the Congregational Church, Northwich, delivered another of the series of lectures on Old Testament Characters, his subject being, "David : the man after God's own heart." There was a good attendance. A distribution of prizes, followed by an entertainment, took place in the Altrincham and Bowdon British Schools, on Friday evening. The prizes were distributed by Mr. T. D. Hall, of Bowdon College; and a very satisfactory report from Her Majesty's Inspector of Schools was read. There were 374 births and 204 deaths registered in Altrincham during the year ending December 31st, 1881. The death rate was 18 per 1,000 and the birth rate 33.2. The return compares very favourably with that of the preceding twelve months. The subsidence still continues in the neighbourhood of Northwich, and the private road leading to Whatcroft Hall Irons the main road between Middlewich and Broken Cross, and which goes under the bridge of the London and North Western Railway Company' has gone in to such a degree, ' that a pool of water to the depth of about three feet six inches has accumulated there. The bridge will be raised, so as to enable the road underneath to be made passable. The spot is just mid-way between Northwich and Middle- wich, it being therefore about WI miles from the town of Northwich. An entertainment was given at the People's Hall, Nant- wich, on Saturday evening, under the presidency of Dr. Munro. There was a large attendance, and a very interesting and diversified programme was gone through. Songs were given by Mr. John Thomas, junr., Miss Speed, of Whit- church, Mr. Reginald Bellyse of Oakfield, and Mr. James Bayley, J.P., of Willaston Hall. Miss Samuel, daughter of Mr. Samuel, Hospital-street, Nantwich, played a selection of pianoforte music, chiefly remarkable as coming from a child of tender years. The entertainment was brought to a close with the National anthem the chairman inviting the audience to join in singing it, and remarking that, in view of the re- cent attempt on Her Majesty's life, the time was most ap- propriate for showing their loyalty. The invitation was most heartily responded to.

IVIGA.N. DISSOLUTION OF A BUILDING SOCIETY. At a meeting on Monday evening of the Southport Permanent Benefit Building Society, which has been in existence for 24 years, it was decided to dissolve the society, its affairs having become deranged. Three trustees were appointed to sell the propery, which is situate at Wigan, Skehnersdale, Prescot, Blackpool, Formby, Southport, and Ainsdale. A sum of 150 guineas was voted to the trustees, exclusive of travel- ling expenses, for their services in winding up the snietv, which it w,is anticipated would take three years. It was decided that when they had £1,200 in hand it was to be divided. WAITE T. WIGAN COAL AND ILION COMPANY.—In the Exchequer Chamber of the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice, Westminster, on Tuesday, the case of Waite v. the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, came before Mr. Justice Field and Mr. Justice Bowen, sitting in banco. This was an appeal by way of special case from the decision of the justices of Wigan, who had held that a legal contract existed under which the appellant was bound to give the respondents fourteen days notice of his intention to quit their employ. Mr. Russell appeared for the appellant, and the Solicitor-General and Mr. Crompton, Q.C., represented the resnondents.—Mr. Russell, in support of the appeal, said the dispute in the present case arose nnder the Employers' and Workmen's Act, 1875, the respondents, who traded as the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, having summoned the appellant for loss alleged to have been sustained in conse- quence of the appellant having, on the 19th November last, absented himself from the service of the company, The respondents contended that the appellant entered into a con- tract to serve them in their California pit, and that the con- tract was determinable at a fortnight's notice, but he argued that the appellant did no such thing. It apPeared that after the appellant had entered the respondents' employ, they posted a notice about the pit to the effect that no contract which had been entered into between them and their work- men could be determinable without fourteen days' notice on , -either side, and the justices held that the appellant was aware ot the notice, and that a legal contract existed under which the apnellant was bound to give the respondents four- teen days' notice of his intention to quit their employ.--Their lordships, without calling on counsel on the other side, dis- missed the appeal with costs, on the ground that there was no point of law for them' to decide.

NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. OBSTRUCTION IN TIIE HOUSE OF ComstoNs.—A petition was on Tuesday forwarded to the House of Commons from the inhabitants of Newton and Earlestown showing that the petitioners are exceedingly grieved at the obstruction of the national business which has taken place for several years in the House of Commons, and which the petitioners regard as wilful and mischievous obstruction to the highest in- terests of the .nation. The petitioners, therefore, humbly pray the House to adopt such rules to govern the proceed- ings of debates as will check the abuses which have existed in the past, facilitate the progress of public business in the future, and protect the rights of the people's representatives. The following reply has been received :—"lndia Office, London, 7th March, 1882.—Sir —I am desired by the Marquis of Irartingtomi to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the Gth inst., and in reply to inform you that his Lordship will present the petition which you forward, on the subject of the Rules of Procedure in the House of Corn- mane—Yours faithfully, W. J. MitrLAND."—P. M. Camp- bell, Esq., Wargrave, Newton-le-Willows. NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, Newton, on Monday. Present: Messrs. F. Gooch (chairman), Glover, Wood, Emmett, Forster, Pardey, Gillespie, J. E. Worsley (law clerk), and B. Brierley i (surveyor).

HIGHWAYS, ETC., COMMITTEE. A meeting of the Highways, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee was held on the 20th ult. Dr. Watkins attended to confer with the committee upon his annual report. Thirty-one cases o,f scarlet fever were reported, four new cases having occurred during the week. Respecting the I proposed new burial ground, it was ordered that Mr. Brierley communicate with the Local Board of Haydock and Ashton to ascertain if they were willing to join Newton in selecting a site for the three townships. It was ordered that Mr. par- dey he informed that the committee were willing to adopt Vista-road as a public highway in substitution for the " Gib- rood " from Newton Common to Haydock, on Mr. Legh consenting to pay the cost of putting the same in repair, which was estimated at £175, and agreeing to provide for . his lessees to flag the footpaths when required by the com- mittee to do so ; Mr. Legh also to make immediate applica- tion for, and obtain the sanction of, quarter sessions to confirm the arrangement, and to indemnify the committee for any responsibility with regard to the Gibraltar Cottages. The committee having viewed and considered Mr. Pardey's verbal application on behalf of Mr. Legh for diverting the footpaths crossing the Mains from High-street, they recom- mended that the Commissioners sanction the altera- tion on the footpath from High-street, Newton, to , the railway arch going to Earlestown across the Mains, pro- vided the footpath from Park-road bridge to the proposed new road near to the Mains water-course be kept open and made straight. It was ordered that Mr. Pardey's atten- tion be called to the wretched condition of Mercer-street, between Mr. Pennington's cottages and Crow-lane, and that he be written to and asked if it was his wish that the committee should sewer and pave the same on behalf of Mr. Legh and the property owners abutting.' It was ordered that the superintendent of police be requested to enforce the provi- sions of the To Nn's Police Clanses Act, especially as to obsnruction by tradesmen exhibiting goods outside their doors and the placing of clothes lines across some of the streets. A communication from the Local Board of West Ham referring to a legal decision upon section 152 of the Public Health Act, 1575, was referred to the next Board meeting. The surveyor baying certified the sum of £l2O clue to Mr. Unsworth on his contracts, a cheque for that amount was ordered to be issued. Mr. Ewer Err moved, and Mr. Woot. seconded, the adop- tion of the minutes. Mr. EMMETT asked:whether the surveyor bad put himself in communication with the other townships about the burial grounds, and what answer, if any, he had received. Mr. BRIF,RDEY said be bad written to the Ashton and Haydock Local Boards. He had received a reply from the Haydock Local Board, which was as follows :--" Your letter of the 24th ultimo was laid before the members of this Board at their last meeting. In reply lam directed to say, 'should sh!on and Golborne be prepared to join such a scheme, the Haydock Local Board will be prepared to give the subject due consideration.'' He had not 'received a reply from Ashton Local Board, but he saw from a report in the newspapers that they declined to combine with them. •Mr. PARDEY: Then one would assume that Haydock will decline too.

The minutes were then passed. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the Gas and Water Committee held on , the 20th February, Mr. Brierley submitted the gas manager's monthly carbonising account, which gave fuel used 248 tons, 14 cwt, gas made, 2,503,900 cubic feet, averaging. 10,050 cubic feet per ton. A letter was read from the Jim T. R.

THE WIDNES THEATRICAL BOOTH. Sir,—You will publish in your columns to-day a report of the proceedings before the Widnes bench of !magis- trates on Wednesday, relative to the application made by a ' person for a license to establish a booth on the waste land adjicent to the Volun- teer Hall. I desire, with your kind permission, to rectify a alight mis-statement made by Mr. Beasley, who, in the course of his observations, said, "I must say in justice to my client that Mr. Kershaw having first let the Volunteer Hall to him for dramatic representations, a few days after- wards accepts the proprietor of the booth as a tenant for the adjacent land." This is not the case, the circumstances being directly vice-versa; and therefore it is by no means fair that such an imputation should have been fora moment cast. As many of the residents are aware Mr. Kershaw is a warm supporter of the drama, but nevertheless I hardly think he will care to figure in so heavy a character as "First Robber" in this the first at- te npt for two years to permanently revive histrionics in the town. Unfortunately, I was called away to St. Helens, on the all important business of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and in consequence was unable to attend the court here and supervise the instruc- tions somewhat hastily imparteil to my advocate. I have been taught to hate shows for the reason that they dispar- age what I dearly love, and on this ground I base my objec- tion. Very few can have felt the need of some place of popular entertainment where the rich and the poor might meet together occasionally through the week, and mutually enjoy an intellectual performance, more than I myself have; and it was the utter absence of such an institution in the place which made me determined to sacrifice the position I now hold and become a puolic caterer. My functions will not, of course, apply exclusively to Wi4nes, but whether I am located here or elsewhere I shall endeavour to prove myself the trusty advocate of the higher drama, which edu- cates while it amuses, and the opponent of anything of a low E. SANSOM.
Ciass. Widnes, March 11, 1882.

The 'necessity of lighting Vitriol-street having been considered, 111 r. Brierly was instructed to ascertain from the Law Clerk the Commissioners' power. On the motion of Mr. GLOVER, seconded by Mr. Forster, the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

A meeting of the School Attendance Committee was held en the 20th ult. The School Attendance Officer read his report with the severatattendances summarised as follows: —For the quarter ending December, 1881, nutaber on the books, 2,174, average attendance, 1,415, absentees, 759, as compared with 2,236, 1,593, and 643 respectively, in the quarter ending September, 1881. The increase in the number of absentees was attributed to the epidemic of scarlet fever and measles prevailing in the district. The minutes were agreed to on the proposition of Mr. FORSTER.

FINANCE COMMITTEE. At the meeting of the Finance Committee held on the 20th ult., accounts amounting to £651 Bs. 6d. were examined, and cheques signed for payment. The minutes were adopted. THE BOARD AND HALF-TIMERS. The LAW CLERK said he was directed at the last meeting, to lay before the Education Department, a case for their opinion as to the refusal to admit a half-timer to an elemen- tary school. In accordance with this direction, he wrote a letter to the Department detailing the circumstances of the Pullen case, and enquiring whether the double fee of Bd. could be imposed by a public elementary school receiving the Government grant. He pointed out that the case was considered a sample case by the School Attendance Com- mittee, and that the reply given would govern their practice upon all further occasions. The School Attendance Com- mittee were making every effort to obtain the due attendance of children at school, but if double fees were to be charged to the persons who could least of all others afford to pay them, inasmuch as children who worked at an early age were almost invariably the children of poor and necessitous parents, their efforts would be greatly hindered. On the 13th February, he (Mr. Worsley) received a reply acknow- ledging receipt of the letter, which, it was stated, would be dealt with in due course.

div.head: COMMUNICATION.
div.p: A COMMUNICATION.

The LAW CLERK read the communication from the West Ham Local Board, as to a legal decision upon section 152 of the Public Health Act, 1875, in reference to a private road being declared a highway. At present, Mr. Worsely stated, private roads had to be sewered, lighted, and completed before they could be adopted by the ratepayers, but the West Ham Local Board asked them to join in petitioning that local authorities should have dis- cretion in deciding as to what portion of the 152nd section should be carried out, before they adopted a road as a high- way. After a short conversation, it was decided to take no action in the matter.

div.p: TRADE NOTES. The block chain makers in East Worcestershire and Staffordshire struck on Saturday for an advance of 10 per
cent. The mule'spindle makers of 3lanchcster. Blackburn, Old- ham, and Bolton have struck work for an advance of 12,k

per cent. The Cleveland Ironmasters' Association, Midalesborough, have issued their monthly return showing that the manufac- ture of pig iron during February was 205,642 tons, and the shipment 66,893 tons. The stocks show a decrease of 6,772

tons. NORTH OF ENGLAND IRON TRADE.—The Board of Arbi- tration for the north of England iron trade have unani- mously decided to ask Mr. J. W. Pease, M.P., to act as arbitrator in the workmen's claim for an advance of wages, in place of Sir Rupert Kettle, who declined the office. The Ironmasters' Association reports that last year's pig iron product of the United States was 4,144,354 tons, an eight per cent increase over 1880. The stock of pig iron un- sold on December 31 was 210,896 tons, against 456,658 tons at the beginning of the year. 'The probable annual con- sumption is 4,982,565 tons, an increase of 1,000.000 tons, On Monday a colliers' conference was held at Netherton, 6,000 colliers being represented. It was unanimously agreed that other district should be helped to overthrow the sliding scale, and that no overtime should be worked in order to secure the district from over-production. Further, it was

-- deemed advisable to play Monday for the future. A letter has been addressed to the Iron Trades Employers' Association (Liverpool branch), by a committee consisting of representatives of the Amalgamated Eagitteers', Steam En- gine Makers' and Metal Plainers' Societies, requesting an advance in wages equal to 73/4 per cent. on present rates, the said advance to date from the 16th inst. The committee state that they feel justified, by the present great activity in every branch of the trade, in asking such an advance. A NEW TRADE WITH AMERICA.—A new spring trade has developed between the North of Scotland and America in tlee export of seed potatoes; and on Sunday the steamer Limos& sailed from Aberdeen for New York with 2,000 tons of "Champions." The cargo is consigned by farmers in the Aberdeen district, and are cleared for about 365. per ton. The duty at New York is £l, and the price expected to be realised in the American markets is from £4 to £4 103. per ton. This is the first venture in the trade by Aberdeen agents. THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE.—Manchester, Wednes- day.—Lancashire makers of pier iron report having secured fair orders recently in Staffordshire, but there are very few new inquiries coming in from this district, and although for delivering equal to Manchester they are still quoting nominally, 495. to 50s. per ton, less 2.A. per cent, for forge and foundry qualities, they would be open to offers at under these figures. In district brands of pig iron very low prices are now being quoted, and Lincolnshire in some cases is offered at 475. 6d. to 48s. We less 21,e per cent. for forge and foundry qualities delivered in this district. Finished iron is easier, and although a few of the leading makers are still holding firmly for £7 per ton for bars delivered into the Manchester district, in some eases where makers, although well sold, are short of specifications orders for prompt delivery would be booked at £6 17s. Gd. or even as low as £6 15s. per ton. The leading engineering firms in the dis- trict continue well employed. THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.—Manchester, Wednes- day.—There is no very material change in the coal trade of this district since the reductions in price announced last week. In the Manchester district some of the colliers have now been put on short time, whilst in the West Lancashire dis- trict a limitation of the output to three or four days per week is becoming very general. The winter is also closing, with large stocks in hand, both under load, on the colliery sidings, and in many cases on the pit banks, and the pros- pects for the ensuing summer are anything but encouraging from a colliery proprietor's point of view. The average prices at the pit mouth remain as quoted last week—the better qualities of round coal Bs. 61. to Os.; seconds, 69. Cxl. to 75.; common coal, ss. to 65.; burgy, 43. Gd. to ss. ; and good slack, 3s. Gd. to 4s. per ton. Here and their collieries are tolerably busy with orders for shipment, but the ship- ping trade generally is very dull, and extremely low prices are quoted both at Gerston and Liverpool. Coke is in fair demand at about late rates. TEE CORN TRADE.—The 31-arl-lane Express says:— 'The rainfall has been heavy enough to cause trouble from flood water, and generally to make heavy soils unworkable for a time. Wheats and other autumn-sown crops now begin to show more rapid growth, but the colour remains good, and they are now only fortunately forward at the commencement of March. As a whole they are not at all dangerously so for the time of the year, which may be said to have fairly overtaken them. Deliveries of native wheat have fallen off considerably, and some of last week's markets have been poorly supplied with farmers' offerings; nevertheless, the demand continues very restricted, and prices continue to droop. Flour, too, comes continually cheaper. excepting, perhaps, better makes, which are not plentiful enough to share to the fullest extent the general downfall of values. Finest descriptions of barley maintain the extreme rates which have been quoted for some time past, but the inquiry is scarcely so good as it has keen for malting samples, whilst rates for malt begin to show weak- ness. Choice samples of native oats are in request, and old. winters are particularly scarce and dear. Beans and peas show no change. Trade for foreign wheats off stands all over the country has continued to droop." THE LABOUR MARKET.—The labour market is hardly in so active a state as it has been for some weeks past. In Lancashire there is a considerable amount of short time re- sorted to in the cotton trade, and in some branches of the iron trade there is a temporary slackness. At Birmingham orders are again more plentiful, and tinplate workers are busier. Wireworkers are well engaged. At Wolverhampton all the works are steadily employed, and at the leading ports shipbuilders are still busy. At Sheffield the electro- plate and silver trader show some improvement, but the coal trade is dull. At Swansea the tinplate workers are restrict- ing the outpat by one day in the week, otherwise the South Wales industries are well employed. Engineers and iron- founders throughout the country are generally well em- ployed, and there is a considerable demand for fitters and pattern makers at several centres. In London the miscel- laneous trades are fairly employed, but there has been a demonstration of unemployed labourers asking for emigra- tion and other special measures on their hebalf. The postal telegraph clerks are again agitating for better terms of ser- vice, and several sections of workers are unsettled. Advices from the 'United States show that agricultural operations have commenced some weeks earlier than usual in lowa and other North-Western States. Chinese immigration is again being vigorously resisted in the Western States. The build- ing trades in New Zealand are again more active.— Labore. News.
