div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. I

The moathly meeting was held on Monday. Dr. Steele presided. and there were also present Messrs. Norman, Lake, Williams, Taylor, P. Speakman, Shaw, Meadowcroft, Hand- ley, Rhodes-, Briscoe, Taylor, Fisher, Hazlehurst, McDougall, J.J. Speakman, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes (secretary), Barker (surveyor), Mouritz (medical officer). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. Mouritz presented his monthly report, which stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month was 31; and three had occurred at Halton- within-Runcorn, making the total 23. Of these seven were due to bronchitis, six to senile decay, four to abdominal complaints, four to diseases of the nersous system, three to diseases of the heart, two to diseases of the lungs, two to premature birth, two to scarlatina, and two to phthisis. Masks and gangrene accounted one each, representing a death rate of 28 per thousand per annum. Sixteen deaths had occurred amongst children of five years and under, and 12 under one year. Three inquests had been held. HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE. It appeared from the minutes of this committee that Mr. Beasley, formerly tenant of Waterloo House, had taken out a summons to obtain an inspection of the Commissioners' minute book; and the committee recommended that the law clerk provide that gentleman with an extract from the minutes. The surveyor reported that he had sunk down to the bottom of the fountain water shaft in Ellesmere-street, and let off the stagnant sediment. It had also been resolved that a manhole should be built, so as to get at the discharge pipe when required in future, without having to excavate. Mr. NORMAN moved, and Mr. P. SPEAKMAN seconded, the

adoption of the minutes. Mr. SHAW was of opinion that it would be wise to let Mr. Beasley see the minute book, in order to save law expense. Mr. LAKE said that if Mr. Beasley were not satisfied with the offer made by the committee he could exercise the powers granted to him under an order to inspect the

Minutes: The resolution in favour of adopting the minutes was carried, with a slight alteration (suggested by Mr. llazle- burst) as to an agreement to be entered into with Mr. W. ..`Ratham, concerning 11 houses in Leinster-street. THE COMMISSIONERS AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD. The Canal Boats and Hospital Ccmmittee's minutes showed that a letter had been received from the Local Government Board enquiring whether the Commissioners desired a loan in respect of the proposed hospital, and stating that the London Board would defer dealing with the proposal as to Waterloo House until the Commissioners were in a position to determine the purpose for which they desired to use it. The committee recommended that a reply should be sent stating that the Commissioners did not desire to take up a new loan, as they had an unexpended balance in hand. They also suggested that the requisite furni- ture, &c., should be provided for the hospital at the ferry pier. After a conversation on the subject of the minutes, it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. TAYLOR, that they should be passed, with the exception of the part relating to Waterloo House, which it was agreed should be considered at the termination of the meeting, in committee.

div.head: PROPERTY OWNERS AND EXPENSES AT FIRES.
div.p: PROPERTY OWNERS AND EXPENSES AT FIRES.

It appeared from the minutes of the General Purposes Committee that a correspondence had taken place with the assessor to the Queen Insurance Co. in respect to the charge for the services of the firemen in connection with the recent fire in Regent-street. Instructions had been given to the secretary to state that unless the account were paid at once it would be charged to the owner of the property. Dr. McDouGALL, in moving that the minutes be passed, remarked that for some considerable time the committee had been under the impression that they had no power to charge costs out of pocket in cases where fires had been ex- tinguished. It, however, appeared that this idea was a mis- taken one, as a case had just been decided in which it was clearly proved that a local authority had power to make owners of property pay such costs. Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion, and it was carried. NEW DISTRICT RATE.-THE FREE LIBRARY.

The Finance Committee reported that tenders had been received for the construction of Ashbridge-street and Per- cival-lane. They recommended that a letter should be sent to the Gas Co. relative to the price charged for gas supplied to the stieet lamps. They also submitted the estimates for the ensuing year, recommending that a general district rate of 2s. in the pound be made, which is estimated to produce £4,105. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN moved the adoption of the minutes, and said that last year the Board decided upon a rate of Is. 9d. in the pound, but this arose from the fact that they had a considerable balance at the bank. In reply to a ques- tion, the speaker said the library rate was included in the 2s. Mr. FISHER seconded the resolution. Dr. MCDOUGALL raised a point, which is not of general interest, as to the Finance Committee having, in his opinion, usurped the powers of the General Purposes Committee in proposing to write to the Gas Co. The speaker argued that the company had lately treated the Commissioners in a very fair spirit. Mr. SHAW contended that Dr. McDougall was not in order in making such observations. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN said the committee wished to econo- mise, and they thought it was possible to get a reduction on the £2 2s. charged by the Gas Co. for each lamp. Mr. HANDLEY observed that the price per lamp at Widnes was 575. _ _ _

Mr. MEADowcßorr was of opinioa that the Finance Com- mittee should Rot be debarred from discharging their duty because the General Purposes Committee had neglected theirs. (Laughter.) Mr. HANDLEY proposed, and Mr. BRISCOE seconded, that the suggestion as to writing the letter be referred to the General Purposes Committee. Messrs. Handley, Briscoe, and McDougall, were the only members who supported the amendment, which was declared lost. .

-Mr. MEADOWCROFT said that Mr. Speakman's statement to the Board on the question of finances was very meagre. He also was at a loss to know why a Is. 9d. rate would not have been sufficient this year, when it appeared that £253 less had to be provided for in the coming twelve months. The general commercial condition of the community in Runcorn could not be considered any better now than it was a year ago, and yet it was intended to increase the rate. He was much surprised that the committee proposed to raise i'l7l by the Library Rate, as he understood at'the public meeting held on the question that the expenses would not exceed £6O or £7O per annum. He moved that the Library Rate be reduced one-half. Mr. HANDLEY believed it could be clearly proved that the is. 9d. rate had been found sufficient during the past year, not because of the balance at the bank but because of the absolute cessation of all improvements in the town. As to Mr. Meadowcroft's amendment, it was not competent for the Board to do any other than provide a rate at one penny in thee, though it did not follow that the sum thus raised would be spent. The CHAIRMAN drew the attention of the Board to the het that the amendment had not been seconded. Dr. MCDOUGALL thought the chairman of the Finance Committee might well exclaim "Save me from my friends." (Laughter.) Mr. Handley had put the matter in a nut shell. He (the speaker) did not think a 2s. rate in a town like Runcorn could be considered a very heavy one. The motion for the adoption of the minutes was ulti- mately agreed toovith the addition of a suggestion from Mr. P. SPEARMAN to the effect that in future the Board should so advertise in the case of street making that if they thought necessary they could macadamisa them instead of letting contractors do the work. BYE-LAWS REVISION.
On the motion of Mr. LAKE, seconded by Mr. NORMAN, Messrs. Fisber, Hazlehurst, Briscoe, and P. Speakman were added to the Bye-Laws Revision Committee. LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

This body reported that the Rev. J. Barclay bad been ap- pointed chairman. It had been resolved that Mr. J. D. Jones, Penketh-lane, should be appointed librarian and secretary to the committee. Mr. D. Worthington had re- signed, and it was recommended that Mr. Charles Pownall be appointed in his placs. Mr. G. Rhodes having also re- signed, in consequence of having been elected a Commis- sioner, it was recommended that Mr. J. R. Frith be elected to till the vacancy. The committee were of opinion that the Commissioners' Board room was the most suitable locality for the Public Library, and they requested that the Board would permit them to use the room, temporarily, for that

purpose. Mr. TACKP considered there was danger of the Board not preserving their balance of power on the committee, and they ought to carefully guard this privilege, as it would ba a matter ot considerable importance in the case of a division upon any important question. Mr. SHAW had a strong objection to electing anyone as librarian and proposing to fix his salary after he had been appointed. Such a proposal was most unbusiness-like. He moved that Mr. Rhodes be retained on the committee, and Mr. Frith elected in the place of Mr. Worthington. Mr. NORMAN: Hear, hear. That will be a good appoint- ment.

Mr. SHAW said that Mr. Rhodes had long been connected with the town's subscription library and the BOOK Depart- ment at the Literary Institute and be had an amount of ability which would do them Li credit. Dr. McDougall proceeded to deliver an explanatory speech, but it was ultimately agreed, on the proposition of Mr. Shaw, seconded by Mr. Lake, that the recommendations should be referred back for reconsideration. DII.3IDOUGALL'S MOTION.

The Cnernmor said the next bn-;in-e-s-s'.a.vas the considera- tion of the resolution of which notice had been given by Dr. McDougall, "That the resolution of the Board passed on the 6th day of February last, confirming the minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee of February 2nd, so far as they relate to the approval of the Bridgewater Trustees' plans of proposed greets on the Sprincb, on land near the Old Quay, and in Cooper's Field, be revoked." .Dr. McDouGALL then asked that certain correspondence ' which had passed between the representatives of the Board and those of the Bridgewater Navigation Company should be r aad. The letters having been read, Dr. McDouaaLL remarked that the original plan submitted was very imperfect, but it now showed the street as 30 feet wide. Seeing that the object he had in view, when he gave notice of the motion, had been gained, he, with the consent of the Board, would withdraw it. It was then decided, on the motion of Mr. Handley, to adjourn the meeting to the 14th inst., at seven p.m., when it is proposed to discuss the letter received from the Local Government Board referred to in the Hospital minutes.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT,
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT,
MOND/Y.—Before Messrs. H. Gaskell, junr., and George

Pilkington. ANOTHER COAL STEALER CAUGHT.—Martha. Hough, was charged with stealing 56 lbs. of coal, the property Of the London and North Western Railway Co., from a Widnes siding. On Saturday morning, P.C. Skinner was on duty in the siding, and he saw the prisoner standing on a wagon from which she was throwing coal to the ground, on which was a half-filled bag. He took her into custody. She was sent to prison one month, with hard labour. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brock (chairman), H. S. Hall, George Pilkington, Holbrook Gaskell, senr., and Holbrook Gaskell, junr. A DISTURBANCE IN THE UNICORN VAULTS.—Michael Doulan, and Patrick Rabbitt were summoned for being drunk and refusing to quit the Unicorn Vaults, Moss Bank, Moss Bank-road, kept by James Cane.—P.C.'s 1,169, and Pitt gave evidence to the effect that on the .23-d ult., at about ten minutes to eleven at night, they heard a great distur- bance in the public-house, and, on entering, saw the land- lord struggling with one of the defendants. The man was requested to leave, but he refused, and he and his companion were only put out with great difficulty. Each defendant was fined 10. and costs. PUTTING PARAFFIN OIL ON A FIRE.—John Beattie was summoned for permitting the chimney of his dwelling-house, in West-street, to be on fire. An officer was called who proved visiting the defendant's house, and finding that the chimney had been set on fire through his throwing paraffin oil upon the fire.—Defendand admitted his guilt, and pleaded in extenuation, that he was led to throw the oil upon the wood in the fire-place, as it was so damp that it would not burn.—The Chairman said this was a different case to those which came before them at times, in which people were charged with permitting their chimneys to be on fire, and defendant must be taught that he could not pursue such a course with impunity. He would be fined 55., and ss. costs.

THEATRICAL MATTERS IN WIDNES. A NEW VERSION OF THE PLAY OF "THE RIVALS."— MR. KERSHAW AND HIS TWO TENANTS. Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, addressing the Bench, said they had been summoned to a special sessions for the purpose of considering an application for a license to perform stage plays in a building which it was proposed to erect upon a vacant piece of land in Bold-street. Mr. Russell was called, and said he was the applicant in this case. He occupied the position of manager to a com- pany of players known by the name of the Pavilion Theatre Company. Mr. Beasley said he appeared to oppose the application, and he cross-examined the witness, who said the building would be put up on the land which immediately adjoined the Drill, or Volunteer Hall, and it would front into Bold- street. The company were in the habit of performing various kinds of plays, amongst which were those of Shakspeare and Bulwer Lytton, and all the pieces of the Dramatic Authors' Society. The building was a portable one, and he had it in Widnes about six years ago. He was quite willing to con- form to any rules laid down by the justices. Superintendent Barker, in reply to the Bench, handed in a communication, dated the 14th inst., from the superintendent of the police at Hyde, stating that he had much pleasure in bearing testimony to the excellent manner in which the Pavilion Company's theatre had been conducted there. During the whole time not the slightest disturbance had taken place. Mr. Beasley: I appear to oppose the application, gentle- men. (To witness) To whom does this building belong? Witness: It is my own property. Mr. Beasley : I appear for Mr. Sansom, stationmaster to the London and North-Western Railway Company at Widnes (who is resigning his post). The Chairman: Mr. ;horn. Mr. Beasley : Mr. Sansom. The Chairman: We want to know what is tke ground of your objection? Mr. Beasley: If you will first allow me to examine the applicant, I shall be able to state that presently. Cross-examination continued: Witness was not prepared to admit that such plays as "Dick Turpin," or "The mur- der in the Red Barn" would be produced at his theatre. The entrance to the building would be about four yards below the Waterloo-road thoroughfare. Mr. Beasley submitted that Mr. Russell's application must fall of the ground, as the Bench could not grant a license in respect of a piece of waste land. The license must be granted to a building of some kind. Mr. Lewin ruled that Mr. Beasley's objection was not a valid one. Mr. Beasley said the notice of the applicant was for a license to perform stage plays upon a certain piece of land. In fact, that document formed the groundwork of the whole case. Mr. Gaskell, sen., remarked that the notice which the magistrates had received from their clerk was to the effect thit a special sessions would be held for the purpose of granting a license for the performance of stage plays, in. a booth to be erected on a piece of land situate in Bold-street, Widnes.

Mr. Beasley: That is the notice to you, but the law re- quires that the applicant shall give a2l days' notice. The license asked for occupies exactly the same position as if it were required for a public-house. I submit that you can- not grant it, for the Act says that you are only empowered to grant a license to a house or other building. Mr. Gaskell, ten.: It is to grant a license to a house to be erected on a piece of land mentioned in the notice. The Clerk: Yes, and the applicant comes before you, and ' then tells you what he wants. Mr. Beasley: I think you will find in the form given by Oke, in his Magisteeial Synopsis-- The Clerk: It is only a clerical error. Mr. Beasley: Oh, no it is not, and you would not say it was so if the application were in respect to a spirit licence. The Clerk: I shall rule that it is as I have stated. The Chairman asked Mr. Beasley to proceed with the

case. In reply to other questions, the Applicant said he called the structure referred to a building, bat it might be described as a booth. Mr. Beasley drew the attention of the Bench to this admis- sion on the part of Mr. Russell. Mr. Gaskell, see.: Well, "a rose by any other name would smell as sweet." (Laughter.) Mr. Beasley observed that there were other grounds on which he had to oppoie the application. He maintained that if the building were placed at the top of Bold-street, it would prove an intolerable nuisance. Mr. Gaskell, sen. : But we are told that the entrance will not be in the main thoroughfare, but in Bold-street. Mr. Beasley : That may be the applicant's present in- tention.

Mr. Gaskell, sen.: But we can limit him to that. Mr. Beasley: Your worships clearly understand that the pieces to be performed will no doubt be of a sensational character,—pieces in which criminals-- Mr. Gaskell, sen.: Mr. Beasley, you are appearing for a rival applicant, are you not? Mr. Beasley: Your worship is quite justified in saying 1 MAL Mr, Gaskell, sen.: I believe your client is going to apply for a license to be granted to the Drill Hall. Mr. Beasley: No, the Drill Hall is already licensed for the performance of stage plays. and Mr. Kershaw has let the present applicant land which immediately adjoins, on which to erect this theatre. Mr. Gaskell, sen., referred to the fact that Mr. Russell had intimated that the plays to be performed would include those of the Bard of Avon. and he scarcely saw how Mr. Sansom was to produce any of a higher class. (Laughter.) Mr. Beasley: Mr. Sansorn intends to produce Sheridan's and Shakspeare's plays, and pieces by other eminent drama tists. Mr. Gaskell, sen.: And the applicant mentions Bulwer Lytton's. Mr. Beasley: Those who would attend the Drill Hall would be an entirely different class from the frequenters of such a place of amusement as that which belongs to Mr. Russell.

Mr. Gaskell, sen., pointed out that the superintendent of police at Hyde said that the pieces produced by the appli- cant there had been of a good character and tone. Mr. Beasley: I admit all that, but they have a very different class of population in Hyde to what we have in Widnes. .

Mr. Gaskell, sen.: Do you mean to say that the popula- tion of this district are not to have any theatre? Mr. Beasley: No, I don't say that. Mr. Gaskeil, sea.: What is the nature of your argument, then? Mr. Russell is proposing to bring a theatre into the district. If he was askin, us to grant him a license for something that people would not attend, he would put him- self out of court.

Mr. Beasley: I will not labour this part of my case further, but, in justice to Mr. 'Sansom, [must explain that some days ago Mr. Kershaw let him the Volunteer Hall, which k licensed for the performance of stage plays; and directly- he has done so he lets the land immediately ad- joining to Mr. Russell, and so brings him into competition. Mr. Gaskell, sen.: You have competition in your pro- fession, and we have it in our trade, and why should there not he competition ? Mr. Beasley : The place where it is proposed to erect the theatre is close to the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel. Mr. Gaskell, Ben.: And vet your own client -- Mr. Beasley: Yes, but 1 say again, his audiences would be of a different class altogether from those which would frequent the applicant's building. Mr. Sansom has had to g.o to the court at St. Helens this morning, or he would have been here to conduct his own case. lam instructed by him. Mr. Gaskell, sen.: I beg your pardon for interrupting you, but you are laying your arguments before us, and I want you to see bow these arguments strike us, so that you may have an opportunity of meeting the objections. Mr. Beasley : But your worships have all seen these theatrical booths that go from place to place, and it is per- fectly well known that theatres of this kind which have been here before, have only been attended by the very lowest of the population. Mr. Gaskell, sen. : That is an argument that does not touch me, for one. I think that the lowest population are entitled to amusement, if it is not of a vicious nature, or immoral character. Mr. Beasley considered that, at any rate, the place of amusement should be put where it would not be a nuisance. If a license was granted to the applicant's building, hundreds of the lowest of the population would be brought together three, and it would not be safe for respectable females to pass.
- Mr. Gaskell, see.: But these performances are not on the Sabbath Day when the places of worship are open.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY MARCH 11, 1832
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY MARCH 11, 1832

The Chairman: Mr. Beasley, that argument of yours would apply to any other place of amusement where the lower class of population would attend. Mr. Russell : We are always in the habit of having a policeman on the premises. In Hyde we paid monthly for an officer wbo was present every night. Mr. Beasley said that he did not know that he need say anything more. He then br:etly recapitulated the arguments which he had laid before the magistrates. Mr. Gaskell, sen. : Have you any plans of the building?

Mr. Russell: No, sir. _ _ Mr. Gaskell, sen. : Will you undertake to erect a building to the satisfaction of the local authorities in Widnes, as respects ingress and egress? Mr. Russell : Yes, we always do so. In reply to a further question from the same magistrate, the applicant stated that the structure he proposed to put up was 96ft. long and 46ft. wide. There were front and second seats, a raised gallery and the place would hold about 1,200 people. In answer to Mr. Lewin, the applicant said he had the same building in Widnes some 6 years ago, and it was put up at the side of the Wellington Inn, at the back of Waterloo- road. Mr. Hall said he remembered the structure, which was a suitable one for the purpose. Mr. Samuel Owens, estate and insurance agent, of No. 50, Victoria-road, opposed the granting of the license, on the ground that he lived within a few yards of the spot where it was proposed to erect the building. He had been in court on other buitness, and this was the first he had heard of the pro- posal. He felt sure that if it had been publicly known that such an application was to be made, there were several other tenants living near to him who would strongly have opposed

it. _ Mr. Gaskell, sen. : Never mind the others ; speak for yourself. Witness: Well, I oppose it on moral and religious grounds. I submit that the granting of the license will very materially injure the neighbourhood. There is likely to be considerable disorder, and on Saturday night I shall have to submit to the clamour and noise which form the accompaniments connected with such a place. lam sorry that I have not had more notice about what it was intended to do. It is a building that we can do very well without in Victoria-road. Mr. Lewin: Are you a member at the Wesleyan Chapel? 1 Witness: I am. Mr. Lewin: And Mr. Cummings is your minister? Witness: Yes. Mr. Lewin: Does be know about this application? ' Witness: I don't know.

In reply to a question from Mr. Gaskell senr., witness said there were only two houses between him and the spot where the building would be put up. Mr. Gaskell, sen. : Your first objection is a personal one, that it will be an annoyance to you; and next you object on moral and religious grounds, which objection will apply to all theatrical performances. Witness: I object more especially as Victoria-road is a main thoroughfare. Mr. Gaskell, sen. : That is a local, and not a moral or religious objection. Witness: I submit that there are several of my neigh- bours who, if they kmew about this. matter, would like to appeal against the granting of the license. , Mr. Barnard Dutton, auctioneer, living at Helsbv, said he was the proprietor of a-place of business at No. 2, Oakland- street, Widnes, and he opposed the application as one of the trustees of the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Victoria-road. He-had only been made acquainted with the fact that the application was to be made whilst listening to the proceed- ings, and,-of course, under such circumstances, he had not been able to communicate with his co-trustees, and take united action, but, individually, he should decidedly oppose the application. The Chairman: Then you simply oppose it as a trustsb of the Wesleyan Chapel? Witness : Yes. The Chairman asked if there was any other objector; but no one came forward.

Superintendent Barker was asked if he wished to offer any objection, on which he said he had not, because during his long experience as a police officer, he had found that theatres were rather a gaod thing in a town than otherwise. The reason of this was that they often attracted young fellows who would otherwise be found in public-houses and who would be far better in a well-conducted theatre than in such

places, where they frequently took too much todrink,and be- came disorderly. Theatres had often the effcct of causing drunkenness to decrease in a town; and, in fact, the only persons he had known to suffer from the fact of their being established, was the publicans. The magistrates retired for a few minutes, and on their return into court, Mr. Brock, addressing Mr. Russell, said : We have considered this matter, and we are unanimous in our decision to grant your application. Mr. Russell then entered into sureties to see that the necessary rules for the good management of the theatre were observed, himself in £lOO, and Messrs. Thos. Gerrard and Wm. Lomax in £5O each. Before Mr. Brock (chairman) and Mr. G,Pilkington.

A VIOLENT YOUNG WOMAN. Mary Cullen, young woman, was charged with assaulting P.C. Pitt, by striking him on the face whilst he was ejecting some men from the Moss Bank public-house, on the 27th ult.—Defendant pleaded guilty, and Superintendent Barker said he had no desire to press the case against her.—The Chairman said she would be fined is. and 7s. ed. costs, and he hoped this would be a warning to her not to interfere with a policeman in the execution of his duty in future. VANDALISM IN WIDNES.-Wm. Riley and John Howard were summoned for wilfully damaging a fire grate in a house belonging to Thos. Hargreaves, on the 23rd ult.— Mr. Owens, agent for the property, prosecuted, and said !that a great amount of this class of damage was done to Iproperty in the town. He called Martin Quinn, who said that he saw Riley in the house, but he did not actually see him injuring the grate, which had been partly pulled down. The oven had also been dislodged from its proper position. —The magistrates did not see that there was sufficient evi- dence upon which to convict, and they dismissed the sum- mons against Riley, but adjourned the hearing of the one against the other defendant until Wednesday next, as it was intimated that a witness could be called who would clearly substantiate the charge against him.—Michael Lee and Jno. Wynn were charged with having done wilful damage to a house, the property of Mr. Mclntyre, by breaking nine win- dows, and damaging a brick wall.—Evidence was given as to the windows having been broken and the wall consider- ably damaged, but the magistrates did not consider it sufficient strong to convict, and the summonses were dis- missed.
YESTERDAY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell and John Brock.

STEALING COAL.—John Cooney, a lad, was convicted, on the evidence of P.C. Murray, of having, en the previous evening, stolen 36ibs. of coal, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company, from a crane on the canal bank.—Prisoner was sentenced to receive Six strokes with a birch rod. ASSAITLT.—James Heath, charged with assaulting Mary Norcott, was ordered to find sureties, himself in £2O and two sureties in £5 each. to keep the peace three months.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit.

A STRANGE CASE.—ALLEGED THEFT OF A FLAT AT WESTON.—James Bushell, a waterman, living in the Hol- loway, who a few days ago was committed for trial at the ' sessions by the Chester county magistrates, was charged ' with having, on the 21st ult., at Weston, stolen a flat known by the name of the Earl, 400Ibs. of rope, a mainsail, foresail, foghorn, three lamps, two anchors, two chains, and other articles, all the property of Messrs. Richard Sutton, Pear- son, and Co.—Joseph Taylor, outdoor overlooker to the pro- secutors, who are flat owners and timber brokers, of 34, James-street, Liverpool, said his masters possessed a flat known as the Earl, which traded between Weston and Liver- pool. The cap.aiu was named Samuel Nash, and the prisoner had. newer been in the employ of the firm.—Samuel Nash stated,that he had been captain of the vessel for about six months, and on Monday, the 20th ult., it was in the canal at Weston Point, near to the Weston Chemical Works. At nine o'clock in the morning she was safely moored, and he went away, leaving ono of his hands, whose name was Carter, in charge. He went to Weston Point on the Wednes- day moraine-, and found that the flat had been taken away. He proceeded to Liverpool, and gave information at his em- ployers' office as to what had Gccurred, and, from what he afterwazds heard, he went to New Brighton, but could not Ind the vessel. He next journeyed •to Ellesmere Port, which is about eight miles from Weston Point, and there found the flat on the beach, where it afterwards remained for about eight days. On going upon the vessel he saw the prisoner, and asked him why he had taken the flat from Weston. Bushell replied that some one had given him charge, or something to the same effect, and he (prisoner) tried to get the flat off, but he could not do so, as the tide was not in. Prisoner was the sole person on board. He (witness) remained there until high water, but could not get the vessel off. Prisoner went ashore about two hours after he went on board. The different articles mentioned in the cllarge were safe on the flat when he last saw her at Weston Point, but some of them were missing when he went upon , her at Ellesmere Port. Amongst the articles missing were a head rope, a lock rope, two spring ropes, two small lines, , half a barrel line, the topsail, halyards, the peak, and the main halyards. There was a farmhouse near to where the boat was on shore, and there he found the peak and main , halyards. He had previously noticed the prisoner visiting the house.—John Turner, stonemason' Weston Point, said that on the 21st ult., whilst near the chemical works at Weston, he saw the prisoner on board the flat Earl, which was at that time in the canal. Bushell shouted to him to get on board, and ride down. The vessel was then adrift, and he jumped on board. Just at that time there was a steam tug

cominE,, down the canal, and one of the men upon it called to the prisoner to give him a rope, and he did so. He rode with Bushell as far as Weston Point, and then went on shore. He afterwords helped the prisoner to take tilt vessel into the basin at Weston, where she was made fast,

and he went ashore with Bushell, who remarked that he was going to Eastham for a cargo of salt.—James Dickens, dock- labourer, Weston Point, said that on the 21st ult., he was at the side of the basin where the flat was lying, and the prisoner came to him and asked him if he wanted work. On saying "Yes," Bushell asked him if he would go with him to Eastham to load the flat with sand. He agreed, and went with three other men, on the same day. They got the flat into the river, hoisted sail, and went down to Ellasrnere Port, the vessel being steered by Bushell. At Ellesmere Port it came on very foggy, and the flat got aground. He and the other men found that the prisoner had nothing to eat on beard, and Bushell went to a grocer's shop, and ordered about 10s. worth of provisions, but when the shop- keeper discovered he had no money, he would not permit them to have the goods. He and the other men then returned _

to Weston Point, leaving the prisoner in charge of the tlessel.—P.C. Wilkinson, of Ellesmere Port, said that on the following Friday morning he toGk the prisoner into custody on the pier-head at Ellesmere Port, and, on being charged, he told him the flat belonged to his mother, as he would find upon inquiry.—Prisoner, who had nothing to say in defence, was committed to the Chester Sessions for trial.—The damage done to the flat amounts to £2O. THURSDAY.—Before Messrs. John Brundrit (chairman)
The minutes were confirmed

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Messrs. Henry Reynolds (chairman) and
C. W. Hazfehurt.

TRANSFER DAY.—The following transfers were granted: —Alehouse. Fleetwood Arms, Church-street, from George Saunders (deceased) to his widow, Martha Saunders. Beer- houses :—Welsh Harp, Cooper-street, from William Water- worth to Robert Beech ; Rose and Crown, Mersey-street, from Michael Thomas Lavelle to Thomas Finnegan. and the Angel Inn, from ,Thomas Hodgkinson to Michael Ryan. —The licence held in the name of Mr. Isaac Speakman, Bridge-street, for the sale of wine, spirits, and beer, was transferred to Mr. Philip Speakman. THE FAMILY TROUBT ES OF A MEMBER OF THE SAL- VATION ARMY. George Oultram and Isaac Bignall, the younger, were summoned for assaulting Isaac Bignall, sen. —Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the defence.—The com- plainant, who is a middle-aged man, living in a street off Cemetery-road, stated that be left home for two days in consequence of a dispute with his wife, caused through his having chastised his son for insulting the Salvation 'Army. He returned on the 18th ult., and a conversation took place between him and his wife, on which the defendants (the elder being his stepson) entered the hoase in a very excited state. His own son lifted a poker which he brandished in his face and afterwards hit him on the shoulders and the head with it. The blow on the skull was so severe that a wound four inches in length was inflicted. Whilst this was going on, his wife came downstairs and shouted " Give it him now you are at it." Defendants continued to beat him some time, and finally ran off to Widnes, and did not return that night.—A young man named Jciseph Santley said he saw complainant come out of the house on the evening mentioned, and he was covered with blood, and said his sons had been kicking and beatit.g him about the head with a poker.--Complainant was then charged, on cross-sum- monses, wail having assaulted his wife, his son Isaac, and his stepson, George Oultram.—Mr. Linaker appeared for the complainants, and called Mrs. Bignall, who said that after her husband returned home, on the evening of the 18to ult., he sat down, and remained mute for an hour and a half, and then began to quarrel, stating that site should never have any more of his money. She went up- stairs out of his way, but he followed her, threw her down on the floor, and struck her on both her shoulders. He likewise cursed her, and used language which she should be ashamed to repeat.—Mr. Linaker asked if it was such as was fit for a soldier in the Salvation Army to use—Witness: I No, sir; it was very bad language.—Geo. Oultram said that lon entering the house during the evening, his step father struck him a violent blow with the poker, and also hit his brother. In the course of the struggle which followed, de- fendant fell with his head against the sofa. Neither of the defendants touched the poker.—lsaac Bignall and Emily Jane Bignall also gave evidence.—Joseph Santley was called on behalf of defendant. —Superintendent Williamson 'stated that when defendant came to the police-station to lodge a complaint against his son, his (defendant's) head i was covered with blood.—Mr Linaker contended that it was quite evident the elder Bignall was a man of very eXcitable , temperament, and it had been clearly proved that he coin- menced the disturbance.—The Chairman said the case re- vealed what was evidently an unfortunate family quarrel. Oultram and Bignall jun. would have to enter into sureties to keep the peace towards the father for six months, them selves in £lO. and two sureties of £5 each. The summonses aciainst the elder Bignall would be dismissed, but he would ' be bound over to keep the peace to his wife for six months, , himself in £lO, and two sureties in £5 each. The parties would have to pay their own costs.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

From the Finance Committee's minutes it appeared the receipts for the month were £33 10s., and the following accounts falling due on the 25th inst. were passed for pay- ment :—Oddfallows' Club, Runcorn, £3 18s. 4d.; John Ball, sen., £5 17s. ; Mrs. Kenwright, £9 15s. 10d.; John Hazle- burst, £39 3s. 4d.; other accounts, £2O is. id.; total, £7B 16s. id.

div.head: INTERMENTS.
div.p: INTERMENTS.

The SECRETARY stated that during the month ending Feb. 25th there had been 31 interments, an increase of four on the corresponding period last year. In the 11 months ending; Feb. 25th there were 231 interments, a decrease of 47 com- pared with the corresponding period last year, whilst the receipts had only decreased 135., the fees received amount- ing to £228 10s. 2d.
'There was no other business.

div.head: RFLIGIOUS TRACT SOCIETY,
div.p: THE RFLIGIOUS TRACT SOCIETY,

The annual meeting, in connection with the Religious Tract Society, was held in Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, on Thursday evening. There was only a mode- rate audience, but one considerably larger than attended the last meeting, when only 25 persons put in an appearance. The Rev. J. Yonge presided, and he was supported by the Rev. R. Butcher, district secretary to the society, and the Rev. E. Moore (Baptist).—ln introducing Mr. Butcher to the meeting, the CHAIRMAN said the society was a perfectly unsectarian one, and he confessed that that by itself had for him considerable charm. Denominational objects were right and good, and ought to be sustained by the members of the various denominations with all the energy and principle which they could command, but societies like the Religious Tract Society and the British and Foreign Bible Society, in which Christians of all sects could meet and work together for one common object, he thought were a very happy idea, and a very blessed means of bringing Christians together to realise practically their thorough oneness as servants of a common Master.—The Rev. R. BUTCHER, after expressing his gratification at the good attendance compared with last year's meeting, spoke of the unsectarian character of the society, whose endeavour, he said, was to provide Christian literature or religious truth in small portions, that any and every Christian might distribute the wide world over. Its aim and purpose was to be helpful to every Christian Church to whatever section it might belong. Last year there were 81 millions of different publications issued from the society at home and abroad. These publications were not all written in the English language, but comprised works printed in 140 different languages. No other society was doing such a work. Last year the total trade receipts of the society were £192,000, which, after paying all expenses, left a profit of £13,000. The latter fund formed part of the society's missionary fund—(hear, hear)—froin whence churches, at home and abroad, drew supplies to help them in their evangelical work. But to that amount was to be added £llOOO received in subscriptions and donations,to which Warrington contributed £6 16e. The expenditure during the year had been £16,000 in round numbers. The circula- tion of tracts last year was 24,000,000, and Mr. Butcher related several interesting incidents of the good which had resulted from their distribution. Mr. Butcher went on to describe the work of the society in France, Spain, Belgium, and in Italy. In the latter country, which had been so long under the denomination of Rome, there were 700 Sunday and 1,300 day schools assisted by the society. Referring to the publications of the society, the speaker said the Boys' Own Paper had counteracted much of the impure literature of the day, which had been the cause of so much crime. They would be pleased to know that in six months after the issuing of the Boys' Own Paper. five out seven of the most obnoxious papers published by one firm had ceased to live—(hear, hear,)—and the remainder had now only a very small circulation. The boys and girls in our day schools, ley means of the society, were being trained to have a taste for something better than mere trash and sentiment, and it was felt that with the advanced education of the young, something higher in tone and matter should be produced for their leisure hours. The influence of the Girls' Own Paper had even exceeded that of the boys, and had furnished to many towns most valuable information, and counteracted a good deal of the light and trivial litera- ture provided for girls. The society made grants of libraries to Sunday schools, coffee rooms, and various institutions, and during the year 551 districts, and parishes, and congre- gations had received libraries, either free or at one half the usual price. Grants had been made to 734 Sunday and day schools, 23 workingmen's clubs and coffee rooms, 246 hospitals, workhouses, prisons, and asylums, and 47 sailor and soldier institutions. Ministers were not forgotten, especially poor ones, and 107 ministers on ordination had , received 107 libraries of £lO value at half-price, and 115 ISunday school teachers had received similar grants. Many foreign missionaries had testified that if it were not for the I help they received from the Tract Society they cculd not carry on the work as they did. The society had a short time ago translated an annotated Bible for China, in which country there were 4,000,000 people ready to recieve their teaching. The rev, gentleman concluded with a reference to the society's work in Japan.—The Rev. E. MOORE, in a short address, referred to his experience as a tract distribu- tor in Liverpool and Manchester, and made an appeal for subscriptions to help forward the good work of the society. ' The proceedings concluded with the singing of a hymn, and , a collection was made in aid of the society.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIA.NS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIA.NS.

Mr. S. Marsh presided at the fortnightly meeting, held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday. Present :—Messrs. W. Tyrer, J. T. Hall, John Fidler, C. J. Paris, T. Eatock, S. Rowe, W. Gil body, J. Fisher, J. Jackson, J. Barnacle, J. Lowe, E. Syder, T. Chambers, W. Birchall, J. Matthews, P. Longton, T. Dobell, T. Sadler, W. Gerrard, James Ransom, Wm. Swift, Richard Tuson, E. Birch, J. Penketh, J. Keit- wright, J. Scotson, W. A. Meadows, R. Leigh, J. Buckley, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).

div.head: DELAYED INQUEST.
div.p: A DELAYED INQUEST.

The MASTER reported there were 512 inmates in the House; last week 537; corresponding week last year 550. There were 134 boys and girls in the industrial school. An inquest was held in the House, on the 7th inst., on the body of George Robinson, who was admitted on the 22nd ult., end' died on the 3rd February.—ln reply to Mr. Fidler, Mr. BICKNELL (the Master) said he was not made acquainted that the doctor could not give a certificate of the cause of death until three days after the death, and he immediately acquainted the police.—Mr. FISHER said the Master should have been immediately acquainted that the doctor would not give a certificate.—The MASTER said he could perhaps throw some light upon the matter. Whenever a case like this had arisen, the doctor himself had acquainted him that he could not give a certificate. In the .present instance it had perhaps been an oversight on the doctor's part, and the nurse had probably forgot to remind him of it. He did not think I blame n ei be attached to anyone.—A MEMBER: It seems curious.—The MASTER said he knew the man was dead, but not that the doctor could not certify the cause of death.— Mr. MEADOWS: The inquest ought to have been held sooner. —The MASTER: The police did not inform the coroner on the night I acquainted them, but let it stand over till the next day.—fn reply to a question by Mr. Fidler, the MISTER said if the friends of the deceased, who had lived in St. Helens, had claimed the body, he should not have had any information to prevent him from allowing it to be removed. —The CLERK suggested that a resolution should be passed that the Medical Officer, in any case in which he could not give a certificate of the cause of death, should as soon as possible inform the Master.—Mr. PARIS moved a resolution to that effect, and, having been seconied, it was carried unanimously.

div.head: MR. J. PRESCOT AND THE BOARD.
div.p: MR. J. PRESCOT AND THE BOARD.

The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board stating that Mr. Knott, as assistant district auditor, had reported that at his audit of the accounts of the Pres- cot Union for the half year ended at Lady Day last, he cer- tified the stun of £Bl 16s 9,1 to be due from Mr. J. Prescot, late relieving officer. The Board wished to be in- formed if that sum had been paid to the treasuter of the Union. The Clerk said be had recovered £59; the rest of the money was due to the credit of Mr. Prescot.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF THE TREASURER.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF THE TREASURER.

The CLERK said Mr. J. Chrimes had resigned the position of treasurer. The Board could not make the appointment that day, but must either advertise or give a fortnight's notice, and• in the meantime consider what arrangement should be made as to the terms of the appointment. —On the motion of Mr. TYRER, a committee consisting of Messrs. J. T. Hall, W. A. Meadows, J. Fidler, and W. Tyrer was appointed to consider the matter.

div.head: RE-APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICERS.
div.p: THE RE-APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICERS.

At the suggestion of the CLERK, notice was given of the re-appointment of Dr. Ricketts as medical officer for.Sutten district, and Dr. Tattersall for Hale. Both appointments would expire on the 26th instant.

div.head: PANTASAPH CONVENT SCHOOL.
div.p: PANTASAPH CONVENT SCHOOL.

Mr. FIDLER said the deputation appointed for that pur- pose had visited the Pantasaph Convent School, and the children looked the picture of health. So far as intellectual culture was concerned, the deputation saw some of the work done and he was sure they could not possibly get a similar education in the Workhouse. The state of discipline and conduct in which the children were kept was such as would make them very respectable members of society when they came out.—Mr. LEATHERBARROW and Mr. RANSOM endorsed Mr. Fidler's remarks.—This concluded the business.

div.head: MANIFE,TO BY Mt BRADLAUGH,
div.p: MANIFE,TO BY Mt BRADLAUGH,

Mr. Bradlaugh has written a lengthy address to the majority which on Monday voted in favour of his beitg refused cermission to take the oath, reviewing his whole case from his first election to the latest motion, with a view to showing that he has not been treated as obnoxious mem- bers such as Wilkes, John Archdale, and Daniel O'Connell were treated, Wilkes's opponent having been pronounced to be duly elected, and Archdale and O'Connell having had the oath tendered to them more than once for refusal. He denounces the conduct of the majority as illegal, reiterates that he has never refused to take the oath nor pressed his heretical views upon the House, inveighs against the per- sonal violence that has been used against him, declares— "The struggle you have commenced,l will not abandon; and now I must ask the country, your master and mine, to arbitrate between us. The violence is yours; the defiance is mine. In defying you I obey the law. You are the law- breakers."
The London address of Wm. Cunliffe Brooks, Esq., M.P. for East Cheshire, is No. 5, Grosvenor-square, Lon- don.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The meeting of this authority was held at Dutton on Tuesday, when there were present the Rev. Canon Barclay (chairman), Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Jno. Ashton, Knowles, Highfield, Rigby, Handley, Challoner, Darbyshire, Midwood, Andrews, G. Dansey (Local Government Board Inspector), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). FRODSHAM SEWERAGE SCHEME,—THE ARBITRATION AWARD.—MORE CLAIMS. Mr. LINAKER said he had received the umpire's award in respect to the arbitration between the authority and Mr. E. A. Wright in connection with the Frodsham sewerage scheme. Mr. Wm. Radford, the umpire, awarded Mr. Wright £175 103. 61 compensation, the Authority to pay their own and Mr. Wright's costs. Mr. CIIALLONER : What is the sixpence for, I wonder. Mr. RiGny : A cigar. (Laughter.) Mr. LINAKER said he had received the following letter, dated February 27th, from Messrs. Wright and Morecroft, and he asked for a cheque for the amount named :—" We have this morning tiken up the award of Mr. Radford, and have paid the charges, £95 3s. 2d., on the understanding that a duplicate award has been sent to you, from which you will perceive that you are forthwith to repay to us that amount. We will thank you to send us a cheque. Our costs of the reference shall be sent you in due course." Mr. CHALLONER : Have you any idea what the costs of the counsel will be. Mr. LINAKER SAid he thought the cost of the reference would be about £440, which was the amount which Mr. Wright claimed in the first instance. Mr. DANSEY : You are not much worse off. The CHAIRMAN: And very little better. Mr. CnALLoNEre : I would rather squander it than it should go to Mr. Wright. Mr. ASHTON : It has been stated that notice was not given to Mr. Wright before the works were commenced. I should like it stated officially by the clerk whether that was so or not.

Mr. LINAKER said Mr. Wright was served with a notice similar to the other landowners in 1879, and subsequently with a tracing showing the line of pipes. Mr. ASHTON: The works were not commenced until October, and did he never intimate that he objected to the cutting through his land? Mr. LINAKER : No. Mr. DARBYSHIRE remarked that Mr. Wright did not object to the seheme until the work had gone so far that the Authority could not diverge from the course they had begun. Mr. CIIALLONER: The scheme was passed bv the Local Government Board Inspector as a reasonable thing, and one that ought to be done, and after that we should not go into litigation. I shall certainly move that the thing be referred back to the Local Government Board, informing them that Mr. Wright did not give notice at the proper time, nor until the scheme had been half completed. Mr. RIGBY : He sees the drain, and then he comes upon us.

Mr. CHALLONER said he thought the excuse given by Mr. Wright for his delay—that the water scheme had fallen through, and he thought this would do the same—a very Door one. Mr. MIDWOOD: It is no excuse at all. Mr. LINAKER, in answer to Mr. Rigby, said the award was final. Mr. RIGBY : Then the Local Government Board have no authority in the matter? Mr. LINAKER : No. It is no use being in a false position. If you show a disposition to question the award, Mr. Wright will make it a rule of court. Mr. CHALLONER: He cannot do any more at RS now. Mr. LINAKER : He can enforce payment of the mon2y, and some extra costs upon it. Mr. CHALLONER : I should refer it to the Local Govern- ment Board before it was paid. The CHAIRMAN: It is no use giving ourselves useless trouble. Here is the representative of the Local Govern- ment Board. Mr. DANSEV said that they might refer the matter to the Local Government Board, but they could not help them out of the liability. It could be enforced in a court of law. The CHAIRMAN jocularly remarked that although the Board would have to pay the sum Mr. Wright originally claimed, Mr. Wright would not get the money, and that was a " moral " victory for the Board, if that was any con- solation. • Mr. LINAKER : I ask for a cheque for £95 3s. 21, the charges for taking the award. Mr. CHALLONER: It must stand over—(hear, hear,)—until we write to the Local Government Board. Mr. RIGBY : I would not pay it unless they sent a hill of particulars. (Laughter.) The CLERK: We cannot legally ask for a bill of par- ticulars. Mr. RIGBY : I would not pay it without. The CHAIRMAN: It is no use throwing good money after bad. If the award is made a rule of court, there will be more expense. Mr. ASHTON said the bill was for the costs of the three gentlemen engaged in the arbitration. Mr. CHALLONER: It will cost as much as the whole scbe me. Mr. ASHTON : We need not discuss that now. (Laughter.) Mr. CHALLONER moved that the Clerk write to the Local Government Board placing before them the circumstances for both sides, and asking if the Authority ought to pay any money at all. Mr. MIDWOOD seconded the motion. The CHAIRmAN : Pay this bill before? Mr. BOOBY: No, they will surely trust us a fortnight. The CLERK said he should require the resulutibn in writing, and he should simply forward a copy when passed. He would not take the responsibility. Mr. CHALLONER (hesitatingly): Very well. Mr. MIDWOOD : Stick up. Mr. Challoner handed in a written resolution. Mr. DANSEY said he could not profess to give his opinion on the question of law, but he did not think the Local Go- vernment Board could help them. Mr. RIGBY : Do you think we are compelled to pay this £95?

Mr. DANSEY : I think so. I don't think you can require a bill of particulars. Mr. RlGpy : It is a very loose way of doing business. It is a complete farce. The CLERK remarked that he thought the general cost of the _arbitration would fall upon the common fund of the Union. Mr. RIGBY : No, no. (Laughter.) That won't wash. (Laughter.) Mr. ASHTON (laughing): Frodsham is going to get off better than we expected. (Laughter.) Mr. LINAKER said the Act of Parliament stated the costs consequent upon reference should be in the hands of the arbitrator or umpire, and the umpire had awarded that the Authority should pay its own costs. Mr. DANSEY suggested that the Board should apply to the Local Government Board to have the expenses made special, and fall upon the district benefited by the scheme. This met with almost general approval,but it was pointed out that there was no immediate necessity for taking action in the matter, and none was taken. Mr. Challoner's motion being put to the vote was carried unanimously. Mr. LINAKER : Well, what have I to do about this bill of £95? . _

-- Mr. CHA.LLONER : I move that it stand over. Mr. RIGBY seconded the motion, and it was carried. Mr. LINAYER then read the fallowing letter:— March 6th, 1882.—Gentlemen.—Executors of the late Mr. Thomas Dutt n. Frodsham Lordship scheme.—The Authority will recollect that when notice was given to the late Mr. Dutton of the intention to lay a sewer through his and at Netherton. and when Mr Wright gave notice for arbitration on his claim, Mr. Dutton through us stated that he would defer making his claim until the award in Mr. Wright's case had bean given, and thereby expense would be saved. Toe award in Mr. Wright's case having now been given, and which he informs us is £175, we are instructed by the executors of the late Mr. Dutton to claim the sum of £BO for the eas-ment through their :and, heing calculated at the same rate as the amount awarded to Mr. Wright, the authority to pay the ex- penses in the usual way.—Yours obediently, H. LINA.RER and Box. The reading of this letter was received with gestures of astonishment from some members, and Mr. Rigby caused much laughter by exclaiming "0 ! crikey. It ought to be good water." • Mr. MIDWOOD: It's a sewer. (Laughter.) Mr. RIGBY : Anybody else a claim, Mr. Clerk ? (Laughter.) Mr. LINAKER read 39 follows : Frodsham, March 6th, 1882.—Gentlemen,—I beg to inform you that the laying of the sewerage pipes iS the main street, Frodsham, has taken the water out of my well. (Laughter.) I have been put to considerable expense to get it back but to no purpose. I therefore claim of the Authority the sum of £5 as compensation.—l am, sours respectfully, Ttimuits BATE. Mr. RIGBY : I propose that we throw the " sponge " up entirely. (Laughter.) It is a regular imposition. Mr. MIDWOOD (dubiously) : You said there were no more. Mr. LINAKEE : This only came in this morning, Mr. RIGBY : Any come in this afternoon? (Laughter.) In reply to a member, Mr. LINAKER said Mr. Dutton's land was of the same nature as Mr. Wright's. If the claim was not allowed Mr. Dutton's executOrs would go to arbi- tration. Mr. MCINTYRE moved that the consideration of the claims be deferred for a fortnight, so that the Authority could come to sornlS conclusion as to'the value of the land. Mr. Minwoon seconded the proposition. Mr. DARBYSHIRE considered the claimants' land was im- proved by sewers passing through. Mr. ,SIITON said the Authority ought not to entertain the claim with regard to the well. If they entertained that they should have no end of claims. He should put one in in respect to his own. A 111Emnnst said the well in question was 15 yards from the sewer. It was decided to repudiate the claim for the well. Mr. MCINTYRE said if Mr. Wright got his claim Mr. Dut- ton was entitled to his. The CHAIRMAN : There seems to be a dispute as o whether the ground is of equal value. Mr. CHALLONER said it was far more valuable than Mr. Wright's. It was worth 15s. per acre more. Mr. LIN:MEM : And he is far more prejudiced by the position of the sewer. Mr. DARBYSHIRE said there was one thing about Mr. Dutton's claim—it had come before the Board with far more grace than Mr. Wright's had. A committee was appointed to consider Mr. Dutton's

div.head: and C. W. Hazlehurst.
div.p: and C. W. Hazlehurst.

ROBBERY BY A. SAILOR—James McAulay was charged with stealing A pair of drawers, a singlet, and a pair of stockings, the property of Win. Mcßride, at Weston, on the Tth instant.—Prosecutor said be was a seaman on the schooner, Mary Jane, at present lying at Weston Point, and the prisoner was employed in a similar capacity up to Tues- day last, when he was paid off. Witness had the clothes, mentioned in the charge, on the aft deck of the vessel, on Tuesday last, and he last saw them safe about ten o'clock in the forenoon. McAulay left Between twelve and one o'clock, and about three hours after he missed the things, and went to Runcorn to find the prisoner, but he did not succeed in doing so until Wednesday night, when he and the mate of the vessel discovered him in a public-house. He asked McAulay for his clothes, when he said that if he accused him of taking them "he would plug him," as he bad not got them. He then went for Sergeant Morris, and saw him search the prisoner's bag and find in it The stolen singlet and drawers.—Joseph Pegg, keeper of the Sloop Inn beer- house, Loch-street, where the prisoner had been staying, was also called.—Sergeant Morris gave evidence as to ap- prehending the prisoner, who said he knew nothing about the stolen things, and was quite willing that his box should be searched.—McAulay said that the various articles on the aft deck must have got mixed, and he put the missing things amongst his own, in mistake. He elected to be summarily dealt with, and was sent to gaol 14 days, with hard labour.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
The meeting was held on Wednesday. Present : Messrs. Coleburn (chairman), James Handley, Norman, Rhodes, W. Littler, P. Briscoe, George Moss, W. F. Salkeld (secretary).

div.head: VICAR OF RUNCORN AND PAUPER BURIAL FEES.
div.p: THE VICAR OF RUNCORN AND PAUPER BURIAL FEES.

Mr. HANDLEY moved the adoption of the Finance Com- mittee's minutes, which contained the following :—" In accordance with the order of the last meeting of the Board, the committee have considered the case in which the Rev. Canon Barclay claims the burial fees paid by the relieving officer on„the occasion of the funeral of Alice O'Neil in the Roman Catholic ground, when the Roman Catholic priest officiated. The committee is of opinion that as ministers' fees for all parts of the cemetery are received at the Board's office as a mere matter of convenience, the Board should not recognise any retonsibility in connection with the said fees, and recommend that a letter to this effect be sent by the secretary to the Rev. Canon Barclay." Mr. NonmAs seconded the motion.
The CHAIRMAN remarked that the committee had passed that resolution believing that the Board were not compelled to receive fees either for the vicar or Nonconformists.

Mr. RHODES: It only seems reasonable that the clergy- men should look to those people who employ them. The CHAIRMAN : We as a committee recommend the Board to remove all responsibility from our shoulders. Mr. lIANDLEY : That is all we can do. We decline the responsibility. Mr. BRISCOE: Did the see et try receive these fees for O'Neil? The SECRETARY: Oh, yes. Mr. HANDLEY: From the opening of the cemetery we have always received them. Mr. BRISCOE: But I understand the Secretary has never been authorised to receive them, though he has received them through kindness. The SECRETARY: Oh, no sir. A MEMBER: It is a voluntary arrangement on account of the Burial Board. Mr. RHODES remarked that Canon Barclay considered the Board were under an obligation to receive money from cer- taid persons, and bound to hand it over to him. On whose behalf, he asked, were the fees for the burial of O'Neil received ? Mr. HANDLEY: On behalf of Father Fennellev because he officiated. Mr. BRISCOE: You will now discontinue receiving fees.

Mr. LITTLER: No, no. Mr. Moss said the committee considered that in the event of any litigation ensuing, the Board ought not to be sued, but rather the persons who were liable at common law to pay the fees.
_ Mr. BniscoE : Have you paid the fees to Father Fen- nelley ? _ _
The SECRETARY replied in the affirmative. Mr. BRISCOE: Then the decision doesn't interfere Nvith this case. . .

--- -- Ihe CHAIRMAN said it was not intended to make any alteration in the payment of fees to Mr. Salkeld. They sim- ply repudiated any responsibility. Mr. NORMA.N made some observations to show that it was optional whether;the fees were paid to Mr. Salkeld or to the officiating minister. Mr. RHODES asked if there was any regulation which made it obligatory for the persons to pay the secretary. Mr. MOSS read the following note from Glen :—" The question has been asked as to whether, the fees payable to the incumbent are to be paid to the Burial Board in addi- tion to the charges made by them for leave to build a vault, Jr,c., under this section, or whether they are to be paid directly to the incumbent by the persons using the ground. The Secretary of State for the Home Department is reported to have stated, in reply to a communication addressed to ,1 him on the subject, that the above section does not impose upon burial boards the duty of receiving ecclesiastical fees in respect of the rites performed under this sectiod, and that 'these dues are not payable in addition to the charges by the board."

Mr. HANDLEY said that was confirmed by the board's table of fees, and the Secretary of State would sanction no other payments. The CHAIRMAN read the following clause from the Act of Parliament :—" Dissenting ministers or Roman Catholic clergymen will not be entitled to fees in respect of burials in the cemetery, and if they perform the burial services for the dead body of any of their members they must look to the persons by whom they are retained for any fees they may claim."

lilt% BRISCOE observed that the committee had not given any opinion with regard to the case of O'Neil. Mr. Moss said the committee did not attempt te decide the question between Canon Barclay. Mr.:NORMAN understood the question to stand thus—that the Board did not hold itself responsible for the past or the future.

Mr. HANDLEY : Just so. If Canon Barclay feels we are responsible he will communicate with us. That is the first step. Mr. lATTLErt: It is left ih his hands whether he will go any further with it or not. In the course of some further conversation, it was stated that the secretary received the burial fees for the conveni- ence of the clergymen, as it avoided the unpleasantness of having to hand over money at the grave.

PAYMENTS. Mr. LINAKER said he should want a cheque signing ft sMewr.erßaagne scheme,croftfo £233 for contract work for the Frodstl and for £l4 Ss. id. FRODSITAN. tot thil VOLUNTEER PAI?.ADE.—On Saturday evening Frodsham Volunteer corps mustered at head quartetsCO half-past six, for marching out exercise, under th mand of Lieutenant B. G. IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the PART- NERSHIP heretofore subsisting between us, the undersigned, WILLIAM ALLEN and MATTHEW WOLSTEN- HOLME, in the business of Stonemasons. carried 0., by U 3 at Greenall-street, off Church-street, Warrington, in the County of Lancaster, under the firm of ALLEN and WOLSTENHOLME, has been DISSOLVED by mutual consent, as from this day; and that the said business will henceforth be carried on by the said William Allen alone, who will PAY and DISCHARGE ALL PARTNERSHIP DEBTS AND LIABILITIES and RECEIVE ALL DEBTS AND MONEYS due and payable to the said firm.—Dated this 3rd day of March, 1882. ELLEN HOWARTH, Deceased.—Pursuant to an Act of Parliament of the 22nd and 23rd Viet., cap. 35, intituled "An Act to further amend the law of property and to relieve trustees." NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that all persons, being creditors or otherwise, having any CLAIMS upon or against the estate of ELLEN HOWARTH, late of Mill Brow, Sutton, St. Helens, in the county of Lancaster, widow, deceased (who died on the 3rd day of February, 1832, and whose will was, on the 24th day of February, 1882, proved in the Liverpool District Registry of he Probate Division of the High Court of Justice, by Noah Greenhough, of Sutton aforesaid, provision dealer, and William Gorton, of Bold, in the said county, farmer, the executors therein named), are hereby required, on or before the Ist day of May next, to send to us, the undersigned, solicitors to the said executors, the particulars of their Claims upon or against the said estate; and notice is hereby furthergiven. that after the day last above rrentioned the said executors will pro- ceed to distribute the whole of the assets of the said deceased among the parties entitled thereto, Laving regard only to the claims of which the said executors shall then have had notice; and that the said executors will not be liable for the as ets so distributed, or any part thereof, to any person of whose claim they shall not then have received notice. And notice is hereby further given to persons who are indebted to the estate of the said deceased, immediately to pay the amount of their respec- tive debts to the said executors.—Dated this Ist day of March, 1882. And sweeter still is the song I sing— 'Tie a song of a Velvet Coat. stitch'd, stitch'd, Perfectly strong and neat, And work, work, work, Not the deftest hand can beat! It's oh! to be well dressed— A duty that none should shirk— For nothing improves a man as much As the tailor's handiwork! Style, style, style, And finish smart and trim; Strength, strength, strength, And colour that ne'er grows dim. Seam, and collar, and scye, Scye, and collar, and seim, Seem all too good for a Sovereign Coat, But are quite as good as they seem! Oh, men with sisters dear! Oh, men, with mothers and wives! You never beheld such a Sovereign Coat, No, never in all your lives! Fit, fit, fit, Perfect from skirt to throat— Lewis's even excel themselves In their "Sovereign Velvet Coat." The meeting concluded with the audience singing "Praise God from whom all blessings flow." The room was afterwards cleared for dancing, which was kept up for some time to the strains of Mr. T. It was decided to close them. HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The MEDICAL OFFICER reported :—"The health of the town is still unsatisfactory, the death rate being very high, being 35.25. This state of things is due to the epidemic of measles, which has carried off 48 children in the month. This ~infectious disease was very prevalent in St. Helens in 1879. In 1880 there was not a single case, and list year was nearly free, till December brought this present epidemic, which has proved very fatal. Mr. BELSHER: Is the cause of this disease to be found in having such a mild winter? MEDICAL OFFICER: It visits the town every three or four I years. The disease makes its appearance at every third or fourth year. THE SANITARY CONDITION or THE TOWN. The SunvEyort,drew attention to the fact that there were main sewers in different parts of the borough, but all house drains did not empty themselves into them. For instance,l along Prescot-road, in the neighbourhood of St. Ann's, there was the sewer in the road, but as vet there was not one house that drained into it. They all drained into the fields behind, into the cesspools and water courses. • I Mr. : Can you not compel them to drain into the sewer? The SURVEYOR: Certainly we can. if the sewer is within a distance of 100 feet away from the houses we can insist upon them making the connection. Mr. CRAIK : That is if they are insufficiently drained in the opinion of the Corporation. The SURVEYOR said he had mentioned one plaee as a , specimen. A similar state of things existed In Park-road and Norman's-lane and other parts of the borough. He mentioned this so that some action might be taken by the Council, as he knew that Dr. Spier, who had been inspecting the town in.respect to the cause of fever, would make a point of it. Mr. BROOK: I think we may attribute our increased death rate to bad sanitary arrangements. The CHAIRMAN thought their sanitary arrangements were very bad indeed, and he had expressed that opinion before. The Surveyor was instructed to make a report of all such cases at the next meeting. Mr. BELSHER remarked that cesspools were only utilised as a necessary evil where there was no sewer. WATER COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting of the Water Committee was held on Wednesday, Mr. T. Cook presiding, and the other mem- bers present were Messrs. Hanson and Johnson. YIELD OF THE WELLS. The returns showed that the total delivery of water for the four weeks, at Eccleston Hill, had been 11,546,580 gallons, the daily average being 412,378 gallons, as com- pared with 421,644 last month. From Whiston the total, delivery was 16,524,160 ; the daily average 590,148 and last month's daily average, 622,143 gallons. The minimum column of water in the well was 18 feet 4 inches. The Sutton-road pumping station yielded for the four weeks 18,424,886; being a daily average of 658,031 gallons as against 653,072 last month. There had been a total delivery (by meter) from the Eccleston reservoir of 3,958,200; the daily average was 141364; last month's daily average, 133,514. The rainfall for the month eßding February 28th was 173 inches, as against 417 in the cor- ' responding month of last year.
